en: The Compendium of the Father and Son Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master from the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Official,
Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master of Propagating the Dharma, and Recipient of the Purple Robe.

Translated by the Śramaṇa臣 (Chen) Rìchēng and others, by Imperial Decree. Chapter One: King Śuddhodana’s Initial Awakening of Faith. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.

Having completed his work of teaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings, he traveled to the kingdom of Kapilavastu. Not far from the city, he stayed in the Nyagrodha Grove together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus. All were arhats whose outflows (*āsrava*) were exhausted; they were free from further afflictions, their minds well-liberated and their wisdom well-liberated. Like great dragon kings, they had accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, exhausted all fetters of existence (*bhava*), and attained mastery over their minds, reaching the supreme, ultimate other shore.
Their names were:
Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Śāriputra, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana—great arhats well-known to all.
Furthermore, there were various categories of those who had abandoned error to return to the right path— non-Buddhists, Nirgranthas, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—
and countless assemblies had all gathered together, namely: the disciplined and their assembly, the tranquil and their assembly,
and those who have successfully crossed to the other shore and their assembly.
Those who dwell securely in peace and those who dwell securely with the assembly; those who have emerged from afflictions and those who have emerged from afflictions with the assembly;

those who are able to leave behind evil and those who are able to leave behind evil with the assembly; those who wash away the stains of sin and those who wash away the stains of sin with the assembly;

those who skillfully transcend the three realms of existence and those who skillfully transcend the three realms of existence with the assembly; and those who remain far removed from the five sensory objects.
Those who dwell far removed from the five sensory objects and those who dwell apart from all obstructions;
those with pure intentions and those who dwell in pure intentions; those endowed with all faculties and those who dwell in the perfection of all faculties;

those liberated from both the adverse and the favorable and those who dwell in liberation from both the adverse and the favorable; those who well protect themselves and those who dwell in the well-protection of themselves.

Those endowed with right mindfulness and the assembly of those endowed with right mindfulness; those endowed with the four bases of psychic power and the assembly of those endowed with the four bases of psychic power;

those who delight in explaining and recording [the teachings] and the assembly of those who delight in explaining and recording [the teachings]; those who clearly understand the conditions and truths and the assembly of those who clearly understand the conditions and truths;
those whose faculties are well-pacified and the assembly of those whose faculties are well-pacified; and those possessed of resolute faith and understanding.
The assembly of those with resolute faith and understanding; the assembly that delights in seeking meaningful benefit;
the assembly that observes selflessness; the assembly that has abandoned all conceptual proliferation;
the assembly that has severed doubt; the assembly whose physical conduct is pliant and serene.
The assembly, the assembly that delights in mastery, the assembly that delights in mastery; the assembly whose minds are well-liberated, the assembly whose minds are well-liberated;
the assembly whose wisdom is well-liberated, the assembly whose wisdom is well-liberated; the assembly that dwells in the noble lineage, the assembly that dwells in the noble lineage.

Thus the assembly, their bodies and minds at ease, finding joy in attaining wholesome benefits, each came with their followers to the place where the Buddha was, like a vast *pāṭala* tree with its branches, leaves, and foliage flourishing, growing, and fully developed, abiding in purity.
At that time, during the first watch of the night, the World-Honored One sat upon the open ground, silent and still, surrounded by the entire assembly in reverent attendance.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata surveyed the assembly of bhikṣus present and asked them:
"Who among you is capable of going to convert King Śuddhodana, exhorting him to generate the aspiration for enlightenment and to give rise to pure faith and understanding?"
Then the Venerable Kauṇḍinya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in salutation, and said:
“World-Honored One!
"I shall make the vow to go there.
The Buddha said, "Kauṇḍinya!"
"You are the foremost among the śrāvakas; you have long understood the meaning of the Truths and possess great renown, being honored by all sentient beings as their teacher.
Let this matter rest; there is no need for you to go."
At that time, the four great Kāśyapas in the assembly, along with Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others, each extended their prostrations and said:
"We are able to go and convert the noble King Śuddhodana."
The Buddha did not grant permission to either, stopping them as before.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"I do not yet know whom the Tathāgata has now dispatched to go to the place of my father, the King."

He then entered meditative concentration and beheld that the light from the Tathāgata’s heart gazed afar upon Udāyin, like the bright sun piercing through a multi-storied pavilion, streaming directly from the eastern window onto the western wall.
Then Maudgalyāyana, having arisen from his meditative concentration, went to where the Venerable Udāyin was and said to him:
"The World-Honored One summons you; go and convert your father, the King."
"Therefore, I have come to inform you. Udāyin said,
"Having truly received your instructions, I shall certainly obey your command."
Maudgalyāyana said:
"The destination to which the Venerable One is going is an exceedingly difficult matter; you should examine it thoroughly for yourself so as not to bring regret upon yourself later. Why is this so?"
He is a consecrated Kṣatriya king, majestic and awe-inspiring, whose nature no one dares to violate; who could guide him, and by what means could he be summoned for an audience?
How much less could he be taught or inspired with faith?
Now, take these various analogies, and you shall understand them fully.

Suppose a hundred men, over the course of many years, carry dry firewood on their backs until it has accumulated into a vast heap; then they set fire to it, and its flames become fierce and blazing, and they further drench the top with clarified butter.
Is there anyone who could walk through this immense mass of fire without being harmed?
Furthermore, it is like a person who wishes to extract the tusks from the mouth of a most excellent dragon-elephant; you should know that such a person will inevitably suffer harm.
Desiring now to go and convert the noble King Śuddhodana is likewise extremely difficult, and it is just like this.
"I have now briefly set forth a few illustrations; when you encounter the matter, deliberate upon them and take comfort in your own mind.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One summoned the Venerable Udāyin and said to him:

"Among my śrāvaka disciples, you are of the Śākya clan, endowed with eloquence and skilled in expounding the essentials of the Dharma. You should now go to convert King Śuddhodana, your father, using skillful means to awaken his aspiration for the Path."
Then Udāyin, having received the Buddha’s metaphorical instruction, replied, “So be it,” and accepted the teaching. He said,
“World-Honored One!”

I shall now depart; I only pray that you, in your great compassion, will not harbor anxious thoughts. Should my father, the King, become angry upon seeing me, I hope from afar that your compassionate light will secretly bestow its protection and aid.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to Udāyin:
"Excellent, Udāyin!
Listen now as I speak."
You possess wisdom and eloquence, and are the foremost among the assembly;
when King Śuddhodana of the Śākya clan sees you, he will surely be filled with joy.
Therefore, you should go and quickly exhort him to resolve his mind [upon enlightenment].
If one can transform the father-king and cause him to give rise to a pure mind,
then all devas and worldly people will together increase their wholesome benefits.
To remain at ease without cultivating goodness is like a crumbling bank about to collapse.
In this present life, one should eliminate pride and doubt;
for wealth and status last but a moment, increasing heedlessness and attachment.
Like a traveler without means, one’s thoughts are nothing but suffering.
Dwelling in the most excellent palace, enjoying exquisite sensual pleasures, they fail to understand the Buddha’s teaching;
when their happiness perishes, they give rise to grief and distress.
Possessing the fourfold army and the retinue of the seven treasures, they [fall].
Moving at will with sovereign ease, you take pleasure in destruction and give rise to sorrowful affliction.
There are yakṣas and spirits who devour the vital essence of sentient beings and cause them to contract various diseases; why do you not protect your own body?
Accumulating various precious treasures like Mount Kailāsa,
they are entangled by defiled wisdom and cannot observe themselves.
Because their minds are shrouded by defiled wisdom, they have no understanding of wholesome dharmas.
As one dwelling within a dream, how could there be any true perception?
Ordinary beings, having lost their clear wisdom, are certain to encounter sorrow and fear,
just like those traveling a long road who lose their companions.
Therefore, Udāyin, you should employ skillful means to encourage the King to establish the banner of faith and destroy his towering pride of self;
others lack such dexterity in exhorting and assisting him to resolve his mind toward awakening.
You possess wondrous eloquence, able to reveal the suffering of the three realms of existence.
I recall a past eon when a king appeared in the world,
his fame pervading the ten directions, known by the name Satyarāśi (Gatherer of Truth).
He governs the world with righteous laws, his realm extending to the very limits of the ocean;
for many koṭis and nayutas of years, ministers and subjects alike offer him their devotion.
In all the villages and cities, various kinds of flowers and fruits abound.
The ground produces only soft grass, free from tiles, rubble, or thorns;
flowing springs and groves of trees surround it on every side,
while hundreds of thousands of gandharvas play various musical instruments for one another.
The noble and holy ones gather therein; both people and things are all abundant and joyful.
There are many assemblies of bhikṣus who rely [on him] and uphold the pure precepts.
Furthermore, there are various non-Buddhists, great seers, and those of great wisdom.
Numbering in the hundreds of thousands, they abandoned their practiced asceticism and all gave rise to true insight;
with faith and joy in the Buddha’s True Dharma,
they feared the three evil realms and vowed to attain the fruit of rebirth in heaven.
That king had a crown prince named Dṛḍhamati,
who had encountered the Buddhas of the past and long planted the roots of all virtues.
Tens of millions (*koṭi-nayuta*) of people all drew near to him in devotion.
Contemplating the faults and afflictions of the five desires, his mind constantly gave rise to weary detachment.
Beholding the king’s residence, which was like a celestial palace,
with the queen and consorts vying to surround him as he enjoyed boundless sensual pleasures.
At that time, Dṛḍhamati immediately addressed his father, the King:
"With a heart of sincere truth, I vow to seek the unsurpassed path;
I feel no joy at all for these female attendants and their retinue."
The youth who is attached to desire finds that when pleasure perishes, suffering immediately arrives;
just like the great seers of old who dwelt among the mountain valleys,
they realized that the five desires are not ultimate and that tranquility alone is true happiness.
The King said to Dṛḍhamati:
"Do not speak thus; if you do not accept sensual pleasures, how can you be called my son?"
The wealth and nobility of that land are like those of the Heaven of the Multitudinous Hearers (Bahudhātuka),
where the various palaces and towers are adorned with many jewels.
Hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens and musicians constantly surround them on all sides.
Possessing the most excellent physical marks, she was no different from a celestial maiden;
her facial features were perfectly complete, her lips were crimson and her teeth even and closely set;
her forehead was broad and level, and her eyes resembled the petals of a blue lotus.
Their physical forms were entirely upright and graceful, their skin as pure as white jade or snow;
they performed various exquisite songs and dances, enjoying themselves together.
Their youth and complexion were fresh and white, like blossoms upon the branches of a tree.
"You should remain here; do not abandon this glory and nobility.
I now tell you truly: whether it be disparagement or praise, O Prince, you must clearly understand that the royal throne is most supreme."
Having heard these words, I resolved my mind to seek liberation from suffering;
regarding those five objects of desire, I did not cling to them, as if they were but a dream or sleep.
I spoke again to the King, my father:
Sunk in the mire of desire, one indulges the passions without shame;
like that blind man laboriously treading a perilous path,
having abandoned the level ground, upon whom can he rely for refuge and rescue?
If one does not understand sensual desires, by what means can one be liberated from the bonds of suffering?
One should leave the perilous path; this mind must not be inverted.
If one can distance oneself from all desires, one will dwell in peace, having eliminated faults and afflictions.
Know that those attached to desire are like the blind who see nothing;
the realm of desire is like a torrential flood, pouring down and difficult to restrain.
Those of wise understanding in this world should give rise to weariness and dread.
“Desire is the cause of manifold sufferings;
its harm exceeds that of a snake’s sting, a sword or staff, or poisoned medicine—it is like a blazing fire.
Prince Dṛḍhamati, filled with sorrow, addressed his father, the King:
"My aspiration lies in the mountain forests, where I seek liberation by departing from desire.
This body is deeply loathsome, bound as it is by the sufferings of old age and illness;
disregarding the royal throne and treasures, I pray that you will grant me permission to leave the home life."
At that time, among the royal clan, there was a youth named Candadatta who,
seeing the Prince renounce the world, also followed him to practice the holy life.
Having renounced the world, the Prince possessed courageous and diligent energy.
Having attained the five supernormal powers and skillfully cultivated the four immeasurables,
the Lion of the Śākyas among men teaches the Dharma without fear;
he transforms all sentient beings, causing them all to enter the Buddha-way.
That youth Candadatta, through skillful means,
demonstrated the faults and perils of the five desires and exhorted the king to resolve upon the Way.
Udāyin, you should know that he was formerly the one of Firm Wisdom.
What do you think?
It is I myself who am now here.
That youth Candadatta, who delighted in practicing the conduct of truth, was he.
Among those of the Śākya clan with whom you once lived, it is now your very self.
Therefore, Udāyin, you should now go and urge the Father King to resolve his mind [on awakening], so that all manner of wholesome benefits may increase.
At that time, when the Venerable Udāyin had heard these verses spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he respectfully received the compassionate instruction, paid homage, and withdrew.

At dawn, taking up his alms-bowl, he went toward the city of Kapilavastu and arrived at the gate of the royal palace. There he saw hundreds of thousands of Śākya kinsmen gathered together in one place. Among that assembly was a Śākya named Candrānana (Moon-Face), who had been an old acquaintance of Udāyin; seeing the Venerable approaching from afar, he went to greet him with consolation:
"For what reason have you come here?"
Udāyin said:

"I have now crawled from the Nyagrodha Grove where the World-Honored One resides, to respectfully carry out the Buddha’s compassionate command by being sent to teach and transform my father, King Śuddhodana, so as to awaken his pure faith."
Having heard these words, he spoke thus:

"In the past, had the Prince not renounced his home, he would certainly have become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin Rāja). He would have governed the four continents with the ten wholesome deeds, and seven treasures would have appeared spontaneously—namely, the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the military-treasure, and the treasurer-treasure.
Furthermore, he would have been surrounded by a thousand sons, and all the people would have revered and honored him."
"Now that he has left the household life and set his heart upon emptiness and stillness, he has lost such vast wealth and honor; this is precisely what we have been discussing in our assembly.
Before he had finished speaking, King Śuddhodana summoned the Śākya clansmen and arrayed them in the courtyard, saying to them:
"You should all know: Prince Siddhārtha has renounced the sovereignty of the kingdom and its supreme pleasures to delight in dwelling among the forests and wilds—how great a mistake this is!"
"From this day forward, you must not go to him to offer worship or show him respect.
Should anyone violate this, they shall certainly be punished with flogging.
At that time, there was a member of the Śākya clan named Sunetra, who was wise, discerning, and possessed of many skillful arts.
Having gone out to the palace gate, he encountered Udāyin; employing skillful means to draw near, he gradually reached a secluded spot where he finally dared to ask:

"Does the World-Honored One, the Teacher, enjoy lightness, ease, peace, and happiness? Are the four elements in harmony? Are you free from much illness and affliction? And in transforming and delivering sentient beings, do you experience no weariness?"
Furthermore, there were two Śākyas named Aśoka and Vigataśoka who went to the Venerable One to inquire after the World-Honored One’s health, as previously described:
“We all wish to go to the presence of the World-Honored One; however, we have just received the King’s decree that none of the Śākyas are permitted to approach and make offerings to the Buddha.”
"If anyone violates this, they shall certainly be subjected to corporal punishment.
Out of fear of these strict commands, none dare to go.
Upon hearing this, Udāyin sighed deeply: "What is the King, my father Śuddhodana, thinking?"

The Tathāgata, the sun of wisdom, has appeared in the world, bringing great benefit to all sentient beings; all the people, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devendra, Brahmā, and others vie with one another to offer him worship, never for a single day neglecting this. I shall seek an audience with King Śuddhodana and relate these matters in detail.
He then entered meditative concentration and observed that the King, his father, had matured his faculty of faith and was certain to be converted.

At that time, the Venerable Udāyin, endowed with all dignified deportment, sat in the full lotus posture and rose into the air to the height of seven *tāla* trees, immediately manifesting various supernatural transformations.
At that time, King Śuddhodana saw from afar the Venerable One approaching through the air; his heart was filled with joy, and he joined his palms in reverent gazing.
He spoke in verse:
"Rare indeed is the accomplishment of such sublime conduct, Manifesting various miraculous transformations and endowed with majestic deportment."
"What is the reason for your arrival here traveling through the air?
We pray that the Noble One will explain it quickly.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin replied in verse:
"I am the son of a noble prince, dwelling in reliance upon the Dharma of the Tathāgata;
I pray that Your Majesty will swiftly give rise to pure faith and offer worship to this supreme field of merit."
The Crown Prince renounced his kingdom to attain the Way of the Buddha;
endowed with supreme auspiciousness and great renown, the light of his body constantly illumines the world, and the light of his wisdom can shatter all darkness of ignorance.
Just as the brilliant sun dispels the veil of clouds and radiates great light everywhere through the sky,
so too does the light of wisdom from the Dragon Prince constantly illuminate the three realms of existence.
Just as the bright moon spreads its abundant radiance, Outshining all the stars and planets wandering through space, So too is the light of wisdom of the Naga Prince;
He is able to subdue all those of external paths.
Just as when a lion roars in the rocky valleys, all the beasts flee in terror upon hearing it;
so too does the Dragon Son proclaim the sublime sound of the Dharma, crushing all heterodox arguments and bringing about awakening and understanding.
The heretical sages who practice asceticism possess false and deluded wisdom; they cannot penetrate or understand the principle of non-self.
They wander through the cycle of rebirth within the three realms because, lacking supreme wisdom, they are deluded regarding the ultimate truth.
All sentient beings in every world, blind and lacking the eye of wisdom, find it difficult to escape;
the Tathāgata has opened up the radiance of knowledge to shatter the cataracts of beginningless ignorance.
The two paths of good and evil are extremely clear: one is level and the other is perilous.
The Tathāgata skillfully points out the way for those who are lost, and can rescue those submerged in the mud.
Just as clouds can contain all waters, universally nourishing the great earth without distinction between high and low,
so too does the Buddha bestow the rain of Dharma, increasing the seeds of goodness among humans and devas.
The rain can thoroughly saturate all the mountain forests, Causing the roots, stems, and branches and leaves of medicinal herbs to flourish,
And causing all manner of exquisite flowers to bloom, Universally adorning the great earth.
Just as the sons of dragons rain down the Dharma rain, They nourish and cause to flourish the tree of the Buddha-dharma’s merits:
The ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities, Maturing the flowers and fruits of bodhi-wisdom.
The Mount Meru of myriad jewels within the ocean stands resplendent and towering, unmoving;
so too the Buddha, seated amidst the great assembly of śrāvakas, possesses a supreme radiance beyond compare.
Śakra, Lord of the Thirty-three Heavens, extensively raised offerings of wondrous adornment;
the majestic Dragon Son, the Great Śramaṇa—whenever the devas beheld him, they all attained awakening.
Desiring to enter the ocean of liberation of the Buddha-dharma and to accomplish the treasury of the jewels of wisdom, one should take precepts and meditative concentration as a boat and raft;
thus one can reach the cluster of mani-jewels of the foundations of mindfulness.
In the past, the Prince practiced various ascetic austerities;
Sometimes dwelling by ponds or lakes, sometimes in mountain caves, Or relying on remote and desolate wildernesses, He thoroughly mastered emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The Muni, the Great Seer, roars the lion’s roar, Guiding the deluded masses toward awakening;
By such power of skillful means, He transforms those difficult to tame, making them pliant and compliant.
The Buddha is the supreme teacher and tamer, Who can bestow upon sentient beings the jewels of all dharmas:
The sublime bliss of tranquility, śamatha, And the firm treasury of the merits of precept and concentration.
If one can practice all deeds in accordance with the teachings, removing delusions and extinguishing transgressions to become pure,
for this reason gods, humans, and asuras always delight in hearing and upholding the Buddha’s true Dharma.
Thereupon, King Śuddhodana spoke this verse to the Venerable Udāyin:
"My son has left home and finds no small measure of joy; Perhaps he lacks food and drink, or perhaps bedding and seats.
He is like a fresh and pure blue lotus flower, Which, if placed upon dry land, will surely wither away."
The Venerable Udāyin replied with a verse:
“The Tathāgata sports in the various supernormal powers, Constantly feasting on the joy of dhyāna, free from hunger and thirst;
By abiding in tranquil and sublime samādhi, He is as firm and solid as a golden lotus.”
At that time, King Śuddhodana spoke again in verse:
"When the Prince was formerly in the imperial palace, Hundred thousand court ladies constantly surrounded him;
Whether sleeping or waking, he always heard the sounds of singing and music."
"What joy is there in dwelling among the mountains and forests?
The Venerable Udāyin replied in verse:
"The Buddha dwells in the supreme realm of liberation, With a profound mind relying upon the various meditative concentrations."
"In his deportment of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, he always gives rise to joy and never experiences suffering.
Then King Śuddhodana spoke again in verse:
"In the past, when the Prince was in the imperial palace, exquisite and wonderful cushions and rugs were spread as his bedding."
"Hundreds of thousands of lamp-flames constantly illuminate, and as evening falls, one has never known darkness.
The Venerable Udāyin replied in verse:
"The Muni extensively cultivated sublime practices, taking the four immeasurables as his bedding."
"His mind constantly seeks the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, and he is free from delusion or dullness regarding neutral objects.
Then King Śuddhodana spoke again in verse:
"In the past, when the Prince dwelt in the deep palace, he enjoyed all manner of pleasures in his play."
"Attended on all sides by guards who welcome you well;
what can one gain by dwelling alone in the mountain forests?
The Venerable Udāyin replied in verse:
“The dwelling place of the Tathāgata is entirely pure and sublime; He delights in abiding in the tranquility of the araṇya.
With an impartial gaze upon the world, He is always honored by devas and nāgas.”
At that time, King Śuddhodana spoke again in verse:
"In former days, when the Prince resided in the royal palace, Bathing attendants vied with one another to serve him,
And exquisite, superior unguents were used to adorn his body."
"What is gained by dwelling in the mountains and forests?
The Venerable Udāyin replied in verse:
"The Muni takes the precepts as his bathing pool, Perpetually washing away all evils until he is pure and stainless."
"Able to bring both self and others to complete purity, Leaving behind all defilements to ascend to the other shore.
Then King Śuddhodana spoke again in verse:
"The exquisite robes worn by the Prince, Adorned with golden thread and strings of pearls,"
"Chandanwood blended with exquisite unguents—
what can one who dwells in mountain forests obtain?
Venerable Udāyin replied in verse:
“The Muni takes shame as his upper garment; The factors of enlightenment are like a string of pearls;
Guarding the precepts is a cooling unguent— With these he adorns the body of merit.”
Then King Śuddhodana spoke again in verse:
“The Prince’s quarters are always strictly guarded; A hundred thousand warriors bear spears and armor, While parasols held aloft in the sky obscure the sunlight.”
"Who will protect you as you go alone into the mountain forests?
The Venerable Udāyin replied in verse:
"The Muni, endowed with the ten powers of knowledge, Is unshakable in mind amidst all fears."
"Compassion universally shelters all living beings; the śramaṇa’s disciples always surround him.
Then King Śuddhodana spoke again in verse:
"Excellent! Well-spoken are the Buddha’s virtues; before long, I shall go to hear the essentials of the Dharma."
"May you first accept my offerings now, and then take this fragrant meal to present to the Tathāgata.
*The Compendium of the Father and Son Sūtra*,
Scroll One *The Compendium of the Father and Son Sūtra*, Scroll Two
The First Chapter, "King Śuddhodana’s Initial Awakening of Faith," Part Two:
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin, knowing that King Śuddhodana’s heart had been moved to realization, spoke a verse in praise and then addressed him, saying:
"Great King!

Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has appeared in the world as the Great Dharma King, fully accomplishing all virtuous merits. Among that assembly of śramaṇas, he is like the full moon surrounded by the host of stars; yet the World-Honored One’s radiance surpasses even theirs."
"Great King!
When the Tathāgata appears in the world, he is like the sun in an autumn sky; its light is exceptionally brilliant, unobstructed by clouds.
Yet, when the Buddha is amidst the great assembly of śramaṇas, his radiance shines even more intensely than that."
Furthermore, just as there is a mountain of radiant light within the ocean whose brilliance outshines all other mountains,
so too does the Buddha, dwelling amidst the great assembly of śramaṇas, radiate a splendor that surpasses even that.
Furthermore, just as Śakra dwells in the Sudharmā Hall surrounded by the hosts of devas, his bodily radiance being more brilliant than that of the other sons of heaven;
so too does the Buddha, amidst the great assembly of śramaṇas, shine with a brilliance that surpasses even that.
Furthermore, just as the Great Brahmā King is surrounded by hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Brahmā hosts, such that no one can equal the radiance of his entire body,
so too does the Buddha’s brilliant illumination within the great assembly of śramaṇas surpass even that.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having heard of the World-Honored One’s such supreme radiance and majestic spiritual power, further recalled to mind:

“In the past, when the Prince first descended from birth, the earth shook in six ways—namely, it moved, moved everywhere, and moved most everywhere; it rose, rose everywhere, and rose most everywhere; it surged, surged everywhere, and surged most everywhere; it quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked most everywhere; it rattled, rattled everywhere, and rattled most everywhere; it crashed, crashed everywhere, and crashed most everywhere; it roared, roared everywhere, and roared most everywhere. His light illuminated heaven and earth, with none equal to him, and he immediately took seven steps without requiring support.”
At that time, two kinds of water rained down from the sky:
one warm and the other cool, to serve as a bath for the Prince’s body.

From within the earth, precious thrones spontaneously emerged, and exquisite parasols hung suspended in the void; various sons of gods, with reverence and respect, stood in attendance at his left and right, holding white whisks in their hands.

Furthermore, for many years, the Bodhisattva left home, grew weary of the pleasures of the five desires, constantly abided in right mindfulness, spoke truthful words, and caused all sentient beings not to harm one another.

With actions determined, courageous, and firm, they vow to achieve unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, so that all who have not yet crossed over may cross over, gradually reaching the ultimate further shore.
Thereupon, King Śuddhodana spoke this verse to Udāyin:
"When a person is first born, Their speech is already definitive;
Since they possess tranquil wisdom, Why would the wise not believe them?"
When the Prince was first born, there was none in the world equal to him;
he is honored by the world—why would the wise not believe this?
Even in his dreams, he has never uttered a falsehood.
If one practices according to what has been taught, why would the wise not believe?
Not giving rise to craving toward sense objects, and not being bound by craving,
disregarding heaps of gold and jewels— why would the wise not believe?
Hatred is like a sharp sword; its fury strikes terror into others.
Since the wise have skillfully abandoned such faults, why would they not believe?
Constantly endowed with supreme wisdom, they cannot be shaken by fear.
Since they are free from the fault of delusion, why would the wise not believe?
Though they enjoy the pleasures of the five senses, they are not bound by them;
With supreme wisdom, they discern well—why would the wise not believe?
The hundreds of thousands of kinds of illusory arts possess not even a fraction of reality;
they are not what the virtuous delight in—how could the wise fail to believe this?
Countless clever words are ultimately but frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
If one cannot be liberated from bondage, why would the wise not believe this?
If one delights in the joy of the Dharma and accords with all that is meaningful and beneficial, one will certainly be able to leave bondage behind; why then would one not believe these words?
With the power of skillful means free from defilement, who among men could have restrained him?
Having scaled the city walls and departed from the Śākya palace, how can one not believe his words?
Having renounced the pleasures of the five desires, he dwells in the mountains like a deer.
He aspired with joy to seek awakening; why do you not believe his words?
For six years he practiced austerities; why do you not believe his words?
To deliver all sentient beings, he sought the supreme awakening; why do you not believe his words?
For six years he ate hemp and wheat, never thinking of fine delicacies;
seeking the supreme bodhi, how can you not believe his words?
For six years he dwelt on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, while the hosts of Māra came to watch for an opening.
If one cannot see even a slight fault, why not believe their words?
Who does not seek profit, yet alone has no small hope;
having skillfully departed from the affliction of greed, why not believe their words?
The unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, if unheard of by others, is difficult to believe and difficult to understand; why do you not believe his words?
Whether it was at the request of Brahmā or spoken by the World-Honored One himself, [it remains the same].
Such is this subtle and wondrous Dharma; why do you not believe his words?
Out of compassion for the Śākyas, he manifested birth in a royal palace to cause all to be liberated from the bonds of suffering; why do you not believe his words?
To those who have not yet reached the further shore, he teaches and instructs them so that they may cross over;
having always made such vows, why do you not believe his words?
In the past, the World-Honored One frequently exhorted and transformed others in this very way.
Know that it is the same now; why do you not believe his words?
Therefore, I now seek to see the King of Dharma;
by observing thus with truthfulness, I have attained purity of body and mind.
When King Śuddhodana had spoken this verse, he reflected further and said to the Venerable One:
"How long has this body been here before you finally gave rise to the aspiration for the Way?"
Then Udāyin spoke these verses to King Śuddhodana:
“Great King, now that you have become the lord of men, You ought to cultivate all that is meaningful and beneficial.
The Tathāgata has praised the cause of generating the resolve for enlightenment; By this, one always attains birth in noble and exalted places.”
If one can give rise to a pure intention and go before the Great Sage, the Muni,
the merit obtained will be immeasurable, increasing the seeds of all goodness for humans and devas.
In the past, when the Tathāgata was a prince, he felt great compassion for all living beings;
he extensively practiced the immeasurable mind of equanimity, remaining unstained by it, just as a lotus flower is not wetted by water.
All sentient beings are submerged in the torrential flood; the Buddha is able to rescue them and bring them to liberation—He is called the Unsurpassed Honored One among Two-legged Beings.
O King, arouse a pure mind and practice skillful self-discipline.
The Buddha’s wisdom is supreme and foremost; it skillfully extracts the arrows of doubt from sentient beings, causing them to forever leave behind all suffering and attain peace and happiness.
O King, arouse a pure mind and practice skillful self-mastery.
The Crown Prince has forever severed the bonds of the three realms of existence, Subdued the hosts of the four kinds of Māras,
And attained the unsurpassed, great Bodhi;
May the King give rise to a pure mind and be well-subdued.
Revealing the nectar-like Dharma of liberation, Śakra and the kings of men all entreated him to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings within the three realms;
the King gave rise to a pure mind and was well-disciplined.
He is able to turn the most supreme and wondrous wheel of Dharma, gathering and transforming all those of external paths,
numbering in the hundreds of millions;
the King has given rise to a pure mind and is well-subdued.
The Tathāgata’s eye of wisdom is utterly pure; Sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance.
By preaching the Dharma, he can eliminate their delusive darkness;
O King, arouse a pure mind and practice skillful self-mastery.
Sentient beings are oppressed by old age and death; the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma to eliminate their sorrow and fear, using skillful means to lead them through the gate of eternal bliss.
O King, arouse a pure mind and practice sublime self-mastery.
The Tathāgata appears in the world, like great clouds pouring down rain from the four quarters of the sky,
able to extinguish the blazing fires of the three poisons;
O King, arouse a pure mind and practice skillful self-mastery.
The light of the Sage’s wisdom of the ten powers Extinguishes the sins of sentient beings across the three times,
Ultimately distancing them from all faults;
O King, arouse a pure mind and practice sublime self-mastery.
The Tathāgata always, with a heart of great compassion, cherishes all sentient beings like his own infant,
causing them all to leave suffering behind and attain liberation;
may the King give rise to a pure mind and practice skillful self-mastery.
The Tathāgata, through skillful means, is able to gather in those sentient beings who are difficult to transform and stubborn;
he causes them to eliminate restlessness and arrogance.
O King, you have given rise to a pure mind and are well-subdued.
Sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of craving, and even the gods are likewise attached to pleasure;
the Buddha, possessing the ten powers, is able to rescue and receive them;
O King, arouse a pure mind and practice skillful self-mastery.
The Tathāgata’s great compassion is peerless, adorned with immeasurable merit;
he can rescue sentient beings from the suffering of the long night.
O King, arouse a pure mind and practice skillful self-mastery.
Through the Tathāgata’s power of great compassion and skillful means, he is like a maṇi jewel that can clarify turbid water;
he excellently removes the causes of strife and defilement,
and the King has given rise to a pure mind for excellent self-discipline.
Just as a mani jewel is pure by its very nature, and all beings rejoice upon seeing it,
so too has the Muni forever abandoned the causes of affliction;
O King, arouse a pure mind and practice skillful self-mastery.
Humans and devas mostly suffer the pain of separation; the Buddha causes them to attain the bliss of tranquility—the cause for escaping the cycle of birth and death.
O King, arouse a pure mind and practice skillful self-mastery.
The Sage has accomplished an ocean of merit; I now briefly describe but a small fraction of it, which is like space, having no bounds.
O King, arouse a pure mind and be well-disciplined.
At that time, having heard the verses of praise, King Śuddhodana immediately recalled:
"Formerly, before the Bodhisattva had left the household life, I personally witnessed him performing sublime deeds; with right mindfulness and a resolute vow, he declared:
'I shall renounce the home and swear to attain the Buddha-way, delivering all sentient beings to the other shore.'"
Then he said to the Venerable Udāyin:
"You are now truly a son of the Tathāgata. After you have finished eating, take this offering separately; only then shall I go to the place where the World-Honored One resides."
At that time, Udāyin was filled with great joy and immediately took the fragrant food to offer to the Tathāgata.
After the Buddha had accepted the offering, he summoned the bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"That Udāyin, whom I dispatched to convert his father, King Śuddhodana, has now attained faith and understanding."
The Buddha then praised Udāyin, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"You have now attained an immeasurable mass of merit; having heard this matter, the gods and humans of all worlds will increase their roots of goodness.
Some bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How much merit does that Udāyin obtain?
The Buddha said,

"Suppose there were as many grains of sand as there are in the Ganges Rivers of the ten directions— immeasurable, boundless, and beyond reckoning— the merit and reward obtained by Udāyin is exactly equal to the number of those grains of sand, without any difference."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, having finished his meal, set aside his bowl, established himself in dignified deportment, and sat cross-legged; he entered meditative concentration to observe that the King, his father, was about to arrive.

He immediately summoned the Northern Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, together with his retinue of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of yakṣa generals. They emerged from their own palace and came through the air; in the time it takes to extend or contract one’s arm, they arrived at the place where the Buddha was, joined their palms in salutation, made offerings to the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus, and stood to one side.

Furthermore, the Eastern Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with his retinue of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of gandharvas, came through the air to the place where the Buddha was. Joining their palms in salutation, they paid homage to the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus, and stood to one side.

Furthermore, from the south, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, together with his retinue of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kumbhāṇḍas, came through the air to the place where the Buddha was. Joining their palms in salutation, they paid homage to the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus, and stood to one side.

Furthermore, the Western Heavenly King Virūpākṣa, together with his retinue of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of great nāgas, came through the air to where the Buddha was. Joining their palms in salutation, they paid homage to the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus, and stood to one side.
Furthermore, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with countless sons of the gods from the Heaven of the Thirty-three, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated, and made offerings.

Likewise, the Yāma devas, Tuṣita devas, Nirmāṇarati devas, Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, Mahābrahmā devas, Ābhāsvara devas, Bṛhatphala devas, and Śuddhāvāsa devas—each of these sons of the gods, accompanied by retinues of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sons of the gods—came to where the Buddha was, bowed their heads at his feet, and, having made offerings and paid respect to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, stood to one side.

Furthermore, the asura king Vemacitrin, together with a retinue of sixty nayutas, dressed in fresh, clean garments and arrayed in full regalia, came through the air to the place where the Buddha was. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, made offerings to the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus, and stood to one side.

Furthermore, the Kinnara King, together with his retinue of eighty-six thousand followers, came through the air to where the Buddha was. Joining their palms in salutation, they paid homage to the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus, and stood to one side.

Furthermore, eighty koṭis of non-Buddhist great seers, brahmins, and others came from all directions to the place where the Buddha was, approaching him to pay their respects and make offerings; they were like the full moon shining beautifully in the sky, its majestic radiance eclipsing the lunar mansions and planets.
At that time, the assembly of devas, nāgas, spirits, and mahoragas there, with one mind and in unison, praised him in verse:
“The Buddha possesses the radiance of wisdom, Supreme and without peer;
He has subdued the asuras And extinguished the darkness of the three poisons and delusion.”
The Buddha’s face is like the full moon, adorned with all the marks of excellence;
possessing supreme eloquence, he is able to refute all heterodox arguments.
His body is wondrously adorned with a hundred blessings; among devas and humans, none can equal him.
He guides all the śrāvakas, like a lotus emerging from turbid water.
Like Śakra, Lord of Devas, surrounded by his sons of heaven, his majestic power surpasses that of all the gods; so too is the radiance of his body.
The Tathāgata, the Honored One among two-legged beings, is constantly surrounded by his sons of the Dharma;
he skillfully expounds the essentials of all dharmas, causing sentient beings to attain awakening.
Like the Lord of Yama, he is constantly surrounded by his retinue.
Seated serenely amidst the great assembly, all the devas pay him their respects.
The Buddha’s body emits boundless light, illuminating the perilous and evil realms;
those sentient beings who have fallen there, upon receiving this light, are all freed from suffering.
The Lord of Tuṣita, constantly surrounded by hosts of devas,
possesses a bodily radiance that alone is supreme due to the karmic rewards of his past merit.
Together with the asuras, as well as the other hosts of nāgas and spirits, [he shines forth].
The radiance of the Lion of the Śākyas is pure and transcends all else.
The Lord of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations and others have all come to the Buddha’s presence;
eclipsed by the Buddha’s light, they are made to realize their own prior meritorious deeds.
Such is the Buddha’s radiance, supreme and beyond compare;
it can transform those who are yet unsubdued, causing them to give rise to pure faith and understanding.
The Lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven is constantly surrounded by a host of devas.
Due to the power of past virtuous karma, his bodily radiance alone is supreme.
The Tathāgata, honored for his ten powers, is perfectly fulfilled in all right conduct;
among all devas and humans, his brilliance is most fiercely radiant.
The Great Brahma King of the Form Realm, His bodily radiance surpasses that of the Brahma hosts;
With his eight kinds of wondrous voices, No deity among the heavens can equal him.
So too is the Tathāgata, the Great Dharma King, To whom the eight classes of beings always pay reverence.
Proclaiming the Dharma-sound of the Four Truths, his light illuminates the three thousandfold world-system.
All the devas, nāgas, and spirits have come to the Buddha’s presence, desiring to hear the Brahma-voice; they pray that the Buddha will open their unawakened minds.
"The great ocean may have its depth measured, The limits of space may be known, Mount Sumeru may even be weighed, But the Buddha’s merit is infinite.

Chapter Two: The King Visits the Buddha. From the *Sūtra of the Combined Collection of Father and Son*, Chapter Two: "The King Visits the Buddha. At that time, King Śuddhodana addressed the Venerable Udāyin, saying:
"Before long, I shall go in person to the Buddha’s dwelling; I trust that the World-Honored One, with his supernormal knowledge of others' minds, has already discerned this beforehand.
He will immediately summon the Śākyas to select an auspicious day, and at the first rising of the sun, I shall prepare my carriage and certainly depart."
When the Śākyas heard the king’s command, they all felt great joy and each said:
“Excellent, Great King!”
"I pray that you will grant me the honor of serving as your attendant.

At that time, King Śuddhāvāsa issued orders to prepare elephants, horses, chariots, and precious ornate litters. He had the road entirely covered with pure yellow earth and yoked a blue chariot adorned with blue jewels. Above the chariot, he suspended a blue parasol, interlaced with jeweled nets, while precious bells chimed harmoniously; exquisite music was played, and various songs and dances were performed.
A hundred brave warriors, clad in blue armor and wearing blue leather sandals, surrounded him on all sides.

Countless attendants, dressed in garments of blue, each held blue banners and blue whisks, their handles further adorned with various jewels; arrayed in diverse ornaments, pure and brilliant in their blue hue, they proceeded forward in orderly ranks with slow and steady steps.

He rode in a yellow chariot, adorned with gold fittings and harnesses; atop the chariot was spread a yellow parasol, draped with jeweled nets from which precious bells chimed in harmony as exquisite music played and various songs and dances were performed.
A hundred valiant warriors, clad in yellow armor and wearing yellow leather sandals, surrounded him on all sides.

Countless attendants wore yellow garments, each holding a yellow banner and a yellow fly-whisk, their handles further embellished with various jewels; thus arrayed in manifold ornaments, brilliant and pure in their yellow hue, they proceeded forward in orderly ranks with calm and steady pace.

He rode in a crimson chariot adorned with red jewels and gold fittings; atop the chariot was spread a crimson parasol, draped with a lattice of precious nets, where jeweled bells chimed harmoniously as exquisite music played and various songs and dances were performed.
A hundred valiant warriors, clad in crimson armor and wearing crimson leather sandals, surrounded him on all sides.

Countless attendants dressed in crimson garments each held crimson banners and crimson fly-whisks, their handles further embellished with various jewels; arrayed in diverse ornaments, their crimson hues bright and pure, they advanced in orderly ranks with slow and steady pace.

He rode in a white chariot adorned with silver fittings; atop the chariot was spread a white parasol, draped with jeweled nets from which precious bells chimed harmoniously. Wondrous music was played, and various songs and dances were performed.
A hundred valiant warriors, clad in white armor and wearing white leather sandals, surrounded him on all sides.

Countless attendants dressed in white garments each held white banners and white fly-whisks, their handles further embellished with various jewels. Adorned in diverse ways, they were pure white and bright, and they advanced slowly and steadily in successive ranks.

They mounted a chariot painted with variegated colors and adorned with various jewels; atop the chariot was spread a painted canopy, draped with jeweled nets from which precious bells chimed harmoniously as exquisite music played and various songs and dances were performed.
A hundred valiant warriors, clad in painted armor and wearing painted sandals, surrounded it on all sides.

Countless attendants dressed in painted garments each held painted banners and fly-whisks of diverse colors, their handles further embellished with various jewels. Adorned in manifold ways, these objects were of brilliant and pure hues; arranged in successive rows, they advanced forward slowly and steadily.

Behind the multitude of chariots were eighty thousand elephants; upon each elephant was a pavilion made of the seven treasures, with golden banners arrayed between them, most lovely and delightful to behold.
Furthermore, behind the elephant were eighty thousand horses, likewise adorned with gold and jewels.

At that time, King Śuddhodana mounted his most excellent elephant and departed from his own palace in the city of Kapilavastu, proceeding toward the Nyagrodha Grove, while the Śākyas followed him in solemn reverence.

At that time, the World-Honored One saw from afar that his father, the King, was approaching with his ministers and assistants, the Śākya kinsmen, and the citizens of the city; he then summoned the bhikṣus to leave the forest and observe the scene.

Upon seeing this, the bhikṣus felt deep sympathetic joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; at first sight, they all thought that Śakra, the Lord of Devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, had come to this place.

The road the king traveled was cleansed and leveled; five-colored flowers were strewn about, and various famous incenses were burned. Canopies and garlands of silk were suspended in the air, and all manner of skilled musicians and performers lined the sides of the road, playing their exquisite music all at once. With a joyful heart, the king proceeded forward to where the Buddha was.

Chapter Three: King Śuddhodana Pays Homage to the Tathāgata. At that time, King Śuddhodana, surrounded by the Śākya clansmen both before and behind him, proceeded to the Nyagrodha Grove. Upon arrival, he immediately alighted from his jeweled carriage and entered on foot, accompanied by his ministers and attendants.

Having understood this, the World-Honored One, wishing to transform his father the King by causing him to abandon arrogance and give rise to pure faith, ascended into the air and manifested signs of supernatural power, moving back and forth with unimpeded mastery.

At that time, Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Sahā world, stood to the left of the Tathāgata, and Śakra, the Lord of Devas, stood to his right. The Heavenly Kings of Yama, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin each held various precious parasols and followed the Tathāgata as they traveled through the air.
The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa and the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra joined their palms in salutation and stood facing the east.
The Heavenly King Virūḍhaka and the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa bowed their heads in reverence and stood facing the west.

Furthermore, the retinues of the various devas of the six heavens of desire rained down celestial flowers—*utpala*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, and *māndārava*—and showered down exquisite, fine powders of *candana* and aloeswood incense. Simultaneously, the various musical instruments of the devas and their wondrous songs and dances all resounded together in the void.

At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal powers, manifested countless pavilions made of the seven treasures, exquisitely adorned and radiating brilliant light, so that the gods and humans in the assembly could pass back and forth and see one another.
At that time, the assembly was filled with great joy, such as had never occurred since ancient times.
King Śuddhodana, beholding these auspicious signs, conceived a sense of wonder and spoke thus:

"In the past, when the Tathāgata was a prince, he felt no lingering attachment to the sovereignty, wealth, and power of a universal monarch over the four continents. Now, as the Great Dharma King of this trichiliocosm, he is fully endowed with the noble treasures and sovereign supernormal powers, constantly surrounded by the reverence of the devas; this surpasses his former state beyond all comparison."
"Now I have only my Śākya kinsmen and the various people as my attendants.

Having spoken thus, he felt immeasurable joy and gave rise to a pure mind; he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, gazed up at the Tathāgata, and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, further saying:
"When the World-Honored One was first born, there was no one to support him; he immediately took seven steps and surveyed the ten directions."
"In this world, I am the most honored and the most supreme; there is none higher than me. Having transcended old age, sickness, and death, I have reached the end of suffering.
When I saw these things at that time, my heart was filled with joy, and I prostrated myself in reverence.

Furthermore, when the World-Honored One was a prince, he went to the fields to observe the farming work and rested beneath the cool shade of a Jambu tree; although the sun had already slanted toward the west, its shadow did not shift.
At that time, there were also devaputras of the six heavens of the desire realm who stood respectfully at his side with palms joined.
I too extended my salutations then; now, beholding the World-Honored One manifesting this auspicious sign, I pay homage to the Buddha for the third time.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, peerless in merit and wisdom, Immediately upon birth, took seven steps and proclaimed:
‘In this world, I alone am supreme. At that time, I once paid him homage."
Furthermore, I observed farmers resting in the cool shade; as the sun slanted, their shadows did not shift.
The devas of the six desire realms attended at his side, and at that time, I prostrated in reverence.
Now the Buddha manifests this sign of supernatural power, out of compassion for me and all sentient beings;
there is none in the world like the Buddha—this is my third prostration with head and face to the ground.
In the past, I established his name, calling him Sarvārthasiddha;
having now attained the fruit of Buddhahood and fulfilled my long-held aspiration, my joy is like drinking nectar.

At that time, the devaputras of the six heavens of the desire realm, knowing that King Śuddhodana was single-mindedly longing to behold the Tathāgata, first prepared a lion throne for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, within the Nyagrodha Garden. That throne was exceptionally high and magnificent, adorned and polished with every kind of precious jewel; upon it, they spread celestial kauśeya silk and exquisite white woolen cloth.
Furthermore, within that grove, various wondrous garments spontaneously manifested, arrayed all around and hanging down in every direction.
Having completed the arrangement of the seats, he invited the World-Honored One to sit upon them.
"From the time I left home until my attainment of Buddhahood, this is the first time I have met with my father, the King."
Having formed this thought, he descended from mid-air.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, having been graced by the reception of the Tathāgata, was filled with great joy such as he had never before experienced; gazing upon the Tathāgata’s sublime countenance, his eyes could not bear to look away for even a moment, as he paid him deep respect, offered praise, and inquired after his well-being with words of consolation.
The Buddha sat upon his seat in the full lotus posture, while the king and the Śākyas withdrew to sit on one side.
At that time, various devas from the realm of form also came to the assembly of the Buddha;
namely, the Brahmakāyika devas, the Brahmapurohita devas, the Mahābrahmā devas, the Parīttābha devas, the Apramāṇābha devas, and the Ābhāsvara devas.
The gods of the Heaven of the Pure Abodes, the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity, the Cloudless Heaven, the Heaven of Merit-Born, the Heaven of Vast Results,
the Heaven Free from Affliction, the Heaven Free from Heat, the Heaven of Excellent Manifestation, the Heaven of Excellent Vision, and the Heaven of the Ultimate Form—
all beheld these auspicious signs manifested by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, for the sake of transforming his father, the King. They all...
Rejoicing and mutually congratulating one another, they each took celestial *mandārava* flowers and *mahāmandārava* flowers and scattered them over the Buddha;
furthermore, they offered worship by suspending various exquisite celestial garments in the air,
as well as various ornaments for adorning the body, such as jeweled crowns, earrings, and finger rings.
Bracelets for the arms, pearl pendants and necklaces, and precious jeweled belts;
some were made of gold with various jewels interspersed as ornaments, while others were made of various jewels with gold interspersed as ornaments.
Such jeweled garlands were strung with golden thread, exquisitely crafted and radiant; these he offered to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, they offered rows of various exquisite jeweled parasols, jeweled banners, and jeweled pennants as an offering.

Having completed their offerings, the sons of the gods bowed their heads in prostration and remained suspended in mid-air, scattering fragrant waters like a fine rain. Each joining their palms, they praised the Buddha with these verses:
"We take refuge in the most supreme Great Being, Who is skillfully able to gather and transform all living beings."
Possessing great merit, wisdom, and renown, There is none in all the world who equals you.
I take refuge in the most supreme Great Being, Whose transcendent wisdom is profound, vast, and inconceivable;
Out of great compassion for all sentient beings, You proclaim the true Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
I take refuge in the most supreme Great Being, Permanently free from the defilements of greed, anger, and delusion;
Majestically adorned with the primary and secondary marks, Like a mountain of gold manifesting within the great ocean.
I take refuge in the most supreme Great Being, Who can crush heterodox arguments without fear,
Causing all to abandon deluded attachments And cultivate right view and pure conduct.
We reflect upon our own past blessings and merit, that we have encountered the Able One appearing in the world;
by dedicating this small root of goodness from our offerings, may we, for ourselves and others, attain Buddhahood.

**Chapter Four: The Prophecy for the Asura Kings** *The Compendium of Father and Son Sūtra, Chapter Four: The Prophecy for the Asura Kings* At that time, after the World-Honored One had manifested these supernatural transformations to convert the father king, there were various asura kings present in the assembly who beheld these auspicious signs; their hearts leaped with joy. Furthermore, seeing the vast offerings made by the devaputras of the form realm, they gave rise to profound sympathetic joy.
At that time, the preeminent Asura King Vemacitra spoke these words:
"I shall now be the very first to make offerings to the Buddha.
By means of his supernormal powers, he instantly manifested within that grove sixty nayutas of canopies made of various precious nets, adorned with diverse colors, which completely covered the sky.

Beneath the jeweled curtains, sixty nayutas of jewel-adorned grounds appeared; upon these jewel grounds, sixty nayutas of exquisite pavilions appeared. Each pavilion had a gateway made of jewels: the golden pavilions had silver gates, lapis lazuli windows, mother-of-pearl pillars, crystal arches, and agate floors, adorned with interspersed ornaments of pearls and other jewels; the silver pavilions had gold gates, lapis lazuli windows, coral pillars, mother-of-pearl arches, and crystal floors, adorned with interspersed ornaments of pearls and other jewels;
and so on, until the agate pavilions had crystal gates.
Thus, the pavilions formed of these seven treasures were adorned in successive order with windows, pillars, and brackets; within each door, there appeared a lion throne made of various jewels.
On both sides of each seat were asura youths and maidens, holding white whisks or precious fans, standing in attendance by their side.

Above each seat was a canopy made of various jewels, and before them appeared jeweled banners of many colors. From the golden gate emerged a blue banner, with a yellow top and a golden shaft; from the silver gate emerged a yellow banner, with a blue top and a red-jewel shaft; from the lapis lazuli gate emerged a crimson banner, with a red top and a golden shaft; and from the gate of various jewels emerged a painted banner, with a multicolored top and a silver shaft. As these various jeweled nets, curtains, jeweled grounds, pavilions, banners, flags, and canopies appeared, they revolved in the air, circling the Buddha three times and then remaining in formation.
Just as the great elephant king Airāvaṇa of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven moves slowly to circumambulate Śakra, Lord of Devas, so too did it proceed here.

Furthermore, they rained down various exquisite celestial flowers, namely: māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers; mañjūṣaka flowers, mahāmañjūṣaka flowers; pāruṣaka flowers, mahāpāruṣaka flowers; karkārava flowers, mahākarkārava flowers; pāṭala flowers, mahāpāṭala flowers; citrapāṭala flowers, mahācitrapāṭala flowers; and they also rained down flowers made of the seven precious gems.
Golden flowers, silver flowers, mother-of-pearl flowers, agate flowers, lapis lazuli flowers, crystal flowers, pearl flowers, and so forth.
Furthermore, they rained down rare and exquisite articles of play and enjoyment, so that everyone present obtained whatever they desired.
Moreover, they rained down various wonderful fragrant waters, ointments, powdered incense, aloeswood incense, and the like.
At that time, the flowers accumulated in the city of Kapilavastu rose seven feet high and extended six *yojanas* in width; mixed with fragrant water, they formed a thick mud.

By the Buddha’s supernatural power, the fragrance permeated and filled the entire trichiliocosm. When the sentient beings therein—whether gods or humans—smelled this fragrance, they all conceived the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and attained the stage of non-retrogression.

Having made these offerings, that Asura King mounted a chariot of the seven precious jewels, circumambulated the Buddha three times, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and praised him with these verses:
"O Most Victorious and Unshakable Honored One, You have perfectly realized the fruit of Bodhi;
Able to transform all sentient beings, You lead them to transcend the triple world."
With a pure mind, I extend this offering before you;
may I become like the World-Honored One, forever liberated from the suffering of saṃsāra.
O Great Sage, Lord of Munis, free from defilement and having eliminated all delusions—
Worthy to be the Teacher of Gods and Humans, Rescuing and delivering others to the further shore;
Skillfully proclaiming the subtle and wondrous Dharma, Subduing all sentient beings,
And crossing over the suffering and calamities of old age and death— Therefore, I praise and pay homage to you.
When the Asura King Vemacitra had finished praising the Buddha with these verses, he thought, "Even now, my heart's desire for making offerings is not yet satisfied.
He then further presented all the priceless jewels found within the ocean to the Tathāgata.

By means of his supernormal powers, he manifested sixty nayutas of exquisite jeweled chariots. Each chariot was drawn by well-trained horses and adorned with ornaments of gold and jewels. Upon each chariot was a wonderful canopy hung with various jeweled bells that emitted harmonious and elegant sounds. On each of these were Apsaras endowed with perfect beauty, performing exquisite songs and dances and playing various musical instruments; their voices were so clear and resonant that those who heard them never grew weary.
By the spiritual power of the Buddha, this music of joy pervaded the entire trichiliocosm;

when sentient beings therein heard these sounds, their bodies and minds became serene, they were freed from all defiled attachments, and none regressed from their resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, having made these offerings, the Asura King, together with his retinue, was filled with great joy. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he spoke again in verse:
"May I always remain close to the Great Guide, the Muni;
By making the most supreme offerings, May I reach the end of all suffering."

At that time, there was another asura king in the assembly named Pramoda, who gave rise to a pure mind and extensively offered worship; each of his offerings was no different from those of the asura king Vemacitra.
Having made these offerings, he mounted a chariot of the seven treasures and circumambulated the Buddha three times. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he praised him with these verses:
"I take refuge in the Unsurpassed Honored One of Ten Powers, Who has fully cultivated boundless and true practices;
He has definitively realized all dharmas And, forever severing all delusions, attained fearlessness."
I take refuge in the Great Teacher of the three realms, Who has liberated himself from the bonds of craving and existence;
Having himself transcended to the supreme shore of Bodhi, He is further able to rescue those who are submerged and drowning.
The Tathāgata skillfully expounds the path of liberation; having heard it, all sentient beings believe and accept it.
He causes them all to be purified and cleansed of all defilements, just as a lotus flower is unsullied by water.
The Sage’s supreme wisdom observes well; he realizes that all phenomena are empty and signless.
He does not cling to any conditioned activities, being like space which has nothing upon which to rely.

At that time, there was another asura king in the assembly named Subāhu, who gave rise to a pure mind and extensively offered worship; each of his offerings was no different from those of the asura king Pramudita.

Having made these offerings, he mounted a chariot of the seven treasures and circumambulated the Buddha three times. Holding golden grains in his hands, he scattered them over the Tathāgata, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and praised him with this verse:
"I bow my head to the Auspicious Teacher and Tamer, Unequaled among gods and in the world;
You thoroughly know that the nature of sentient beings is fundamentally empty, Existing only as false conceptions, like a mirage."
No agent, no recipient, and no sentient beings; No self, no person, and no distinction between "this" and "that.
Without speech and without description, the intrinsic nature is empty; All phenomena are from the beginning eternally quiescent.
When one seeks all phenomena and finds them unattainable, one then enters well into the understanding of the Buddha’s teaching;
such a person is named a Prince of the Dharma, following the conduct of the Buddhas of the past.
I now extend this offering to the Buddha, who tames all sentient beings difficult to transform;
by means of these roots of goodness from this brief praise, I dedicate them so that both myself and others may all become Buddhas.

At that time, there was another asura king in the assembly named Mahābala, who gave rise to a pure mind and extensively offered worship; each of his offerings was no different from those of the asura king Subāhu.

Having made these offerings, he mounted a chariot of the seven treasures and circumambulated the Buddha three times. He scattered various precious flowers over the Buddha, joined his palms toward him, and praised him with these verses:
"I bow my head to the Great Dharma King, Whose eye of wisdom illuminates the three realms of existence.
Having already crossed the ocean of birth and death, You have reached the ultimate further shore."
He instructs all sentient beings, removing delusion and dispelling fear;
having crossed the four floods, he has reached the place of peace and security.
With profound and subtle wisdom, he has fathomed the very source and bottom of the world.
Knowing the desires of sentient beings, who are deeply attached to inverted perceptions,
he constantly uses a mind of great compassion to reveal and instruct them toward awakening;
he shatters their false and deluded wisdom so they may possess the vision of reality.
Thoroughly realizing all phenomena, Stainless and free from attachment,
Like illusions, mirages, And like the moon reflected in water—
The Muni, the most supreme Honored One, Regards all sentient beings as his own children.
Causing all to cultivate correct practice, Without attachment to the three periods of time.
The Tathāgata appears in the world, Realizing that all phenomena are false and provisional;
Their own nature is unattainable, And their other-nature is entirely empty.
"Just as worldly fools experience sensual pleasures in a dream, which are ultimately unattainable, so too should one reflect according to the truth.

At that time, there was another asura king in the assembly named Rāhu, who gave rise to a pure mind and extensively made offerings; each of his offerings was no different from those of the great asura king Mahābala.

Having made these offerings, he mounted a chariot of the seven precious gems and circumambulated the Buddha three times. He then scattered exquisite *citrā-puṣpa* flowers over the Buddha and, with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised him in verse:
“Lofty is the Unsurpassed One, The radiance of his body most brilliantly shines;
Among all devas and worldlings, None can equal the Buddha.”
Just as if one were to compare a mustard seed to Mount Meru,
or the water in a cow’s footprint to the vast ocean,
so too the Tathāgata’s wondrous physical marks have no equal in the world.
Each individual mark is so dignified and beautiful that those who behold it never tire of looking.
These wondrous marks are inconceivable, transcending all other forms;
like the sun illuminating the world, all other lights are eclipsed.
The Buddha’s majestic power and radiant light Outshine the hosts of all the devas;
Like the moon appearing in the vast sky, The starlight is all rendered dim and obscure.
His wisdom is as deep as the great ocean, And his physical marks are like a mountain of gold.
"The light of the Buddha’s body-wisdom is peerless throughout the three realms.

At that time, there was another asura king in the assembly named Śuddhaśīla (Pure Precept). He gave rise to a pure mind and extensively offered worship; each of his offerings was no different from those of the asura king Rāhu.

Having made these offerings, he mounted a chariot of the seven precious gems and circumambulated the Buddha three times. He then scattered *mahā-utpala* flowers over the Buddha, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and praised him with these verses:
“The Muni possesses the radiance of supreme wisdom, Able to shatter the darkness of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Having accomplished the most excellent *śamatha*, He pours down the rain of Dharma to nourish all beings.”
The Tathāgata’s adamantine seat and place of enlightenment Blazes with the torch of wisdom, illuminating the three realms of existence;
It can burn away the firewood of sentient beings’ afflictions, Leaving nothing remaining but ashes.
Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of eons, you have accumulated and upheld the treasury of the sublime Dharma;
you bestow it universally upon all beings tormented by feverish affliction, so that all who hear it are as if drinking nectar.
The Tathāgata appears in the world, able to show sentient beings the eye of the True Dharma;
amidst the long night of ignorance and saṃsāra, the maṇi-jewel of wisdom can illuminate all.

At that time, there was another asura king in the assembly named Priyayuddha (Joyful in Battle), who gave rise to a pure mind and extensively offered worship; each of his offerings was no different from those of the asura king Śīlavat (Pure Precepts).

Having made this offering, he mounted a chariot of the seven precious gems and circumambulated the Buddha three times. He then scattered exquisite *pāṭala* flowers over the Buddha, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and praised him with these verses:
"I take refuge in the Holy Lord, the Lion of the Śākyas, Who has attained fearlessness among all phenomena.
Like a valiant general donning his armor, He subdues the enemy forces without any timidity."
The faculties of the Sage are ever tranquil, Unperturbed by the afflictions;
Having forever exhausted the three poisons and all stains, Residual habits no longer arise in succession.
The Tathāgata surveys sentient beings six times over, Without attachment, without aversion, and without discrimination;
Abiding in vast, unconditioned compassion, He regards enemies and kin with complete equanimity.
The Buddha knows the various perceptions of sentient beings, Revealing them each according to their needs to dispel all delusions;
He causes them all to dwell well in right reflection, Realizing that the mind is like an illusion, free from attachment.

At that time, there was another asura king in the assembly named Sunetra (Wonderful Eye), who gave rise to a pure mind and extensively made offerings; each of his offerings was no different from those of the asura king Priyadarśana (Joyous Battle).

Having made these offerings, he mounted a chariot of the seven precious jewels and circumambulated the Buddha three times. He then scattered *mahāpattrala* flowers over the Buddha and, with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised him in verse:
“O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, You have thoroughly realized the true nature of all phenomena;
That which is called ‘all phenomena’ Exists only because of causes and conditions.”
Neither existence nor non-existence can be found through seeking;
if there were any dharma that could be spoken of, such speech would be merely a provisional name.
These various characteristics are, from the very beginning, eternally quiescent.
Without name and without mark—this is what the Muni has taught.
Though he speaks, there is nothing spoken; not even a fraction can be found.
Since the speaker is likewise non-existent, the listener is also thus.
"One who thoroughly understands such meanings and does not cling to any phenomena is able to perform the great practice; such a person is called a true son of the Buddha.

At that time, there was another asura king in the assembly named Transcending the Three Times (*Trailokyasamatikrānta*), who gave rise to a pure mind and extensively offered worship. Each of his offerings was no different from those of the asura king Wondrous Eye (*Sunetra*).

Having made these offerings, he mounted a chariot of the seven treasures and circumambulated the Buddha three times. He then presented the Tathāgata with exquisite pearl necklaces, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and praised him in verse:
“The Tathāgata is fully endowed with all merits; His pure precepts and majestic deportment are entirely perfected.
The four kinds of demonic armies have been subdued and eliminated by wisdom; Within the three realms, none are equal to the Buddha.”
The Tathāgata’s power of concentration cannot be shaken; it is beyond the fathom of those of shallow wisdom.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, he remains in accord with meditative absorption, manifesting various miraculous feats for the benefit and happiness of all.
The Tathāgata’s supreme wisdom is unsurpassed; amidst the great assembly, he roars the lion’s roar.
