Skillfully expounding the sublime Dharma, he shatters all doubts and gathers in and transforms all those of external paths.
The Tathāgata’s physical form transcends the three realms of existence, Universally adorned with all manner of marks and signs;
His radiant brilliance blazes like a mountain of gold, Attained through the extensive cultivation of the giving of alms.

At that time, there was another asura king in the assembly named Puyao (Universal Radiance), who gave rise to a pure mind and extensively offered worship; each of his offerings was no different from those of the asura king Yue San-shi (Transcending the Three Worlds).

Having made these offerings, they mounted chariots of the seven treasures and circumambulated the Buddha three times. They then scattered various exquisite jewels over the Tathāgata, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and praised him with these verses:
"We have renounced the pleasures of the five desires And come to the presence of the Buddha to offer worship.
Each of us sees the Tathāgata standing before us; This uncommon virtue is inconceivable."
The pure Dharma expounded from a single voice may be explained extensively or briefly;
each understands it according to their own inclinations—this uncommon virtue is inconceivable.
The pure Dharma expounded from a single voice is understood by each according to their own disposition;
the Tathāgata’s skillful adaptation to their capacities is an uncommon virtue difficult to conceive.
The pure Dharma expounded from a single voice may cause some to practice, others to be disciplined, and some to attain the benefits of various fruits; this uncommon virtue is inconceivable.

At that time, there was another asura king in the assembly named Mucilinda, who gave rise to a pure mind and extensively made offerings; each of his offerings was no different from those of the asura king Puyao.

Having made these offerings, he mounted a chariot of the seven precious gems and circumambulated the Buddha three times. He scattered red pearls over the Buddha and, with palms joined toward him, praised him in verse:
“The Tathāgata has skillfully transformed the Father King, Causing him to abandon pride and false views, And to give rise to firm and pure faith; He is the most supreme and peerless son.”
Dharmas lack intrinsic nature and arise from conditions; like the pleasure experienced in a dream, they are not real entities.
One should know that such pleasure arises following mental conceptions; this is what is called understanding the nature of all dharmas.
Just as drifting clouds arise in the autumn sky, The deluded mind’s attachment to existence is not solid;
Relying upon the teachings of the Muni, The wise should not increase their pride.
When the mind observes well and is not negligent, it will have no attachments within the world;
this is called dwelling securely within the Buddha-dharma, and one shall realize the illusion-like samādhi.

At that time, having made their offerings, the various asura kings each joined their palms, stood before the Buddha with serene body and mind, and having attained great and wholesome benefit, they all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the various asura kings, manifested a smile amidst the great assembly. He immediately emitted five-colored light from his face, which illuminated all buddha-worlds; the light circled the Buddha three times and then re-entered through the crown of the World-Honored One’s head.

Then, having beheld these signs, the Venerable Aśvajit rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and prostrating with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what cause and condition has this auspicious sign appeared?
Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he asked in verse:
"O Lion of the Śākyas, supreme among men, this appearance of an auspicious sign is not without cause."
I pray only that you, out of great compassion, will speak for me, so that upon hearing it, all may find their minds at peace.
Sixty *nayutas* of asuras have offered worship with vast and pure hearts;
could it be that the Tathāgata will grant them a prophecy, so that upon hearing it, they may give rise to joy?
At that time, the entire assembly thought to themselves:
"The emission of this radiance is not for a minor cause; we pray only that the Tathāgata will take pity on us and explain the reason for manifesting these signs."
"Have they already resolved to attain bodhicitta, or have they merely first given rise to pure faith?
The Tathāgata knows each and every one of them; we pray that you will resolve the doubts of the assembly by speaking swiftly."
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“Excellent, Mahābhikṣu Aśvajit! You are able to inquire about the matter of emitting light.
I now wish, amidst this assembly, To prophesy the most supreme and true fruit.”
All the asuras cultivate meritorious deeds, Resolving to seek the unsurpassed, great bodhi;
Having completely eliminated the defilements of greed and anger, They are unimpeded, like a hand touching empty space.
From this, a pure intention arises, and one extensively performs boundless, wondrous offerings;
later, one shall cast off this asura body, always being born in superior realms and increasing clear wisdom.
In the future, after kalpas as numerous as the sands of that river, they shall attend upon and serve all Tathāgatas;
in their final bodies, they shall become Kings of the Dharma, attaining Buddhahood one after another with identical names.
All were titled Tathāgata Supreme Lamp; their fame pervaded the ten directions.
They taught and transformed sixty nayutas of sentient beings, all of whom attained liberation upon hearing the Dharma.
The land is vast and exceedingly pure, encompassing the entirety of a trichiliocosm;
the sentient beings therein who receive transformation are fully endowed with merit and wisdom,
they commit no unrighteous deeds, and all cultivate the practice of equanimity and peace.
Those Buddhas all preach the Dharma free from contention; those who hear it are without attachment and without obstruction.
The lifespan of each Buddha is sixty nayutas, and the life-span of sentient beings remains equal and no different.
When those Tathāgatas have completed their work of transformation, they enter parinirvāṇa in accordance with the resonance of sentient beings' capacities;
in succession, they will inherit and uphold the Dharma to become Buddhas, with lands and lifespans exactly the same as theirs,
likewise transforming all such sentient beings and causing them to receive and uphold the True Dharma as their Buddha-sons.
The Sutra of the Union of Father and Son, Volume Three.
The Sutra of the Union of Father and Son, Volume Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu.
Translated by the Imperial Edict by the Court Gentleman for State Ceremonial, the Master of Dharma from India, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject Nichiren, et al.

Chapter Five: The Original Deeds of the Tathāgata At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, seeing all the asura kings within the assembly of the Buddha manifest vast offerings through their supernormal powers, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and thought to himself:
“What roots of goodness did the Tathāgata plant in the past while practicing the bodhisattva path, such that he was able to obtain such a supreme and most excellent fruition?”
Having formed this thought, he entered *samādhi* and observed with single-minded concentration;

through the Buddha’s empowerment, he was able to recollect immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) eons, wherein the World-Honored One, in various places throughout his past lives, diligently cultivated immeasurable, boundless, and vast meritorious deeds, each of which appeared clearly before him, understood with certainty and free from doubt.

Suppose that all sentient beings in as many worlds in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River were to all attain human bodies, and for as many eons as there are grains of sand in those rivers, each and every being were to offer individual acts of worship; even the mass of merit possessed by such a Vemacitra Asura King would not equal the merit of a single instance of a Tathāgata’s generation of the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—it could not be compared to it.
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having arisen from meditative concentration, joined his palms with joy and praised the Buddha in verse:
“In the past, the Great Sage King, the Muni, Vowed to seek unsurpassed, supreme Bodhi.
Though the asuras offered extensive worship, It did not equal the merit gained by the initial resolve.”
The Tathāgata’s holy virtue transcends the three realms; among gods and humans, there is none equal to him.
Like a mountain of piled sandalwood as vast as Mount Sumeru, he is worthy of receiving such a great offering.
The most excellent and pure ointments, vast and deep as the great ocean,
are worthy of such a grand offering for the Lion among Men who has appeared in the world.
Some scatter various kinds of exquisite flowers, heaped as high as the summit of Mount Cakravāḍa;
the Tathāgata’s holy virtue is wondrous and inconceivable, worthy of receiving such great offerings.
Taking the waters of the great ocean as oil, and making Mount Sumeru the size of its wick, one lights a lamp and offers it to the Great Teacher;
such a one is worthy of receiving this great offering.
Or with countless exquisite flower garlands, they offer them to the Tathāgata and his shrines;
the Buddha, possessing vast and supreme majesty and virtue, is worthy of receiving such great offerings.
Even if one were to offer ten billion exquisite jeweled canopies throughout immeasurable koṭis of kalpas,
the Tathāgata, having skillfully transformed his royal father, is worthy of receiving such a great offering.
Throughout inconceivable billions of eons, filling the worlds of the ten directions with jeweled banners,
the Tathāgata has accomplished the gateway of great compassion and is worthy of receiving such a sublime offering.
Furthermore, throughout immeasurable koṭis of kalpas, with banners of exquisite silk as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
you, O Muni, who bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, are worthy of receiving such great offerings.
The Tathāgata skillfully expounds the essentials of all dharmas, And sentient beings are all able to hear and receive them;
A King of Dharma with unimpeded eloquence, His skillful speech has no equal.
Even if all sentient beings within as many Gaṅgā-sand worlds as there are,
were each to become a Teacher of Gods and Humans endowed with the Ten Powers, and together emerge into the world to attain the Buddha-way—
should such countless Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the river, each miraculously manifest immeasurable heads;
Each head manifests a hundred thousand mouths, and within each mouth there are a hundred thousand tongues;
even throughout eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, praising the ocean of the Tathāgata’s merits—
his lifespan, wisdom, and the generation of the bodhicitta— one could not comprehend even a tiny fraction of it.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! Kāśyapa!”

Now, among this assembly of śrāvakas, you have fully cultivated the holy life, thoroughly understood all phenomena, realized the limit of reality through direct experience, and attained tranquility of mind.
You are well able to enter into and comprehend the mass of merit I have realized, contemplating and examining it with wisdom.
I have already accomplished an immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable accumulation of merit and have reached the supreme, foremost shore.

Kāśyapa! If the mass of merit resulting from the Tathāgata’s single arousal of the great mind were to possess a physical form, the river-sand worlds of the ten directions would not be able to contain it.

Even if as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges Rivers of the ten directions were to appear in the world simultaneously, and were to continue for that same number of kalpas as the sands of the Ganges to describe the merit of a single instance of the Tathāgata’s initial resolve for great awakening, they could not exhaustively describe it.

Why is this so? When the Tathāgata formerly practiced the bodhisattva path, there was not a single thought of enlightenment that was not for the sake of gathering in, benefiting, and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings. Because the realm of sentient beings is limitless, the Tathāgata’s generation of the thought of enlightenment is likewise limitless;
because the realm of sentient beings is ultimately inexhaustible, the Tathāgata’s generation of the thought of enlightenment is likewise inexhaustible.
Therefore, I now receive such offerings from the devas, humans, and asura kings.

Even if every single sentient being in as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges throughout the ten directions were to offer worship equal to that of those asura kings, they still could not equal the merit obtained by generating this great mind even once.
Why is this? Because those sentient beings have impure minds and are attached to karmic retribution. Kāśyapa!

One should know that when the immeasurable Buddhas of the past appeared in the world, their initial generation of the Great Mind was entirely for the sake of compassion for all sentient beings, to cause them to escape saṃsāra and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa;
what I now do is likewise the same.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!

I recall that in the past, immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and inconceivable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Dīpaṅkara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."

All sentient beings within that buddha-field do not commit evil deeds; their minds are free from distraction, they do not give rise to perverse thoughts, and they are devoid of inverted views or arrogance. Their actions of body, speech, and mind are ultimately pure; having subdued and eliminated afflictions and severed the causes for rebirth in the evil realms, they practice with diligent effort and mutually exhort one another.
Within the long night of birth and death, they are able to give rise to a courageous mind, delighting in the Mahāyāna, hearing the true Dharma, and practicing according to the principle.
Within that Buddha-field there are five kinds of joy:
first, the joy of desire.
Second, the bliss of renunciation;
third, the bliss of meditative concentration;
fourth, the bliss of meditative equipoise.
Fifth, the bliss of bodhi.
Those sentient beings constantly enjoy such happiness; yet, though they experience that bliss, they do not become attached to it.
Just as a bee gathering nectar from flowers merely sustains its life, and just as a bird flying through the sky encounters no obstruction, so too are these sentient beings.

Furthermore, those sentient beings are free from the various evil karmas of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the afflictions and their attendant faults; they experience pleasure in accordance with their prior wholesome karma. Why is this?

When that Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path, the sentient beings he transformed were exclusively of virtuous conduct; even if they possessed unwholesome karmic residues from previous lives, the power of their present roots of goodness caused these to be dissolved and suppressed so that they would not arise.
Therefore, all sentient beings in that land experience only the manifestation of pleasant sensations.
Furthermore, that Buddha-land is free from various hardships, such as violent winds and rains, or extreme cold and heat; whenever desired, sweet rain falls at will.
Furthermore, those sentient beings always delight in hearing the Dharma; each is able to comprehend it, honoring and revering it.
Whether walking, sitting, or standing, they contemplate its meaning and penetrate deeply into the flavor of the Dharma, never becoming weary and never falling asleep.
Within the four modes of deportment, he practices with diligent effort; because of his delight in the Dharma, no weariness or hardship arises.
He cultivates only the right abandonments and possesses no inverted views; should any error occur, he immediately reforms and repents, and thus there is no painful sensation.

"Furthermore, when that Tathāgata was practicing in the past, his actions of body, speech, and mind were never erroneous; whatever he did was preceded by wisdom, and he taught the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas to transform all sentient beings.

Having heard the Dharma, they followed it through the practice of wisdom; the benefits they performed were not conjoined with delusion or craving, and therefore they experienced neither painful nor pleasant sensations."
The sentient beings of that land possess minds of equanimity and abide in accordance with reality in all circumstances; therefore, they suffer no pain from encountering those they dislike.
Furthermore, those beings have no sense of "self" or "other," and their minds are unattached to any phenomena; therefore, they suffer no pain from being separated from those they love.
Furthermore, because those sentient beings do not give rise to contempt for any wholesome dharmas nor disparage them, they lack the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
yet, as the sentient beings of that land are subject to conditioned change, they experience only the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
Why is this? Because that Buddha constantly teaches the subtle Dharma of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
When that Tathāgata Indradhvaja appeared in the world, his lifespan was immeasurable and boundless, lasting for as many *kalpas* as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;

the sentient beings therein each possessed vast eloquence and were skilled in expounding the essential points of the Dharma, having all been taught and brought to maturity by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, before being reborn therein.
Kāśyapa! What do you think?

Could any sentient beings who lack faith, lack ethical discipline, lack meditative concentration, lack wisdom, are of little learning, or are indolent ever be born in such a vast, majestic, and pure buddha-field?
Kāśyapa replied:
"No, World-Honored One."
“Kāśyapa! What do you think?

In such a vast, majestic, and pure buddha-field, could beings who possess only subtle roots of goodness, inferior roots of goodness, or weak roots of goodness—those whose karma and afflictions are governed by suffering, and who perform impure dedications of merit—be born there?”
Kāśyapa replied:
“No, World-Honored One!”

Those born within such a Buddha-field are endowed with roots of goodness, pure and free from defilement; they abide in right reflection, are liberated from all suffering, are learned and diligent, and have made pure dedications of merit—all having been long ago transformed and delivered by previous Buddhas.
It is such sentient beings who attain birth therein.
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa,
excellent, excellent!”
As you have said, it is so.
Regarding that former Tathāgata, King of Banners—what do you think?
Do you know who he was?
At that time, the bhikṣus remained silent and offered no reply.

At that very moment, to the east, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a land named Moonlight Adornment. Therein dwelt a Buddha named Mass of Radiance, who was currently preaching the Dharma.

In that Buddha’s assembly was the youth Mañjuśrī, who, hearing from afar the causes and conditions of the inquiry in this world-system, knew that none among the great multitude were able to answer it.
At that time, the youth addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I shall now go to the Sahā world to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha, and for the sake of that assembly at that time, I shall answer their question.”
Then the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna said to the youth, "Go as you please.

At that moment, the youth vanished from that place and, by means of his supernormal powers, reached the world of Sahā where Śākyamuni Buddha resided in the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
Then the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke to the youth, saying:
"By what causes and conditions have you come here?
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī joined his palms and said:
"I have come from afar to answer the questions previously asked by this assembly.
Was that former Tathāgata, King Banner (Dhvajarāja), anyone else?
He is none other than the present Tathāgata Śākyamuni."

Why is this so? Because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is fully endowed with inconceivable and subtle merits, possesses skillful means, and out of compassion for sentient beings, causes them all to dwell securely on the path to enlightenment.
When the assembly heard this, they all praised him together,
saying: "Excellent,
young man!"
You have answered this question well, resolving the web of doubts for the assembly.
What you have now spoken is the correct teaching, the true teaching, and the supreme teaching.
At that time, the youth spoke these verses for the sake of the assembled multitude:
“The Holy Lord, the Lion of the Śākyas, Endowed with courageous diligence,
Out of compassion for the world, Manifests inconceivable deeds.”
That Muni, the World-Honored One, in the past,
already served eighty koṭis of Buddhas; he brought all sentient beings to maturity and,
with a mind of constant great compassion, purified the Buddha-lands.
Those of shallow understanding cannot comprehend the various skillful means;
Without abandoning the initial resolve for enlightenment, they manifest in response to the capacities of beings.
Furthermore, in future ages, they will again manifest infinite bodies.
Sometimes appearing as Śakra or Brahmā, sometimes manifesting as the Māra King,
among all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, none can know even a small portion [of his deeds].
Sometimes appearing born in a royal palace, attaining enlightenment and turning the wheel of Dharma.
Even unto entering nirvāṇa, they manifest the virtues of a Buddha;
or, according to their kind, they appear in the form of women,
yet remain unstained by worldly dharmas, like the nature of a lotus which is inherently pure.
Some weep and wail in sorrow; some sing, dance, and play;
some travel back and forth through the air—all these perform the work of a Buddha.
Those who are fearful are brought to peace and security; those who are arrogant are made gentle and compliant.
To benefit those sentient beings, he manifests various means of subduing them.
He causes the deluded to leave behind their delusion and shows wisdom to the ignorant;
to benefit those sentient beings, he employs skillful and expedient means.
The mad regain right mindfulness, and the lame attain easy movement;
for the benefit of those sentient beings, you manifest various miraculous feats.
Therefore, I prostrate to your inconceivable diligence.
Universally transforming all sentient beings, Causing them all to enter the Buddha-way.

Chapter Six: The Prophecy for the Garuḍa Kings. *The Compendium of Father and Son Sūtra*, Chapter Six: The Prophecy for the Garuḍa Kings. At that time, within the assembly, there were sixty-eight thousand Garuḍa kings. Having witnessed the various Asura kings making their offerings and having further heard the Tathāgata bestow prophecies upon them, they gave rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and extensively prepared offerings. By means of their supernormal powers, they immediately manifested sixty-eight thousand exquisite pavilions. Each pavilion was composed of the seven treasures—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, and crystal—and each had seven tiers. On the first level, the pillars were made of yellow gold; the rafters, eaves, capitals, and brackets were made of white silver, all intricately inlaid with various jewels.
The second tier has pillars of white silver, with rafters, eaves, capitals, and brackets made of gold, all adorned with various jewels;
continuing thus up to the seventh tier, which has pillars of coral, interspersed and embellished with various treasures such as pearls.
Each of these pavilions was likewise covered above with jeweled nets—some made of golden nets, some of silver nets, and even those made of pearls.
Furthermore, countless exquisite jeweled bells were suspended; when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produced sounds that listeners never grew weary of.
Additionally, sixty-eight thousand precious canopies appeared, interspersed with various treasures, their radiance shining brilliantly.
Furthermore, sixty-eight thousand jeweled banners appeared, their various colors intermingled and adorned with pearls and gems.
Additionally, sixty-eight thousand silk streamers appeared, variegated in five colors and most delightful to behold.
Furthermore, sixty-eight thousand precious canopies appeared, some constructed from golden threads,
while others were exquisitely adorned with silver threads, lapis lazuli threads, pearl threads, and so forth.

Then the Garuḍa King immediately offered to the Tathāgata the sixty-eight thousand seven-jeweled pavilions, various jeweled nets and curtains, and jeweled banners, pennants, and canopies that had appeared as described above. Arranged in successive rows in the midst of space, they moved slowly in a circular motion, circling the Buddha three times. Like the great dragon-elephant king Airāvaṇa of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven circling Śakra, they then stood to one side.
At that time, the King of the Garuḍas joined his palms toward the Buddha and praised him in verse:
"I bow my head and take refuge in the Unsurpassed One, Whom none in all the world can equal;
You are able to transcend the causes of birth, old age, sickness, and death, And liberate [beings] from the various sufferings and calamities of saṃsāra."
May I swiftly accomplish the Buddha-body, Fully endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks,
Universally adorned with the eighty secondary signs, Possessing the firm strength of Nārāyaṇa.
May I be like the Buddha, with a body of true golden color, And a fathom-and-six-foot halo constantly illuminating;
Amidst the majestic deportments of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, May I gather and transform sentient beings, leading them to liberation.
May I firmly uphold all the prohibitive precepts, Dwell in the supreme and most excellent samādhi,
And through the wisdom of skillful means benefit all sentient beings, Causing them all to attain the path of Bodhi.
May this body of mine forever eliminate and sever [afflictions], so that I may serve as a vehicle for others while subduing the mind of anger;
may I, like the Buddha who is fully endowed with great compassion, attain the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharmas).
Fully understanding that all phenomena arise from conditions, Like a child’s play, a dream, or an echo,
The Great Guide, the Muni, has extensively revealed this To those among gods and humans.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the minds of the Garuḍa kings were deeply resolved and thoroughly understood, and that their will was firm and diligent, manifested a smile and emitted light of five colors.
At that time, the bhikṣu Aśvajit, having witnessed this event, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, joined his palms in reverence, and asked in verse:
“I take refuge in the unsurpassed Teacher of gods and humans, Who manifests this rare and inconceivable deed.
This emission of light is not without cause; Out of compassion for us, please explain it.”
The King of the Garuḍas offers worship, with jeweled canopies covering the sky;
such as the world has never before seen or heard—may the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings explain this meaning.
Now this assembly of humans and devas, with palms joined in joy and filled with hope,
wishes to hear you expound for the sake of that Garuḍa King the fruit of liberation in the future.
The Buddha is the most honored among gods and humans, able to fulfill the desires of all sentient beings;
we pray that the Tathāgata will proclaim this teaching, so that this great assembly may have their doubts and fears dispelled.
If the assembly is freed from doubt and fear, they will be able to give rise to a heart of joy;
if they hear the Tathāgata’s words of prophecy, they shall fully practice all the Buddha's teachings.
We only pray that your great compassion will bestow protection and mindfulness, dispelling our doubts and increasing all roots of goodness;
with palms joined, each of us yearns to hear how the King of the Garuḍas attained the Way of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣu Aśvajit:
“Excellent, Aśvajit, that you have asked so well about the cause of the emitted light and the manifestation of the smile.
I shall now speak; listen attentively, so that you may cast away doubt and give rise to joy.”
The hosts of garuḍas cultivate meritorious deeds, Vowing to seek unexcelled, great bodhi;
They shall become venerable ones of fearlessness and the ten powers, Attaining this supreme name known as "Buddha."
By virtue of making offerings with that pure mind, one will certainly be adorned with the marks and signs of excellence;
possessing the inconceivable eighteen unique qualities, one shall be liberated and mount the vehicle of Nārāyaṇa.
By thus firmly upholding the pure precepts, dwelling securely in the pure samādhi,
and cultivating supreme wisdom and the six supernormal powers, they adorn and purify all Buddha-fields.
Because they made offerings to me with a pure mind, In their final body, they were freed from this animal rebirth;
Ultimately never passing through births in the evil realms, They constantly enjoy the supreme blessings and happiness of gods and humans.
After passing through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, having made offerings to and served all Tathāgatas,
and having skillfully disciplined the gates of their faculties, they shall all thereafter attain Buddhahood.
All are equally named Merudhvaja Tathāgata, complete with the ten titles;
their lands are pure and adorned, their kalpa is named Spontaneous Birth, and in those realms there are no three evil destinies.
All sentient beings therein possess a dignified and extraordinary appearance, free from any deficiency;
that Buddha’s lifespan is exceedingly long, lasting eighty-four thousand *koṭi* years.
In this manner, they shall successively attain Buddhahood;
their lands and lifespans shall all be equal, and each shall transform and deliver beings numbering eighty nayuta-koṭis.
Causing all to abandon the habit of arrogance, Completely dispelling the fetters and hindrances to attain cool serenity,
Abiding securely in the gate of liberation of non-arising, Distant from dust and free from defilement, their minds are pure.
Because he was originally possessed of a golden body and relied upon his great power to give rise to arrogance,
he became a Buddha for the sake of sentient beings and first caused them to sever the dharma of pride.
In the past, throughout incalculable eons, they were great seers who practiced austerities;
numbering sixty-eight thousand, they constantly delighted in cultivating supernormal powers.
Once those sages had attained supernatural powers, they considered themselves masters of the world and rare among men;
though they maintained their prohibitive precepts and were endowed with dignified deportment, they dwelt in mountain forests while giving rise to conceit.

Because of this, they fell among the garuḍas; though they possessed great power through their past supernormal faculties and beheld my body due to their observance of the precepts, they forgot the cause of bodhi because of their pride.
I now bestow upon you the prophecy of attaining Buddhahood; I have briefly explained the prior causes to bring about awakening.
For the sake of the vast benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, May all who hear this together give rise to joy.
The Compendium of the Father and Son Sūtra, Volume Four;
The Compendium of the Father and Son Sūtra, Volume Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu.
Translated by the Imperial Edict by the *śramaṇa* of Purple Robes, Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Ritsū (Jichō), and others.

Chapter Seven: The Prophecy for the Dragon Girl At that time, within the assembly, there were ninety-six *koṭis* of dragon girls. Having seen the Asura King and the Garuḍa King make offerings to the World-Honored One, and having further heard the Tathāgata bestow upon each of them the prophecy of attaining Buddhahood, their hearts were filled with great joy and they leaped for immeasurable delight. With pure minds, they extensively arranged offerings.

By their supernormal power, these nāga maidens manifested ninety-six koṭis of blue parasols. Each parasol had a thousand ribs made of vaidūrya gemstone, skillfully arranged with handles of gold, nets of pearls, hanging flower garlands, and adorned with various precious ornaments.
He further manifested ninety-six koṭis of excellent, noble horses, likewise adorned and embellished with various jewels, with Vaiḍūrya gems serving as their bridles and halters.

Furthermore, he manifested a canopy of various jewel nets, sixty yojanas in circumference, which completely covered the entire assembly of those who had gathered. Beneath this precious canopy appeared a singular and exquisite mani-jewel, its radiance shining forth so brightly that nothing remained obscure.
Furthermore, ninety-six koṭis of flower garlands made of various jewels were manifested, exquisitely and marvelously crafted, hanging down everywhere.

Moreover, countless jeweled bells were suspended and attached; when stirred by a gentle breeze, their sounds were harmonious and elegant, like celestial music, such that those who heard them never grew weary.

Furthermore, they scattered fine powders of *tamarapaṭa*, *candana*, and *agaru* incense over the Tathāgata; they also scattered *utpala* flowers and *campaka* flowers, as well as immeasurable, exquisite garments, various kinds of immeasurable multicolored necklaces, and various kinds of immeasurable multicolored flower garlands.
Each of these dragon maidens mounted one of those horses, unfurled parasols, and circumambulated the Buddha three times through the air.
They further performed various kinds of music from the dragon palaces; the sounds were clear and elegant, a delight for all to hear.
Furthermore, in the city of Kapilavastu, various ointments and diverse perfumed waters descended like rain; these mixed with the fragrant flowers to form a mud sixty yojanas in length and breadth.
Through the majestic empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of that Tathāgata, this sound of music and the fragrant mud shall be made to be heard throughout the trichiliocosm.
All sentient beings therein who hear this sound and fragrance shall attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
After these nāga girls had made their offerings, they prostrated with their heads at his feet in reverence, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and praised him in verse:
"By our past merit we have encountered the Buddha; With pure hearts and joyful minds, we have performed meritorious deeds.
We make offerings to the Great Teacher, the Muni, Hoping to escape this retribution of being born as nāga girls."
He emanated ninety-six koṭis of exquisite parasols adorned with various jewels, making offerings to the Unsurpassed Tamer of Men; through these roots of virtue, he sought liberation.
Furthermore, he manifested ninety-six koṭis [of horses], well-tamed and skillfully guided, with dark-blue steeds adorned with exquisite blue jewels;
all were for the purpose of making offerings to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, ninety-six koṭis were emanated, with blue jeweled banners revolving in the sky;
each, through body, speech, and mind, prostrated with head and face to the ground and extended their dedication of merit.
The exquisite sounds of music from all the dragon palaces, Played simultaneously with voices pure and penetrating;
As the Muni appeared in the world, He was worthy of such a great offering.
Such various sounds of musical instruments resound far and wide throughout the trichiliocosm;
if the sentient beings therein should hear them, they shall all attain the stage of non-retrogression toward Bodhi.
Furthermore, he manifested a vast canopy of a single precious jewel, sixty yojanas in length and breadth,
extending everywhere throughout the sky, providing broad cover for the great assembly of those who had gathered.
In the center appears the supreme maṇi jewel, its blazing radiance illuminating all;
throughout the great assembly of devas and humans, they offer worship with pure hearts and joyful delight.
By means of these few roots of goodness, we resolve to seek the fruit of tranquil enlightenment;
may we, just like the Great Teacher, the Muni, achieve profound and subtle wisdom.
He transforms and benefits all sentient beings, liberating them from the bonds of worldly toil and afflictions;
like the Unsurpassed Honored One endowed with the Ten Powers, he expounds the boundless, pure Dharma.
All conditioned phenomena are like illusions and transformations; They are also like masses of foam, lacking solidity.
Like bubbles arising when rain falls from the sky, Their intrinsic nature is false and devoid of a master.
The wise contemplate all worldly phenomena as like reflections appearing in a mirror;
the essential nature of sentient beings is likewise so—only a Buddha realizes this through direct perception and speaks it according to reality.
Fools, failing to understand, claim these things are real; they give rise to attachment toward illusory objects.
Yet all phenomena are fundamentally empty from the beginning; these deluded ones only deceive themselves.
Because of that delusion and ignorance, they do not realize the true nature of all phenomena;
for this reason, the Tathāgata has appeared in the world to demonstrate that there is no self and nothing to be apprehended.
Just as drifting clouds arise in the autumn sky, appearing for a moment and vanishing in an instant, know that the mark of self is originally non-existent;
when the wise observe with discernment, what could possibly exist?
All such phenomena of the world lack intrinsic nature and are not real;
they can only deceive the gates of the sense faculties, whereby the foolish increase their madness.
The Muni transcends the three realms, realizing that the nature of all phenomena is non-discriminative;
if one follows and practices the Tathāgata’s teaching, all the world shall be liberated.

If a person hears this profound and wondrous Dharma, And gives rise to joy and correct contemplation in their mind, They will be able to transcend and leave the mire of birth and death; This is not the realm of the foolish.
Therefore, I now prostrate with my head at the feet of the Teacher of Gods and Humans, who is free from afflictions;
his great compassion can rescue suffering sentient beings, serving as a boat, a shelter, and a refuge.
We make offerings to the Tathāgata for the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi;
may you proclaim the essentials of the Dharma to awaken the deluded masses, and universally pray that both self and others may attain the Buddha-way.
At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the nāga girls and their hope for a prophecy of enlightenment,
immediately manifested auspicious signs and emitted a great radiance.
At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit, having beheld this sign, prostrated his head at the Buddha’s feet and, with palms joined toward the Buddha, asked in verse:
“O Supreme Knower of the mundane and supramundane, You have suddenly manifested a divine transformation and emitted radiant light.
The assembly beholding this calls it auspicious; It cannot have arisen without cause or condition.”
O Supreme Sage, Lord among men, pray explain the origin of these radiant signs;
when the devas, humans, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits have heard them, they shall all give rise to thoughts of joy.
The Tathāgata, majestic and holy among the holy, who understands all worldly phenomena without exception,
out of compassion gathers in and protects all sentient beings, and thus speaks of this miraculous manifestation of emitting light.
The Tathāgata’s power of wisdom is subtle and inconceivable; it exhaustively penetrates the meaning of the true mark of all phenomena.
The assembled multitude gaze up in reverence, desiring to hear, so that each may know for themselves and their minds find peace.
The Muni has long since attained perfect enlightenment and is able to bring benefit and welfare to all living beings;
for what reason do you emit this great radiance? We pray that you will speak, so that all may have their doubts dispelled.
Now this great assembly’s minds are tranquil, capable of receiving and understanding the profound meaning of the Dharma;
with single-minded devotion they gaze upon the Tathāgata, and having heard it, each has resolved for Bodhi.
If a person has not yet reached a definitive understanding of a matter, their mind will waver and distress will arise;
because of this, they all fall into the net of doubt—may we only hope that your great compassion will swiftly provide an explanation.
Who today has resolved upon the Great Mind?
Which Buddha in another direction is preaching the Great Dharma?
Who has attained Bodhi and shattered the armies of Māra?
The emission of this radiance is most rare;
who is it that extensively generates pure meritorious karma?
Out of compassion for us, the Buddha emits this pure light.
The Holy Lord, the Lion, Honored One of Ten Powers, speaks fearlessly amidst the great assembly.
If we are graced by the Buddha’s revelation, we shall be free from all doubt and terror, our minds at ease;
with hearts of pure sympathetic joy, we shall each practice according to the Buddha’s teaching.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the Venerable Aśvajit:
“Excellent, great bhikṣu Aśvajit! That you are able to inquire about the matter of emitting light— I shall now, within this assembly, Proclaim the future fruit of the nāga girl.”
All of you, with a single mind, listen attentively; Free yourselves from all causes and conditions of distraction and defilement.
Hear me explain the cause of this emission of light, Which increases the manifold benefits of goodness for humans and devas.
The minds of these nāga maidens were opened and awakened; With wisdom they were able to contemplate the true mark of reality.
They understood that the inherent nature of all phenomena is empty, And thus they did not cling to worldly karma or its retributions.
There is no person, no self, and no sentient being; Nor is there an agent or an experiencer.
The *pudgala* is empty of intrinsic nature, Like a mirage or a reflection in a mirror.
These nāga maidens have planted roots of virtue and together performed vast and pure meritorious deeds;
they are well-established within the Buddha-dharma and understand that all worldly phenomena are like illusions.
Having thus performed these various offerings, she vowed to seek the great enlightenment of Buddhahood;
thereafter, she would cast off this female dragon body and be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three,
where she would become the sovereign of Śakra’s celestial palace, enjoying sublime bliss beyond reproach.
Possessing a lifespan as vast as that of the gods and a great renown, he further proceeds to dwell in the Yāma Heaven.
Having been born in the palace of the Yāma Heaven, he fully experiences its exquisite and wondrous pleasures;
the Son of the Buddha, dwelling securely within this heaven, attains mastery over his full lifespan.
Thereafter, he was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where he was constantly loved and revered by the celestial hosts;
though he experienced bliss, his mind remained unattached, like a lotus whose nature is inherently pure.
Due to their past cultivation of supramundane wisdom, they constantly contemplate all phenomena as empty and quiescent;
like carvings on stone that endure for long, they abide in right mindfulness without wavering.
In a future life, one will be born among the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, constantly surrounded by celestial sons and daughters;
one will not be disparaged by others and will possess a renowned reputation, completing the full span of that lifespan without premature death.
Experiencing those supreme pleasures of the five desires, yet remaining constantly in accord with right mindfulness,
one skillfully cultivates the three gates of liberation and ultimately enters into the realization of the dharma of true emptiness.
Reborn again in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, They receive the constant reverence of the celestial hosts;
Abiding therein with pure intentions, They uphold the True Dharma with an unshakable mind.

Whatever they desire to enjoy is all transformed by others; without giving rise to stained attachment or deluded craving, these sons of the Buddha dwell peacefully in those celestial palaces and reach the very limit of that heavenly lifespan.
Through weariness with sensual pleasures, one seeks the stage of meditative concentration to subdue all afflictions;
by attaining the various dhyānas and doors of liberation, one is thereby reborn in the Brahma heavens.
From that meditative concentration, various roots of goodness arise; for one intermediate kalpa, they enjoy joy and bliss.
The sublime satisfaction within that concentration is inconceivable, and one is gradually able to advance upon the path to enlightenment.
Dwelling in that Brahma palace for an eon, he exclusively cultivates pure conduct free from defilement;
through skillful means he benefits sentient beings, maintaining a mind of equanimity without notions of enemy or kin.
He fully masters all sublime joys and delights, yet remains unattached to the flavors of various meditative concentrations.
Skillfully awakening and pacifying all the sense faculties—such is the supreme son of the Muni.
That Brahmā speaks of a "natural dharma" that does not accord with the principle of karmic fruition;
only this true gate of liberation ultimately transcends the three realms.

If a person develops faith and understanding in this life, they will be able to skillfully guide all sentient beings to swiftly attain unsurpassed, wondrous Bodhi; such a person is called the Eye of the World.
Those nāga maidens were reborn in the Brahma realm, where they benefited and brought joy to all devas and humans;
through their teaching, they caused them to give rise to pure minds, and all were able to advance toward the path of bodhi.
He shall travel to infinite Buddha-fields, making offerings to and serving all Tathāgatas;
after that future Star-Constellation Kalpa has passed, he will attain Buddhahood together with them, named Śāntendriya (Tranquil in All Faculties).
Having heard the Buddha’s prophecy, their minds were purified and they leaped for joy with firm resolve;
the entire assembly gave rise to hearts of gladness, and each bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet in salutation.

Chapter Eight: The Prophecy for the Dragon Kings. *The Compendium of Father and Son Sūtra*, Chapter Eight: The Prophecy for the Dragon Kings. At that time, the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda, together with their retinue of nine hundred million dragon beings, having seen the various dragon maidens make offerings to the Tathāgata and receive their prophecies, felt their bodies and minds become serene. Attaining what they had never experienced before, they praised the Tathāgata:

"You have reached ultimate fulfillment in vast majesty, virtue, and unimpeded supernormal powers. You are able to know the thoughts in the minds of sentient beings; you hear and know all the deeds they perform, each one manifesting realization, with nothing that you do not fully comprehend."

Nevertheless, through the predominance of that Tathāgata’s great compassion, he may preach the Dharma without waiting for a request, or preach at an inappropriate time; all this is for the purpose of teaching and maturing sentient beings, so that they may eliminate the heat of afflictions and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.

When the Dharma is bestowed at random, it inevitably causes one to attain the fruit; even women whose minds are agitated and whose natures are dominated by lust, anger, and ignorance—though they may not comprehend the essential points of the Dharma upon hearing them—still receive the transformation and deliverance of the Tathāgata. If even those sixty koṭis of dragon girls obtained their prediction of enlightenment, how much more so should we not receive benefit?

When that dragon king had finished speaking thus, he conceived a sense of the rarity of encountering the World-Honored One. By means of his supernormal powers, he raised a great cloud of fragrance that filled Jambudvīpa, completely covering all the mountains and the great oceans. He rained down various fragrant waters and powdered sandalwood incense, the scent of which was wafted far throughout the entire Buddha-world.
Furthermore, in that city of Kapilavastu, red pearls rained down, accumulating to the height of the knees, extending sixty *yojana*s in length and breadth.

Moreover, throughout the Nyagrodha Grove, immeasurable *nāgendra* flowers were scattered everywhere; as they were scattered again and again, they transformed into a flower palace, its dimensions likewise spanning sixty *yojana*s.

The pillars were fashioned from alternating seven precious gems, and the ground was paved with *nala-kānta-maṇi* stones; these stones were soft and cool to the touch, a sight for all to behold, unlike anything found in the world.

Furthermore, ninety koṭis of flower garlands made of various jewels appeared, hanging down all around; additionally, robes of many colors and famous fabrics were suspended, as well as various skillfully crafted silk banners, fragrant garlands, jewel garlands, pearl garlands, and so forth, adorning the surroundings everywhere with exquisite purity and beauty.
Furthermore, countless treasuries of jewels surged forth, arranged in rows within the hall as an offering.
Moreover, there appeared supreme, priceless mani-jewels, fashioned into mirrors whose inner and outer surfaces were so translucent that they reflected one another without exception.
Everything up to the city of Kapilavastu, the great assembly gathered at that time, and their various offerings and sublime adornments—all were clearly reflected within that mirror.
Furthermore, there were ninety *koṭi* of dragon-horses, with exquisite and rare jewels serving as their bridles and bits, and countless jeweled bells chiming as they stepped forward.

Each of these dragon kings, having mounted his horse, circumambulated the Buddha three times in mid-air. They then performed immeasurable music from the dragon palaces and rained down various kinds of extraordinary and wonderful jewels, scattering them over the Tathāgata and the assembly of śrāvakas.

Having made these offerings, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet; gazing up at the World-Honored One, he did not for a moment turn his eyes away, and with the roots of merit and goodness he had accumulated, he made this vow: "May all sentient beings together attain the Way of the Buddha."
Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he praised him in verse:
"Having long cultivated the practices of loving-kindness, patience, and great compassion, You have achieved the adornment of the marks of a hundred merits.
Leaving home beyond that city of Kapilavastu, Your resolve remained firm in seeking the Unsurpassed Way."
For six years he demonstrated the practice of asceticism, subduing all non-Buddhist teachers without weariness;
proceeding directly to the Vajrāsana site of enlightenment, he universally bestowed the nectar-like Dharma upon all living beings.
In the past, the Tathāgata, the Teacher and Subduer, Abandoned the exquisite pleasures of the royal palace,
Shaved his crown hair and dwelt in the mountain forests, His mind indifferent to the world’s fleeting glory.
In the past, the Muni sacrificed his head and eyes; through the accumulation of merit, he fulfilled the causes for Bodhi.
If ordinary beings find no cause even upon hearing or seeing this, how much less could they emulate his ascetic practices?
As the Buddha once was the Sage of Forbearance, Who was unjustly harmed by King Kali;
Though his ears, nose, and limbs were severed, He gave rise to no anger, but remained joyful at heart.
At that time, there was a foolish brahmin who came to weigh his own flesh and fell down;
when he spoke of these difficult practices and ascetic austerities, we were filled with sorrow and distress upon hearing them.
For what reason does the Tathāgata not give rise to anger, but instead loves sentient beings as his own children?
Because those who harbor harmful intentions fall into the hells, the Compassionate Honored One is able to extend salvation to them.
The Tathāgata is endowed with unsurpassed wisdom; toward those who harm him, he does not retaliate.
Because he formerly cultivated vast causes for peace and happiness, his limbs have been restored as they were before.
We all give rise to pure faith and praise the Tathāgata’s true conduct;
just as that Muni benefits sentient beings, we all vow to swiftly ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the various dragon kings possessed firm faith and understanding and had made great vows, immediately emitted various rays of light from his face; these lights shone universally upward as far as the Brahma Heaven, and then re-entered through the crown of the Tathāgata’s head.
At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit joined his palms, knelt down, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is the natural law that when all Buddhas emit light, there must be a specific purpose for it."
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will skillfully expound this.
Then that Venerable One spoke these verses:
"How great is the Fearless Lion of the Śākyas! By what causes and conditions has he emitted this light?"
The Gate of Compassion extensively benefits all devas and humans; I pray that the Tathāgata will explain this for me.
These dragon kings along with their retinues, as well as those in this assembly, are all in solemn reverence;
we only hope that the Muni will vibrate his Brahma-voice and speak of this rare event of emitting light.
Who, within the Dharma of Śākyamuni, has first resolved upon the Great Mind to evoke such an auspicious omen?
Who is able to crush and destroy the armies of Māra, causing them all to flee in terror and despair?
Could it be that the host of nāgas, having practiced for a long time, have attained inexhaustible merits?
We pray to hear the cause and conditions for this manifested omen, so that our doubts may be severed and our minds purified.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"With my most supreme and excellent merit, And with the eight kinds of profound Brahma-voices, I speak what is true to benefit sentient beings;
You should listen attentively to the matter of emitting light."

These dragon kings possess profound and pure faith; they have prepared a great offering, rare in this world, with sincere hearts aspiring to realize the Buddha’s Bodhi for the sake of delivering all living beings.
Constantly observing the world with a heart of compassion, he causes all sentient beings everywhere to escape suffering and calamity;
never for a single moment has weariness arisen in his mind, as his firm and resolute diligence never regresses.
Cultivating pure śamatha, endowed with invincible power of wisdom, they dwell securely in the three gates of liberation: namely, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Having attained the Buddha’s unsurpassed, profound wisdom, He realizes that all phenomena are entirely empty and false;
With great compassion, he takes pity upon all sentient beings, Free from notions of enemy or kin, regarding them all with total equality.
After the passage of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they will successively attain Buddhahood and appear in the world,
all bearing the same name, Tathāgata Śāntamati, fully endowed with the ten titles, in lands of sublime purity.
He constantly preaches the nectar-like Dharma of non-self;
Free from all external paths and demonic adversaries, With skillful means he responds to the capacities of beings, Without contradicting worldly conventions while discoursing on the ultimate truth.
When these sentient beings have heard the Dharma, they realize that the self-nature of all phenomena is entirely empty.
Through great compassion and skillful means, he expounds the three vehicles; yet within the ultimate reality of the Dharma, there is nothing to be said.
This Dharma does not arise spontaneously; even if one seeks it, not even a fraction can be found.
Yet, there is not a single sentient being who, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, does not understand it.

By drinking the nectar-flavor of liberation, one is able to transcend birth, old age, death, as well as sorrow, lamentation, and the banner of self-conceit; all this is due to hearing the Brahma-voice of the Buddha.
The Śākya Sage, the fearless Holy Lion, Expounded the minds of the nāgas and answered their questions;
The Sons of the Buddha always follow the practice of wisdom, And swiftly attain the unsurpassed fruit of Bodhi.
The Tathāgata bestowed predictions upon those nāgas; having heard this, the assembly was filled with joy and celebration.
Each took refuge in the Honored Muni, their minds becoming tranquil within the Buddha-dharma.
