Chapter Nine: The Prophecy of the Kumbhāṇḍa Kings At that time, there were eighteen koṭis of kumbhāṇḍa kings within the assembly. Having witnessed the various asuras, garuḍas, and nāga kings making their offerings, they conceived a heart of joyful affection.

Furthermore, hearing the Tathāgata bestow prophecies upon them, they leaped for joy with unprecedented delight and spoke in unison in praise: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of the repetitive liturgical verses of praise found in the source text.*

“The Tathāgata has attained supreme wisdom; regarding all phenomena, he is free from doubt, without joy or anger, and does not give rise to discrimination. He is worthy of receiving the vast offerings of devas and humans. Just as the great ocean is deep and wide, full to the brim, unmoving and unswelling, serene and tranquil, so too are the merits of the Tathāgata.”
Then that Kumbhāṇḍa king, together with his retinue, each gave rise to a pure mind and offered worship.
By means of their supernormal powers, they manifested eighteen koṭis of jeweled canopies;
these jeweled canopies were exquisitely and superbly crafted, all adorned in successive layers with precious threads, namely canopies of golden thread, white [thread], and so forth.
There were canopies of silver thread, canopies of vaidūrya, canopies of crystal, canopies of red pearls, canopies of musāragalva pearls,
and canopies of aśmagarbha pearls; where canopies of gold thread hung with garlands of silver flowers,
canopies of silver thread hung with garlands of gold flowers, canopies of vaidūrya hung with garlands of crystal, and [canopies of] crystal...

There were canopies of lapis lazuli garlands and canopies of red pearls with mallet-stored pearl garlands; canopies of mallet-stored pearl garlands and canopies of red pearls with horse-stored pearl garlands;
and canopies of horse-stored pearl garlands with various jewel garlands, arranged in alternating patterns that were exceedingly delightful.
Furthermore, he miraculously manifested eighteen koṭis of exquisite chariots made of various jewels—namely, chariots made of gold, up to those composed of the horse-treasure jewel (*aśvaratna*).

Upon each of those chariots appeared eighteen koṭis of supreme and wonderful parasols; each parasol was marvelous and skillfully crafted, with a hundred ribs adorned with various jewels, having handles made either of pure gold or, in succession, even of *vaiḍūrya*. Beneath these parasols hung various flower garlands, ranging from garlands of golden flowers to those made of *maṇi* jewel beads. These parasols were further provided with nets fashioned from red pearls, intricately interlaced.

At that time, each of the Kumbhāṇḍa kings mounted their respective magnificent chariots adorned with various jewels, holding parasols and performing various musical offerings. In the midst of the sky, they circumambulated the Buddha three times and scattered seven-jeweled flowers over the Tathāgata;

having scattered them again and again, they descended from their chariots, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and stood to one side. Joining their palms toward the Buddha, they praised him in verse:
"The Sage, the Holy Lord, has appeared in the world, Like Mount Meru rising majestically above the great ocean."
Free from all sorrow and fear, unshakable and surging forth, They are able to receive such sublime offerings.
Constantly abiding in the samādhi of tranquility, They expound all dharmas without attachment.
Having abandoned the defilements of pride and arrogance, They observe that the world consists of nothing but names and concepts.
Knowing all phenomena to be like illusions and transformations, Just as one experiences sensual pleasure within a dream,
And like the moon in water whose essence is not real— The wise person should conduct such an investigation.
The city of the gandharvas is fundamentally non-existent; it cannot be found when sought in any direction or place.
One should know that it is spoken of merely by way of conventional designation; all worldly phenomena are just like this.
All the offerings we have made— jeweled chariots, jeweled parasols, jeweled canopies,
and various sounds of song and music— the Tathāgata regards them as being like echoes in a valley.
May I attain Buddhahood like the World-Honored One, And for the sake of sentient beings, preach the Dharma that is like an illusion;
May I cause them all to distance themselves from the causes of delusion and karma, And lead them all to realize the path of tranquil Bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the kumbhāṇḍas and others, immediately emitted a great radiance from his mouth.
When the bhikṣu Aśvajit beheld this light, he joined his palms toward the Buddha and asked him in verse:
"The Tamer’s manifestation of transformation is never without cause; Beholding this pure radiance, it is inconceivable."
At that time, the assembly, wishing to know its cause, Solely hoped that the Tathāgata would swiftly proclaim it.
Beholding this auspicious omen appearing from the Buddha’s face, All the devas and humans were filled with doubt.
May the Buddha, out of compassion for all sentient beings, Explain this rare event of emitting light.
Who today has resolved upon the Great Mind, delighting to hear the True Dharma from the Buddha?
Who has offered worship to the Buddha?
Please explain the various merits thereby obtained.
Who can master those conditioned formations and, in a single instant, be free from all faults?
Who realizes the gateway of the true nature and remains unmoved in their tranquil intention?
Who has attained the Way and subdued all demons?
Who extols the merits of the Buddha?
Who has severed delusions and transcended the three realms of existence, with all fetters and obscurations stilled and the mind serene?
The great assembly all gave rise to a mind of reverence, Awaiting the hearing of the Tathāgata’s subtle and wondrous voice:
"For what cause do you emit this pure radiance?
We pray that you resolve our doubts by explaining it in detail."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣu Aśvajit:
“Excellent, Aśvajit, that you ask about this meaning;
For the sake of benefiting the world, I shall now explain from where this light comes. You all should listen with single-minded attention.”
Now these hosts of kumbhāṇḍas, extensively performing acts of pure merit through offerings,
stand before me with palms joined, abiding securely in the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) with unmoving minds.
Through the power of wisdom, you have skillfully practiced cultivation; Arousing great compassion, you benefit all living beings.
Later, you shall be liberated from this body of the ghost realm, And will certainly be reborn in a supreme place.
He shall become the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Attending upon and serving all Tathāgatas;
Thoroughly understanding all dharmas without doubt, Like lighting a great torch in the midst of darkness.
In the future, passing through further koṭis of kalpas, you shall adorn and purify boundless Buddha-fields;
making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, you shall don the armor of diligence and cultivate all practices.
Benefiting and gathering in all sentient beings, he knew with certainty that he would become a Buddha;
and because he was born in such a region, he was thus named the Buddha Who Dispels Doubt.
He constantly proclaims the supreme Dharma of tranquility; Those who hear it purify their minds and leave all doubt behind.
All aspire to seek the Great Bodhi, To rescue and deliver all sentient beings to the further shore.
I have now answered your question, universally bringing peace of mind to all present in this assembly;
therefore, I bestow this prediction upon the kumbhāṇḍas that in a future age they shall become buddhas.

**Chapter Ten: The Prophecy Bestowed upon the Gandharva Kings** *The Sūtra of the Combined Collection of Father and Son, Chapter Ten: The Prophecy Bestowed upon the Gandharva Kings.* At that time, within the assembly, there were thirty-six koṭis of gandharva kings. Having witnessed the asuras, garuḍas, nāga retinues, kumbhāṇḍas, and others making offerings to the Tathāgata, and having further heard the bestowal of the prophecy of their attainment of buddhahood, they were filled with unprecedented joy and leaped for gladness. Furthermore, hearing the praise of the Tathāgata’s dharmatā—its primordial stillness, its purity and stainlessness, and the fact that not even the slightest phenomenon is manifested therein—they all developed profound faith and understanding for the sake of increasing the roots of goodness in sentient beings. Abandoning all stinginess and avarice, they immediately gave rise to the mind set on unsurpassed bodhi.

At that time, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, the Gandharva kings, by means of their supernatural powers, manifested thirty-six koṭis of great nāga-elephant kings named Airāvaṇa. Each elephant king had six tusks; upon each tusk were seven ponds; within each pond were seven lotus flowers; each lotus flower had a thousand petals; between each petal were seven celestial maidens; and each celestial maiden was further attended by seven servant girls.

Furthermore, upon the head of each dragon-elephant, he manifested thirty-six koṭis of exquisite parasols with nets of the seven precious gems, their jeweled garlands reflecting one another; moreover, each was covered by a jeweled canopy, with various flower garlands suspended everywhere throughout.

Within those lotuses, the goddesses performed songs and dances, played musical instruments, or recited verses (*gāthā*) praising the Buddha’s merits; some scattered powdered incense of *candana* and aloeswood, some scattered various kinds of exquisite celestial flowers, some scattered various kinds of superior and wonderful garments, and some scattered various ornaments for the body, such as earrings, bracelets, jeweled garlands, and golden belts. Some held various jeweled banners, multicolored pennants, and canopies, while others scattered various kinds of pure perfumed water that fell from the sky like rain. This mingled with the incense and flowers to form a fragrant mud that covered the entire city of Kapilavastu, sixty *yojanas* in extent; wherever the wind blew, its fragrance reached everywhere.

At that time, those Gandharva kings each mounted a great dragon-elephant king and vied with one another to play hundreds of thousands of exquisite musical instruments. Moving slowly through the air, they circled three times to the right. By means of their supernatural power, they caused the sounds of the music along with the preceding fragrant wind to pervade the trichiliocosm; all sentient beings therein who heard the music or encountered that fragrance attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Having completed his circumambulation of the Buddha in the air, that Gandharva king descended from his elephant and approached the Buddha’s presence. He circumambulated him three times more, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he praised him in verse:
“The Tathāgata is endowed with all sublime marks; Within the triple world, none can equal him.
He has liberated himself from the causes of affliction and birth-and-death, And has reached the ultimate end of the suffering of saṃsāra.”
Manifesting boundless great majestic power, Most rare among gods and humans,
Having accomplished the gate of tranquil liberation, No non-human being can disturb or agitate them.
The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the pure path; fundamentally there is nothing realized and nothing to be spoken.
The Buddha-nature is truly eternal and inherently serene; it is only through conventional truth that one makes provisional distinctions.
When future Buddhas appear in the world, they too shall abide in this Dharma:
that phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are empty by their very essence, devoid of an agent or a sovereign controller.
To know that self and others have nothing to do is to be a wise person in the world;
though all phenomena are mutually unaware of one another, the Buddha demonstrates activity within the unconditioned.
Just as a chariot is assembled from many parts, And each part does not know its own function,
Yet receives the name "chariot" only through its capacity for transport— The Buddha’s teaching on the mark of self is likewise so.
That Dharma has no dharma that can be taught or summoned; That Dharma has no dharma that can be contemplated;
That Dharma has no dharma that can bring about liberation; That Dharma has no dharma that can cause transformation.

Having understood this thus, the Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings, speaks according to worldly convention, revealing the gateway of conditioned phenomena; yet even that conventional characteristic is unattainable.
Through successive analysis of the nature of all phenomena, I enable those of shallow wisdom to eliminate their doubts:
All phenomena are without marks and without names; Ultimately they are without abiding and without action.
May we, in future ages, attain Buddhahood like that Honored Muni,
with bodies adorned by boundless merit, and may we always preach such supreme Dharma of ultimate truth.
For those wise ones who bring benefit and happiness to the world, as well as for all sentient beings with wrong views,
may they always give rise to such great compassion, causing them to emerge from the ocean of saṃsāric birth and death.
All sentient beings in this world suffering and distressed, Arise from crooked minds and false wisdom;
Like monkeys, they are restless and find no moment of peace— Only the Buddha’s great compassion can deliver them.
Relying on greed, hatred, delusion, and pride, they are constantly adrift upon the waves of consciousness;
repeatedly sinking and drowning in the ocean of suffering, only the Great Compassion of the Buddha can deliver them.
Sentient beings are deluded and lack the eye of wisdom; unaware of their own karma, they fall into evil realms.
Having forever lost the gateway to liberation for humans and devas, only the Buddha’s great compassion can rescue them.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the gandharva kings, immediately emitted a great radiance from his mouth, which universally illuminated the entire assembly.
Thereupon, the Venerable Bhikṣu Aśvajit, having beheld this light, joined his palms toward the Buddha and asked in verse:
“The Tathāgata now manifests this auspicious omen, Tranquilly emitting a great radiance everywhere.
The assembly looks at one another, all struck with wonder and doubt; Never before have they seen such a rare occurrence.”
Who, having been taken into the Buddha’s care, gives rise to great joy and is freed from all obstacles?
Now the Buddha emits this pure radiance, causing their power of faith and understanding to become firm.
Who is it that practices the Great Dharma, Without deviation from what the Buddha has taught?
Now the Buddha emits this pure radiance; He bestows empowerment and extends his protective mindfulness upon them.
This great assembly, filled with longing and thirst, Wishes to hear the Buddha explain the causes and conditions of the light;
With palms joined, they stand before the Buddha, Gazing upon his venerable countenance without a moment’s distraction.

The Tathāgata acts as the eye for the world; Free from all defilements and from sorrow and fear, With great compassion he takes pity on all living beings, Causing them to cast off the net of doubt so that their minds become pure.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣu Aśvajit:
“Excellent, Aśvajit, that you ask about this matter!
For the benefit of the world, so that all may cause their roots of goodness to increase, I now emit this radiance and bestow upon you this prediction.”
The Venerable Aśvajit, the great bhikṣu, having heard the Buddha grant permission to explain the reason for the light,
rejoiced with palms joined and undistracted mind, hoping for the sequential discourse of the Brahma-like voice.
"The Gandharva King raises offerings, For the sake of hearing the true and pure Great Dharma.
This Dharma relies solely upon the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); Its original self-nature is without increase or decrease.
If a person grasps at signs and makes distinctions, That [Dharma] is like a phantom and cannot be apprehended."
This Dharma is neither real nor unreal; because the nature of phenomena is empty, the Buddha has nothing to teach.
Having made such offerings as these, one shall in a future life become a Śākyamuni;
this shall be one's final body in saṃsāra, as one advances in pure conduct with a mind free from indolence.
Traveling from one buddha-field to another, Serving as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
And transforming and liberating beings by the nayuta, One fulfills the fruit and attains the state of a Buddha free from dust.
That Buddha Viraja appeared in the world, Abiding for a lifespan of *nayuta* eons;
He constantly taught that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, And was further able to manifest all-encompassing wisdom.
Thus, the names of those various Buddhas, the duration of their stay in the world during the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma,
and their preaching of the Dharma to transform and benefit all sentient beings, are all identical to those of the previous Buddhas, without any difference.
Aśvajit, because you asked about the causes and conditions of the light, I have thus briefly explained those merits;
in this way, as they successively attain Buddhahood, they shall subdue countless tens of billions of heavenly Māras.
Once the Gandharva King had received his prediction, the assembly was freed from doubt and their hearts were filled with joy;
they all took refuge in the Honored Muni and stood to one side with palms joined.

Chapter Eleven: The Prophecy of the Yakṣa Kings. *The Compendium of Father and Son Sūtra*, Chapter Eleven: The Prophecy of the Yakṣa Kings. At that time, there were eighty koṭis of great yakṣa kings within the assembly. Seeing those asura kings, up to the gandharva kings, making extensive offerings to the Tathāgata, and further hearing the World-Honored One bestow prophecies upon them, they leaped for joy with unprecedented delight. With reverence and respect, they conceived the thought that such an encounter was difficult to find. They praised the profound and far-reaching wisdom of the Tathāgata; regarding the Dharma he taught, their minds attained understanding and entry, giving rise to deep love and joy, and developing pure faith. By means of their supernormal powers, they manifested vast and exquisite offerings, which were no different from the offerings previously made by the asura kings.
Then the Yakṣa King, having made his offerings, circumambulated the Buddha three times and stood to one side. With palms joined toward the Buddha, he praised him with these verses:
"O Lion of the Śākyas, peerless among men, Possessing great supernormal powers and wisdom, As deep and vast as the ocean, beyond measure— Therefore, I now prostrate my head at your feet."
Mount Sumeru may be measured, and the limits of the blazing conflagration at the end of an eon may be known;
yet the Buddha’s power of wisdom is subtle and inconceivable—none can fathom its ultimate extent.

Throughout all worlds of the past, present, and future, among all classes of sentient beings in every realm of existence, the Buddha knows fully their performance of wholesome and unwholesome deeds; none can equal him in this regard.
Some delight in dwelling in forest hermitages, practicing the conduct of tranquility to eliminate clamor;
according to their various modes of cultivation and differing natures, the Buddha knows them all thoroughly, with none equal to him.

Whether they possess the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion, or engage in various evil deeds such as pride and envy—whether these are present in equal measure or one predominates—the Buddha knows them all completely; none can equal him.
Some may lose their way on the Right Path, sinking into the retribution of suffering with no end in sight;
others possess faith and understanding and practice in accordance with the Dharma—the Buddha knows them all completely, for none can equal him.
Sentient beings delight in performing various evil deeds; those karmic actions follow them and do not leave.
When they reach the time of death in terror and fear, only the Tathāgata can deliver them.
Some maintain pure precepts and go to the celestial palaces; others create black karma and undergo manifold sufferings.
The retribution for good and evil is without error in principle; only the Tathāgata knows and sees them all.
Some, possessing wisdom and seeking liberation, Have gone forth within the Buddha’s Dharma;
Delighting in cultivating the Noble Path for the benefit of sentient beings, They have attained the realization of the unconditioned bliss of nirvana.
Furthermore, there are foolish persons who, though they have left the household life and dwell relying upon the Dharma of the Tathāgata, are unable to understand the profound Dharma;
due to their lack of wisdom, they instead give rise to slander.
They harbor contempt for the Buddha's teachings and create immeasurable causes and conditions for suffering;
at the end of their lives, they fall into the great hells, and when the kalpa ends, they are reborn again in other realms of misery.
If a person possesses true faith and a resolute mind, delights in hearing the True Dharma and is able to protect it,
thoroughly understands that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, and is free from all marks without attachment.
Knowing that the world is not solid, and that this body is like an illusion or an echo,
one constantly benefits all beings through compassionate vows, never regressing from the Buddha’s bodhi.
I now praise the Buddha’s merits, which are unsurpassed by anything in all the worlds;
dedicating this slight virtue to sentient beings, may we together attain the path of Buddhahood in the future.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the yakṣa kings and others, immediately emitted a great radiance from his mouth, which illuminated the buddha-field everywhere.
At that time, the bhikṣu Aśvajit, having seen this light, joined his palms toward the Buddha and asked in verse:
"How great! O Most Victorious One, Honored among Two-legged Beings, You have suddenly emitted a pure light, inconceivable.
This rare light does not arise without cause; Its radiance illuminates the world, surpassing the full moon."
Now this entire assembly stands with palms joined, In unison extolling the Buddha’s virtues;
We pray that the Tathāgata will vibrate his Brahma-voice And explain the reason for this radiance.
Who has given rise to pure faith in the Buddha?
Who has awakened to and entered the truly pure Dharma?
Who has made their bodhicitta firm and steadfast?
I only pray that the Tathāgata will explain this in detail.
The Great Compassionate Lord has appeared in the world, able to sever the dense web of doubts of all living beings;
when the devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans hear it, their hearts will give rise to great joy and celebration.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣu Aśvajit:

“Excellent, great bhikṣu Aśvajit! That you are able to inquire about such a meaning— Through this light, you have made a request for the benefit of gods and humans, Causing them all to abide securely in the vision of reality.”
That Yakṣa King has presented offerings, increasing his roots of virtue through superior seeing and hearing;
therefore, I emit this pure radiance, and now I shall grant him the prophecy of attaining Buddhahood.
Thus, that host of yakṣas fully understands that all phenomena arise from conditions;
by the power of their vows they have assumed these bodies, and their minds always abide securely on the path to enlightenment.
Able to observe with wisdom and skill, Knowing that the aggregates, bases, and elements are all false and illusory,
One transcends the causes of cyclic existence and its suffering, Just as a lotus flower is unsullied by water.
The causes and conditions that defile oneself and others are blended together; one awakens to all things as being like illusions.
Observing that the intrinsic nature of form is likewise empty, one realizes the principle of unconditioned nirvana.
If one can awaken to the emptiness of all phenomena, And likewise penetrate signlessness and wishlessness,
Then regarding these three doors of liberation, One will observe them with impartiality and universal clarity, free from obstruction.
When one can perceive that the nature of wisdom is fundamentally empty, what objective realm could there possibly exist?
To realize that both mind and its objects are entirely non-existent—this is the fulfillment of the practice of bodhi.
When the devas and humans hear this Dharma, Joy arises in their hearts such as they have never known before;
Each, with faith and understanding, practices in accordance with the Dharma, Gradually able to cultivate all-encompassing wisdom.
Thus, these hosts of Guhyaka Yakṣas, being able to offer worship with a pure mind,
shall later cast off this body of an evil rebirth and be born among the devas to experience sublime bliss.
In a future age, they shall behold immeasurable billions of Buddhas;
the Tathāgata named Śāntamati shall dwell in the world for an exceedingly long lifespan.
He transforms and guides countless śrāvakas, Like stars appearing in the void;
Those endowed with all wisdom are born therein, In a land adorned and pure, where there is no suffering.
All people and non-people in the world listen to what the Buddha speaks without weariness;
they all give rise to courageous and pure minds, and are liberated from the fetters of afflictions.

**Chapter Twelve: The Prophecy of the Kinnara King** At that time, within the assembly, there were eight *koṭis* of Kinnara kings. The foremost among them was named Mahādruma (Great Tree). Seeing all the asura kings, down to the hosts of yakṣas, making extensive offerings before the Buddha and hearing the Tathāgata bestow upon them their respective prophecies, they were struck with wonder and doubt. Exclaiming that it was unprecedented, they thought:

"If the Buddha says that all the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) of the world exist merely as provisional names and do not have even the slightest portion that can be seen by sentient beings, then neither Buddhas nor Bodhisattvas can be seen either."

Why is it that the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, bestows sequential predictions upon the devas and nāgas, and further causes immeasurable sentient beings to be transformed and delivered? How is it that they travel from one buddha-field to another, paying homage to the Tathāgatas for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, extensively cultivating all practices until they attain the path of Buddhahood, endowed with the primary and secondary marks, with the adornments of their lands, the duration of their lifespans in kalpas, and the True and Semblance Dharma, until finally, when their conditions are exhausted, they enter parinirvāṇa?
"Since you have stated that all phenomena are entirely empty and quiescent, how can the matter of bestowing a prophecy be established?
At that time, the Great Tree Kinnara King gave rise to this doubt, unable to reach a definitive understanding. He joined his palms toward the Buddha and asked in verse:
"I have heard the Tathāgata speak thus, Yet in my mind I harbor a doubt regarding the Buddha’s wondrous wisdom."
Having already spoken of emptiness, you further grant a prophecy; this meaning is so profound that it cannot be fully comprehended.
Again, you say that the dharma-realm is fundamentally empty and quiescent, yet you speak of it as being like the moon appearing in water.
Having spoken of emptiness and stillness, you again manifest form; this meaning is so profound it cannot be fathomed.
How is it that while all phenomena are fundamentally unborn, you further speak of those who joyfully seek bodhi?
Since it is said that there is no arising, how can there be seeking? This meaning is extremely profound and cannot be understood.
How is it that all phenomena are fundamentally inexhaustible, yet you further speak of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa?
I now inquire of the Muni-Bhagavān, for this meaning is profound and beyond my comprehension:
How is it that all phenomena are like illusions, yet you further say that one who dies here may be reborn in heaven?
Since it is said that all things are like illusions, how can there be any arising? This meaning is extremely profound and difficult to comprehend.
If all phenomena have no basis, why then do you speak of relying upon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra)?
Since it is said that there is no basis, why rely on a person? This meaning is extremely profound and cannot be understood.
How can it be that the world has no creator, yet one can still speak of someone capable of severing all delusions?
Since it is said that there is no basis for the cessation of the unconditioned, this meaning is so profound that it cannot be understood.
How is it that while the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, one further speaks of attaining liberation through the contemplation of emptiness?
Since you have already spoken of emptiness, what further is there to contemplate? This meaning is so profound that it cannot be understood.
How can all phenomena be momentary in their cessation, yet also be said to be eternal and non-ceasing?
Since you have stated that there is both transformation and occasional constancy, this meaning is so profound it cannot be understood.
How can it be that meritorious karma is not an accumulation, yet it is said that through cultivation one achieves *bodhi*?
Since it is said that there is no accumulation, how could anything be established? This meaning is extremely profound and cannot be understood.
How can it be that while all phenomena are ineffable, one is still told that slandering them leads to falling into the evil realms?
Since it is said that there is no teaching, how can slander arise? This meaning is so profound that it cannot be understood.
It is what has been proclaimed by the Unconquerable One; its various distinctions are difficult to comprehend.
With the pure Buddha-eye illuminating the world, he universally bestows the flavor of ambrosia upon all living beings.
There is no one else capable of resolving for us the matters we have doubted as above;
only the Tathāgata can sever them. Therefore, I prostrate to the Omniscient One.
At that time, in order to resolve the doubts of the Great Kinnara King Druma, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"O Kinnara King, as for what you have asked: Since all is empty, upon what basis can a prophecy be bestowed?"
Because he has realized that the nature of phenomena is fundamentally empty, The Tathāgata has granted him this prophecy.
For what reason is this said?
If all phenomena possessed a real intrinsic nature, They would neither decrease nor increase, And would never undergo change at any time.

Just as a round mirror suspended in space manifests forms and images due to the conditions of external light, so too, O King of Kinnaras, you should know that the self-nature is pure from the very beginning.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is stainless and eternally serene; it is without agitation or transformation.
Observe the causes of meritorious karma through making offerings: in what phenomenon does their characteristic reside?
One should know that the dharma-realm is fundamentally quiescent; the wise observe that phenomena cannot be apprehended.
Ordinary worldlings who grasp at signs are unable to understand this through doubt;
you ask about the fundamental non-arising of all phenomena, yet speak again of generating the mind to seek the Buddha-way?
Kinnara King, you should know that the wondrous wisdom of the Ten Powers is inconceivable.
Foolish beings are submerged within the three realms, giving rise to attachment toward all objects of desire;
because they constantly give rise to inverted minds, they undergo the various sufferings of birth and death.
From of old they have not heard the True Dharma; even if they have heard it, they do not understand it.
May they be established in the midst of true wisdom, so that they may gradually seek to attain the fruit of Bodhi.
You ask: "If all phenomena are fundamentally without cessation, why is there the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata?
It is to shatter the eternalist views of sentient beings that [it is taught] there is not even the slightest phenomenon that is permanent.
You ask why all phenomena are like illusions, yet harbor doubts because you see those born in the heavens?
It is to transform ordinary and ignorant beings who, relying on what they possess, give rise to arrogance.
You ask how all phenomena are without support, yet you see them as depending upon a spiritual friend?
If one does not rely upon a teacher of the Dharma, there will ultimately be no escape from the world.
You ask how it is that while all phenomena lack a sovereign, one perceives an agent in the world?
One should observe that a chariot is composed of many parts, yet it performs the functional activity of transporting a load.
In order to transform those sentient beings who are attached to a self, as well as those who cling to "mine," I have taught them that [the self] is incapable [of such clinging];
therefore, it is merely a conventional designation and a mental construct.
You ask how all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, yet you speak of attaining liberation through the contemplation of emptiness.
Because of that mind of conceptualization and attachment, one cannot comprehend the meaning of emptiness.
You ask how all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) perish moment by moment, yet you also say that the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) does not perish?
This is to destroy the attachment of sentient beings who conceive the notion of purity regarding what is impure.
For example, when gazing from afar at a mirage, the thirsty person rushes toward it seeking water;
all such things arise from the conceptualization of false imagination—know that the substance of water cannot be found.
In the place of a mirage there is fundamentally no water; within the purity of intrinsic nature there is fundamentally no defilement.
Yet, due to the inverted minds of those deluded beings, they are bound and entangled by craving.
"You ask about all phenomena being ineffable, yet you also say that those who slander fall into evil realms?
When fools hear this, they harbor fear and doubt; when the wise hear it, their obstacles are removed."
All phenomena in the world are fundamentally empty and quiescent; Those lacking wisdom falsely conceptualize them and cling to them as a self.
If such people hear that all phenomena are empty, They will give rise to the fearful notion of annihilation.
If a person slanders the Dharma of emptiness, it is entirely due to their attachment to the signs of a self and a person;
they are like one who attempts to bind empty space, increasing their ignorance and falling into the evil realms.
Some say that virtuous karma leads to rebirth among the devas, while others are born in the human realm to experience happiness;
yet the agent is not real, for karma does not perish—it is like the objects in a dream, created solely by the mind.
Know that all realms of existence are like dreams; because of delusion regarding reality, one does not perceive them as such.
Within a dream, how can there be coming or going? Yet the ignorant falsely claim these to be real objects.
Although I speak of the karma created by beings, if one searches throughout the ten directions, no creator is to be found.
Just as a violent wind blows upon tree branches, fire is produced through their mutual friction.
Yet that wind and wood have no thought, nor do they say, "I am able to produce fire."
Because these two are mutually dependent, fire arises; likewise, there is originally no creator.
You ask how the fruit of Bodhi can be attained when meritorious karma does not accumulate.
Just as there may be a person in the world who is a hundred years old, though time has passed, there is no accumulation of years.
You ask how all phenomena can be inexhaustible, yet why do you further say that karma can be exhausted?
Those who contemplate the principle of emptiness speak of it as infinite; yet within the realm of worldly convention, it has its limits.
Although I expound upon the true reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), beings seek it outwardly due to their inversions;
because the conditions for the obstacles of karma and delusion are so deep, they cannot comprehend this ultimate dharma (*paramārtha-dharma*).
Kinnara King, you should know this: well-abiding in this ultimate truth, all characteristics are but a single characteristic;
one who has thoroughly mastered it is said to be "without characteristics."
The practice of all Bodhisattvas consists in the fact that all phenomena are without action;
this is the dhāraṇī-gate of the syllable A, by which one enters into the understanding of all phenomena.
Kinnara King, you should know that all phenomena are fundamentally quiescent;
this is the teaching on the gateway of the signless dhāraṇī, which is entered through understanding by means of the letter A.
Kinnara King, you should know that all phenomena are without discrimination;
this is called the gate of the dhāraṇī of equality, entered and understood through the gateway of the letter A.
Kinnara King, you should know that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature;
this is the teaching on the gateway of the pure dhāraṇī, which is entered through and understood by means of the letter A.
Kinnara King, you should know that all phenomena are inexhaustible;
this is the teaching on the gateway of the dhāraṇī that transcends obstacles, entered through the gateway of the letter A.
Kinnara King, you should know that all phenomena are beyond conceptual thought;
this teaching of the dhāraṇī gateway of the true nature is entered through and understood by means of the letter A.
Kinnara King, you should know: all phenomena have no destination;
this is called the gateway of the dhāraṇī of liberation, entered through the gateway of the letter A.
Kinnara King, you should know that all phenomena are fundamentally unmoving;
this is called the gateway to the dhāraṇī of realization and purity, entered through understanding by means of the letter-gateway A.
Kinnara King, you should know that all phenomena are spoken of as mere provisional names;
this teaching is the gateway to the true dhāraṇī, entered through and understood by means of the letter A.
Kinnara King, you should know that all phenomena are unattainable;
this is called the Dharani-gate of the Departure from Characteristics, which is entered through and understood by means of the letter A.
Kinnara King, you should know that all phenomena are free from conceptual thought;
this is called the gateway of meditative concentration and dhāraṇī, which is entered through and understood by means of the letter A.
This Dharma is neither a view nor an antidote; seeking those two characteristics, they are found to be non-existent.
Realizing that there is neither characteristic nor name, one is then able to fulfill the path to enlightenment.
If a phenomenon is visible or subject to antidotes, that phenomenon is neither real nor equal;
the intrinsic nature of such phenomena transcends verbal expression, being like space with which it has no resemblance.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has no manifold characteristics; It is neither a single characteristic nor diverse characteristics.
It possesses neither the characteristic of cold nor the characteristic of heat, Just as a reflection in a mirror cannot be apprehended;
It possesses neither the characteristic of curvature nor the characteristic of straightness, And furthermore, it is devoid of the characteristics of light and darkness.
Far removed from the marks of male and female, this is called entering into the understanding of the true mark.
It is without flattery, without deception, and without agitation; it has no marks of expansion or contraction, nor even subtle marks.
It is without marks of anger or joy, nor marks of cowardice, nor marks of arising and ceasing.
There is no mark of entering nor of emerging, Nor any mark of advancing or retreating;
It is neither the mark of waking nor of sleeping, And further, it lacks the marks of past, future, or present.
It is not the mark of the eye nor of gazing, Nor is it blindness, sightlessness, or cataracts.
Neither compliant nor rigid, neither concealed nor manifest,
neither moving nor still— it is free from all conceptual proliferation and is eternally serene.
The wise should contemplate in this way: this is called knowing the realm of the Buddha.
For the sake of taming the world, they provisionally differentiate the ineffable Dharma;
by thoroughly understanding this ultimate truth, they are able to penetrate all phenomena.

At that time, having heard how the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had resolved all doubts and having heard the exposition of the gateways of the dhāraṇī syllables, the Great Tree Kinnara King attained profound understanding and was filled with great joy at such an unprecedented experience.

By means of his supernormal powers, he manifested eight koṭis of exquisite pavilions, so ingeniously and wonderfully crafted that some rested upon mountain peaks, some relied upon groves of trees, and some were manifested atop lotus flowers. All these multi-storied pavilions were adorned with canopies made of the seven precious gems suspended above them; each was further embellished in succession with various jeweled banners, streamers, precious curtains, and flower garlands.

These eighty million kinnara kings each ascended their respective pavilions, circumambulated [the Buddha] three times to the right in the midst of the air, and further scattered exquisite flowers from both land and water upon the Buddha.

Having finished scattering [the flowers], he immediately descended from the multi-storied pavilion and went to where the Buddha was. He circumambulated him three times, gazed upon the Honored One’s countenance without averting his eyes for even a moment, and stood to one side with palms joined in single-minded devotion, contemplating the immeasurable, most supreme merits accumulated by the Tathāgata in the past and present.
The Buddha, having known this, emitted pure light from his mouth.
At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit Bhikṣu, beholding this sign, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and asked in verse:
“The Tathāgata now emits a radiant light, Pure, wondrous, inconceivable, and most rare.”
At that time, the assembly gazed intently upon the compassionate countenance, as if beholding the full moon through the parting of clouds.
Who among those present before the World-Honored One now delights in hearing the most supreme and subtle Dharma?
Having understood it well through true wisdom, who has emitted this radiance to bestow their seal of approval?
Who was it that first resolved upon Bodhicitta, To move the Buddha’s empowerment to manifest such auspicious signs?
We pray you will explain the causes and conditions of this light, To subdue all non-Buddhists and cause them to give rise to faith.
At that time, all those gathered in the great assembly, each with joyful hearts and pure minds, hoped to hear the pure nectar-like voice;
having heard it, they shall practice according to the Buddha's teachings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the venerable bhikṣu Aśvajit:
“Venerable Aśvajit has asked about this meaning; Listen with a single mind, free from other distractions, As I now bestow upon that kinnara The prophecy of his future attainment of Buddhahood.”
The questions he has asked are extremely difficult to understand; they are all for the sake of the benefit and happiness of all the world.
Now, in order to sever his doubts and cause him to dwell securely in the Buddha-dharma, I shall explain them.
This Great Tree Kinnara King, together with his retinue of eighty million followers,
through the cause of pure merit arising from their offerings, shall at the end of life be reborn in the heavens.
Successively enjoying sublime pleasures within the heavens for ninety *koṭi* years,
they attained the five supernormal powers as they wished and drew near to serve Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Having traversed nayutas of lands, constantly proclaiming the supreme Dharma of ultimate truth,
he has transformed and liberated nayutas of sentient beings, attaining the path of unsurpassed bodhi.
He is titled the Tathāgata Immeasurable Light; the name of his eon and his land are all identical.
This lion among men, honored for his ten powers, is fully endowed with boundless great wisdom.
All the bodhisattvas in that land have fully perfected their cultivation of roots of goodness;
there are none who seek the two vehicles, for all are in their final birth before attaining buddhahood.

Thus, that assembly of bodhisattvas, each harboring compassionate vows to benefit all living beings, is able to act as a source of illumination for the world; hereafter, they shall successively attain Buddhahood.
Those lands are supremely adorned, free from all impurity and affliction;
like the celestial palaces of Tuṣita, they enjoy purity and know contentment.
All faults and the eight states of no-leisure have never even been heard of by name;
sentient beings dwell therein in peace and security, constantly partaking of the flavor of the Dharma and the joy of meditative concentration.
How great is the Sugata, the God among Gods! Having bestowed upon the Kinnara the prophecy of Buddhahood, the assembly, having heard it, felt their minds become serene;
they prostrated themselves and paid homage to the Unsurpassed One.

13. Chapter on the Prophecy for the Deva Ratnamālā. *The Compendium of Father and Son Sūtra*, Chapter Thirteen: The Prophecy for the Deva Ratnamālā. At that time, there were eight koṭis of devas named Ratnamālā within the assembly. Seeing the great offerings made by the asuras, up to the kiṃnaras, within the Buddha’s assembly, and hearing the Tathāgata bestow prophecies upon them, their hearts were filled with supreme joy at this unprecedented occurrence.

At that time, the sons of the gods, in order to make offerings to the Buddha, gave rise to a courageous and resolute mind. They circled the city of Kapilavastu for a distance of sixty *yojanas* and rained down *mandārava* flowers from the midst of the sky; they fell in profusion until they accumulated to the height of the knees. Having made these offerings, they circumambulated the Buddha three times, stood to one side with palms joined toward him, and praised him in verse:
“O Honored One of Great Compassion and the Ten Powers, Who is able to save all sentient beings, Whose faculties are tranquil and who radiates light— Therefore, I pay homage to the Sage among Sages.”
The devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans, who have conceived love and joy for the Buddha’s Dharma—
therefore, I now take refuge in and pay homage to the Supreme Muni, the Great Teacher.
The Tathāgata appears in the world, Like the full moon among the myriad stars;
His body is adorned with boundless merit and wisdom, And sentient beings never tire of beholding him.
Fully endowed with various pure dharmas, With the six supernormal powers, the three knowledges, and the four fearlessnesses,
And the eighteen unique qualities beyond measure— Therefore, I now take refuge in you and pay homage.
The thirty-two marks are all perfectly complete, And the eighty secondary signs exquisitely adorn his body;
Majestic and towering like the banner of the Lord of Devas, Therefore, I now take refuge and pay homage to him.
Having accomplished the most supreme samādhi, Able to sever all fetters of saṃsāra,
Subduing countless billions of māra armies, He dwells serenely with an unmoving mind.
The Tathāgata’s power of wisdom is firm and steadfast; He constantly proclaims the true Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
He is extensively able to transform and benefit all humans and devas, Causing them all to transcend to the other shore.
The Lion of the Śākyas, supreme among men, who has shattered all false views and heterodox arguments—
may I likewise become like the World-Honored One, preaching the Dharma to bring about liberation from the darkness of ignorance.

Transcending the world, you have attained perfect enlightenment; You constantly give rise to the four immeasurable minds, Compassionately gathering and sustaining all sentient beings, So that together they may realize the unsurpassed path of Bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the deep thoughts in the minds of the devaputras, immediately emitted a great radiance from his mouth.
When the Venerable Aśvajit Bhikṣu beheld this sign, he joined his palms toward the Buddha and asked him in verse:
“The Muni has manifested this rare sign; the assembly, having gazed upon it, their hearts are filled with joy.”
Each one reverently beholds Your face of great compassion; We pray that You will explain the reason for emitting these rays of light.
The Tathāgata now emits this pure radiance; Surely it shall bring about vast and beneficial deeds.
We prostrate to the Unsurpassed Honored One; We only hope that Your profound voice will grant us instruction.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣu Aśvajit:
“Excellent, Aśvajit, that you ask about this meaning; I shall now explain it to you in detail.
For the benefit and happiness of all humans and devas, I bestow upon the deva Mālinī the prophecy of Buddhahood.”
If the Tathāgata did not speak because of being requested, there would be no means by which to predict the destinies of his disciples;
by answering your question, he has stilled the doubts of the multitude, and with those doubts dispelled, their minds abide in peace.
The deity Ratnamālā, with a pure intention, extended offerings to me;
from this, she was successively reborn among the various heavens, constantly surrounded by hundreds of thousands of devaputras.
Furthermore, taking exquisite celestial incense and flowers, He made offerings to immeasurable koṭis of Buddhas;
In the presence of those Buddhas he gave rise to a pure mind, Delighting in the practice of the bodhisattva path.
Having thus made offerings with such diligence, they shall further perform the work of a Buddha in the future;
they will attend upon nayutas of World-Honored Ones and constantly recite verses in praise of the Buddhas' virtues.
By extensively cultivating pure conduct in accordance with reality, one attains the firm body of Nārāyaṇa;
born during the Kalpa of Joy, one fully realizes and perfects all-encompassing wisdom.
He shall be named the Tathāgata Supreme Flower Banner, possessing a great reputation unequaled by any;
together with eighty million other sons of heaven, they shall all become Buddhas within the same eon.
In that Buddha-field there are no hells, Nor the realms of hungry ghosts or animals, Nor the arrogance of asuras;
It is free from the eight difficulties and all perilous sufferings.
The buddha-fields of those sons of gods shall all be like the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
their lands will be rich, blissful, and universally adorned, and their lifespans will all be similarly long.
Since even the name of the evil realms does not exist in that land, how much less could there be those who commit evil deeds?
Each sentient being follows the practice of the Dharma, all abiding in pure conduct free from contention.
The sentient beings to be converted are boundless, exceeding in number the sands of the Ganges;
when that Buddha appears in the world, he constantly proclaims the supreme Dharma of ultimate truth.
Thus, having completed his work of transformation and returned to quiescence, he widely distributed his relics to erect stūpas and shrines;
each relic was supremely inconceivable, and within them all were present the physical marks of the Buddha’s body.
Each extolled the Buddha’s merits, dwelling in mid-air and manifesting spiritual transformations;
they taught and transformed immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to resolve upon supreme bodhicitta.
By the power of skillful means of the Muni endowed with the ten powers, he bestowed the prophecy of enlightenment upon those devaputras;
when the great assembly heard the Buddha’s words, they dwelt in right reflection with minds serene.

**Chapter Fourteen: The Prophecy of the Four Great Heavenly Kings** At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, together with their retinues of ninety thousand devaputras, all witnessed the various asura kings, up to the gods of the Jewel Necklace (*ratnāvalī*), each making offerings to the World-Honored One. Furthermore, hearing that they were granted the prophecy of attaining Buddhahood, their hearts were filled with great joy at such an unprecedented occurrence. Beholding the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they conceived deep reverence; desiring liberation within the Buddha-dharma, they gave rise to a courageous and vigorous mind, practicing with diligent application.
It is, for example, like a person who boards a clay boat and enters a swift current, wishing to reach the opposite shore.
That person immediately reflects:
"This clay vessel is inherently not solid; it will soon be destroyed. I must cross quickly, exerting effort to seek deliverance, so that I may escape this peril."
The four Great Kings and the various devaputras were weary of and terrified by birth and death, seeking swift deliverance with such courageous resolve.

At that time, the four Great Kings and the devaputras, in order to make offerings to the Buddha, used their supernormal powers to instantly manifest ninety thousand jeweled canopies. Interspersed with myriad colors and adorned with various precious gems, they were vast, magnificent, and rare in the world—namely, canopies of red pearls, mani-jewels, lapis lazuli, diamond-gems, and yellow gold. Having manifested these various jeweled canopies, they circled the Buddha three times in mid-air.
They further manifested ninety thousand celestial musical instruments, which again circled three times in mid-air, producing exquisite sounds of music as an offering.

Furthermore, they rained down *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, scattering them over the Buddha; having scattered them, they scattered them again, circumambulated the Buddha three times, stood to one side, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and praised him with these verses:
"Homage to the Honored One among bipeds, The savior of the world, who has abandoned Excitement and lethargy, As well as desire, flattery, and deceit."
Able to sever all fetters of existence, To uproot the poisonous thorns of the sense-faculties,
To strike down the banner of pride, And to shatter the darkness of ignorance;
The four elements are well-harmonized, Free from the impurities of excrement and urine.
Not struck by poison, the nine apertures are ever pure;
liberated from the bonds of affliction, they forever reach the end of all suffering.
Even those who are stubborn and difficult to transform, the Muni skillfully gathers and sustains.
We, the devas and humans, have all come to the presence of the Buddha;
gazing upon the Buddha’s merit, we find it beyond the reach of praise.
Regarding the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—
Only the Buddha can realize and know it, penetrating it without obstruction.
That suchness, the limit of reality, is the support of all phenomena;
yet when foolish people even hear of it, they are like deer terrified of a hunter.
Sentient beings grasp at various signs, unable to penetrate the nature of phenomena;
they give rise to the four kinds of inversions, which constitute the conduct of saṃsāra.
The Buddha fully realizes the nature of phenomena and views the world as an empty fist.
The aggregates are empty from the very beginning; the sense bases and elements are likewise so.
Whether phenomena or non-phenomena, they are spoken of by means of names;
yet regarding all such phenomena, the Buddha has never uttered a word.
Just as a great illusionist conjures various forms and images,
which in reality have no master and exist only as provisional designations,
so too are the aggregates, the sense bases, and the eighteen elements.
All arise from illusion and delusion; their essential nature is not solid.
It is like a skilled painter who creates the image of a woman, with every limb complete and every feature perfectly beautiful.
These marks do not exist as reality; they merely deceive the eyes of the foolish.
The wise understand them well: the dharma-realm is fundamentally equal.
Those who have skillfully entered the Buddha-dharma harbor no doubt regarding this.
Just as an amra fruit placed within one's own palm,
so does the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom illuminate all classes of sentient beings;
he turns the most supreme wheel of Dharma, causing them to attain awakening and understanding.
"May I, when I attain Buddhahood, likewise preach such a Dharma,
transforming all sentient beings so that they together achieve unsurpassed enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the devaputras, immediately emitted a great radiance from his face, universally illuminating the entire assembly.
Having beheld this sign, the Venerable Bhikṣu Aśvajit joined his palms toward the Buddha and asked in verse:
“O Great Sage, Unsurpassed Honored One, For what reason do you manifest this auspicious omen?”
This must surely have a cause and condition; we pray that you will explain it for us.
Now these kings of the devas, along with their retinues of sons of gods, seeing the Buddha emit this pure light, have all given rise to doubt and confusion.
Who has resolved upon the Great Mind? Who shall receive the prediction of enlightenment?
Who now subdues the various Māras?
We pray that you will explain this for us.
Who was it that made such vast offerings before the Buddha,
whose faculties were so well-subdued, and who thus received this manifestation of the Buddha’s auspicious signs?
Could it be that the World-Honored Buddha has bestowed a prophecy upon him and the various devas?
May the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings speak, so that all who hear may rejoice;
may all sentient beings bring every benefit and purpose to maturity,
seeking to realize great enlightenment, equal and no different from the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣu Aśvajit:
“Aśvajit, great bhikṣu, you have asked well about such a matter.
I shall now emit a radiance and reveal it clearly for you.”
Those nine hundred million devaputras all came to my presence and explained the causes and conditions of this light;
I then conferred upon them the prediction of their attainment of Buddhahood.
These various devaputras have for a long time encountered and served many Buddhas.
Thoroughly realizing the emptiness of all phenomena, he spoke this verse in praise:
Abiding securely within the Buddha-dharma, with a mind of faith and understanding firmly resolved,
He has aroused courageous diligence in his quest for great enlightenment.
Furthermore, in future ages, I shall reverently behold Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
if I do not make offerings to them, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.
Having made these offerings, I shall surely realize the Way of the Buddha.
Named Holder of Radiance, he was the most supreme in the world.
When that Buddha appeared in the world, he shone constantly like a lamp;
he delivered and liberated a multitude of śrāvakas, numbering eighty full assemblies.
These bhikṣus have well cultivated the wisdom of suchness;
dwelling in their final bodies, they have all attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Within that Buddha-land, all classes of sentient beings—
His lifespan was exceedingly long, reaching a full eight koṭis of years.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all who followed him cherished him with longing and devotion;
they constructed countless stūpas and temples to extend their offerings and show their reverence.
Nayutas of sentient beings protect and uphold the Buddha’s True Dharma;
some have resolved upon the Great Mind, while others have entered parinirvāṇa without remainder.
Those Four Great Heavenly Kings have received the Tathāgata’s prophecy.
Their hearts were filled with great joy, and they paid homage by bowing their heads in reverent submission.

Chapter Fifteen: The Prophecy for the Gods of the Thirty-three Heavens, from the *Pitṛputrasamāgama-sūtra*. At that time, Śakra, the Lord of the Gods of the Thirty-three Heavens, together with his retinue of eight hundred million devaputras, came to the assembly where the Buddha was. There they saw the various asura kings, up to and including the four great heavenly kings, making vast offerings to the World-Honored One. Furthermore, hearing the Tathāgata bestow prophecies upon them, they developed an even greater love and delight for the Buddha’s Dharma; they conceived a sense of wonder and sought the unsurpassed path.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, used his supernormal powers to manifest eighty koṭis of jeweled canopies. These jeweled canopies were most extraordinary; they were all adorned with necklaces made of various jewels—some with necklaces of red pearls, some of vaidūrya, some of maṇi gems, and some of gold—all of which hung down in profusion across the entire extent of the canopies.

Furthermore, he manifested eighty koṭis of pure pavilions, their doors, windows, and railings adorned with various jewels; they were successively embellished with parasols, banners, and streamers. Within each pavilion was a sublime lion throne, covered above by nets of bells made of various jewels, and beside each throne stood countless celestial maidens in attendance.

Behind the multi-storied pavilion, he further manifested eighty koṭis of exquisite chariots made of various jewels; upon each were suspended canopies of diverse colors, and they were drawn by well-trained horses.

Furthermore, he further manifested eighty koṭis of great nāga-elephant kings named Airāvaṇa. Each elephant king had eighty koṭis of heads; each head possessed six tusks; upon each tusk were seven ponds; within each pond were seven lotus flowers, each with a thousand petals; within each petal were seven celestial maidens; and each celestial maiden was further attended by seven servant girls, their bodies adorned with necklaces of various jewels.

Upon those lotus petals and within the pavilions, there were celestial maidens who held up banners, streamers, and precious canopies; some performed songs and dances, others played musical instruments, some scattered sandalwood and aloeswood incense, and others scattered heavenly *māndārava* flowers as well as flowers made of the seven precious gems, raining down from the void like a shower throughout the city of Kapilavastu, which measured sixty *yojanas* in length and breadth. Having been scattered again and again, they accumulated to the height of the knees.

At that time, eighty koṭis of devaputras, for the sake of making offerings, likewise used their supernatural powers to manifest eighty koṭis of nāga-elephants; upon each elephant was a canopy, all magnificently adorned with various jewels.
They further manifested eight hundred million exquisite jeweled chariots, eight hundred million exceptionally beautiful celestial maidens, and eight hundred million celestial musical instruments.

These celestial maidens each mounted jeweled chariots, performing music, singing, and dancing, scattering various fragrant flowers; they circled three times to the right through the void, just as the offerings previously described by the Asura King were performed, without any difference.
At that time, after the Lord of Devas and the sons of gods had extended their offerings, they reflected thus:

"These emanated goddesses, having made these offerings, understand that all phenomena are like illusions as the Buddha has taught; furthermore, they observe that their own bodies are likewise like illusions. They know that those offerings and the body of the Tathāgata are also like illusions, and that all the teachings spoken by the Buddha are entirely illusory."

Having understood this, he was freed from all doubt and confusion. He circumambulated the World-Honored One three times to the right, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet in reverence, and stood to one side. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he praised him with these verses:
“The various offerings made by the emanated beings, Their skillful manifestations are peerless;
Even when observing the characteristics of their own bodies, They are entirely like illusions, no different.”
That which the Buddha has taught regarding all phenomena, as well as the matter of bestowing predictions of attaining Buddhahood,
which causes the various devas to give rise to hearts of joy— all these are identical to magical illusions.
This explains that the Muni’s pure body and the Dharma he teaches are both like illusions;
we pray that the Tathāgata will sever all doubts and cause our minds to open to understanding regarding this prophecy.
Those foolish ordinary beings are deluded regarding the true practice of what they undertake;
because they do not understand that phenomena are like illusions, they claim that there is no prophecy concerning the world.
Those who are still training and those beyond training, as well as seekers of pratyekabuddhahood and the śrāvakas—
all of them understand that all phenomena are like illusions, and they have no doubt regarding the Buddha-dharma.
If there are those who delight in practicing the conduct of tranquility, seeking alone to realize the fruit of a pratyekabuddha,
they are able to understand that all phenomena are like illusions, and they harbor no doubts regarding the Buddha’s teachings.
If there are those who joyfully practice the bodhisattva path, benefiting and bringing happiness to the world without negligence—
such sons of the Buddha understand that all phenomena are like illusions, and they remain free from discrimination regarding all dharmas.
The Supreme Sugata, the Tamer of Men, is endowed with peerless great compassion;
his ten powers and sublime wisdom are wondrous and inconceivable, as he has realized the intrinsic nature within this Dharma.
Some may dwell in forest hermitages, free from all feverish afflictions and devoid of longing;
they are able to understand that all phenomena are like illusions, and thus harbor no doubts regarding the Buddha's teachings.
If one realizes that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, such that not even the slightest phenomenon can be apprehended as real,
then one will be far removed from all doubt and shall give rise to reverence for the Buddha's teaching.
May I attain Buddhahood and transcend the world, Constantly teaching that all phenomena are like illusions,
Causing all to be liberated from the causes of delusion, And to dwell securely in the realm of the true and eternal Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the deep thoughts in the minds of the Lord of Devas and the various sons of gods, emitted pure light from his face.
Having observed this sign, the Venerable Aśvajit Bhikṣu joined his palms toward the Buddha and asked him in verse:
“O Muni, endowed with great renown, Why have you now suddenly emitted pure light?”
This sublime light does not arise without a cause; I pray that you, O Greatly Compassionate One, will explain it to us.
As the Tathāgata’s face manifested this auspicious omen, Those present in the assembly, having seen it, were all filled with doubt.
We pray that you will tell us whence this light comes, So that those who hear it may all attain purity of mind.
The devas extol the Buddha’s virtues and extensively arrange the most supreme and wondrous offerings;
could it not be that the Tathāgata has emitted this light to cause the hearts of these sons of gods to rejoice?
The Buddha emits boundless, stainless light; this radiance is pure, surpassing the white moon.
Is it not that the various devas have mastered the art of illusion, and the One of Ten Powers has bestowed his seal of approval upon them?
The Muni has accumulated the practices for awakening, Constantly practicing the gift of Dharma with a heart free from stinginess;
I pray only that the Tathāgata will resolve the doubts of the assembly, Causing them to dwell securely within the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣu Aśvajit:

“Excellent, great bhikṣu Aśvajit! That you are able to inquire about the matter of emitting light— I shall now explain its causes and conditions, And how the sons of the gods were granted the prophecy of Buddhahood.”
Thus those hosts of devaputras, being able to realize that all phenomena are like illusions, have accomplished boundless pure wisdom and clarity;
they extinguish the darkness of ignorance and eliminate all doubt and confusion.
In the past, throughout the cycle of birth and death, you have personally attended and served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
from them you heard the Dharma and practiced right reflection, whereby you came to understand that all phenomena are like illusions.
Now, extending this offering before me, you also know that all phenomena are like illusions;
having become free from all doubts regarding the Buddha-dharma, you have attained a resolute mind that is never diminished.
In a future age, they shall attain the path of supreme enlightenment;
they shall be named Tathāgatas, Kings of the Imperial Banner, their majestic virtues most lofty and manifest.
He transforms and guides ten million nayutas of sentient beings, preaching for them this dharma that is like an illusion;
these sons of heaven, all bearing the same name, shall each in turn attain Buddhahood.
"You gods, abandon negligence and contemplate all sensory realms as being like illusions;
by gradually practicing śamatha, you shall swiftly attain the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi."

Chapter Sixteen: The Prediction for the King of the Yāma Heaven. *The Compendium of Father and Son Sūtra*, Chapter Sixteen: The Prediction for the King of the Yāma Heaven. At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven, together with four koṭis of devaputras, came to the place where the Buddha was. He saw the asura kings and even Śakra, the Lord of the Thirty-three Heavens, making great offerings to the World-Honored One. Furthermore, hearing that the Tathāgata had granted them predictions of enlightenment, he was filled with joy and exultation, experiencing what he had never known before, and conceived a profound love and delight for the Buddha’s Dharma.
He then formed this thought:

"The Buddha has realized the supreme nectar, the foremost Dharma; there is not the slightest phenomenon in all the worlds that he does not know, nothing he does not see, nothing he does not comprehend, and nothing he does not directly realize, for that Tathāgata has clearly and thoroughly penetrated both the conventional truth and the ultimate truth without any limitation or obstruction."
As for that mundane [knowledge], it refers to worldly activities—whether karma or its retribution, whether already arisen or yet to arise—all of which he knows without any error.

That ultimate reality is supremely pure; it cannot be identified, cannot be known by cognition, cannot be expressed in words, and cannot be demonstrated. It is neither seen nor heard, neither grasped nor abandoned, neither moving nor still, neither attained nor lost, neither departing nor arriving, neither light nor heavy, neither disparaged nor praised, neither profiting nor declining, neither lauded nor reviled, neither pleasant nor painful, neither form nor non-form, neither numerical nor non-numerical, neither conceptualization nor free from conceptualization, neither affliction nor free from affliction. It is beyond all conceptual proliferation and transcends all verbal expression; even so-called "characteristics of form" cannot be apprehended, and the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise cannot be apprehended.
The characteristic of the eye is unapprehendable; the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise unapprehendable.
The characteristic of form is unapprehendable; the characteristics of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena are likewise unapprehendable.
Eye-consciousness is unapprehendable; ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness are likewise unapprehendable.
Eye-contact is unapprehendable; ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are likewise unapprehendable.
The various sensations produced by eye-contact are unapprehendable; the various sensations produced by ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are likewise unapprehendable.
The perception of forms is unapprehendable, up to and including the perception of mental phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*), which is also unapprehendable.
The earth element cannot be apprehended; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements likewise cannot be apprehended.
The characteristics of the desire realm cannot be apprehended; the characteristics of the form realm and the formless realm likewise cannot be apprehended.
The characteristics of the conditioned cannot be apprehended, and the characteristics of the unconditioned likewise cannot be apprehended.
If a person seeks those phenomena and their intrinsic nature within this ultimate dharma, they cannot be found.

Furthermore, when unlearned, foolish worldlings hear this dharma, they harbor fear and dread; they give rise to regret and affliction regarding the Buddha-dharma, thereby falling away from omniscience. They are universally despised and reviled by both gods and humans; such persons dwell perpetually in saṃsāra, bound and entangled by manifold sufferings.
At that time, King Yama and the various devaputras observed that all sentient beings in the world constantly dwell within birth and death, oppressed by manifold sufferings.

They conceived a profound sense of reverence for the Buddha’s True Dharma and, through their supernormal powers, performed a great offering that surpassed the offerings previously presented by the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

When these devaputras had finished making their offerings, they circumambulated him three times to the right, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and stood to one side. With palms joined toward the Buddha, they praised him in verse:
"Observing that all the aggregates of the Buddha are empty and quiescent, The dharmas of the sense bases and elements are likewise so;
The faculties and their objects are eternally serene— Thus one perceives the Tathāgata’s true nature."
The wise ones of the world, regarding the true nature of phenomena, attain realization through their own nature rather than by depending on others;
namely, the conventional and the ultimate—apart from these, there is no third dharma.
The Tathāgata appears in the world and, according to their capacities, expounds the conventional dharmas;
if sentient beings give rise to a pure mind, they will constantly obtain the various joys of humans and devas.
The Lion of the Śākyas, fearless among men, speaks of the six realms according to conventional truth:
the devas, humans, and asuras; the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal kingdom.
Those of wealthy abundance and noble lineage, those of low birth and impoverished households,
servants, messengers, and musicians, as well as those who are infirm, crippled, or afflicted by various diseases— [may they all attain peace].
The conventional dharmas thus explained are for the universal benefit of ordinary people;
because sentient beings give rise to craving and attachment, they are unable to transcend the eight worldly concerns—
namely, gain and loss, defamation and praise, as well as fame and insignificance, pleasure and pain.
Those who gain increase their hearts of joy; those who lose constantly give rise to burning affliction.
This is spoken according to conventional truth regarding the ultimate truth:
because of defiled wisdom, they give rise to perversions—taking the impure for the pure, suffering for pleasure, and grasping at what is non-self among phenomena as self.
Regarding impermanent phenomena as permanent, they give rise to false conceptualizations and become attached to them.
Even if such persons should happen to hear the Buddha’s words, their minds will be struck with terror and they will not believe or accept them.
Because they slander the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, they shall undergo extreme suffering within the hells.
Thus do those deluded by craving and ignorance Succumb to one another’s influence, sinking without rest. If there be one who,
within the Buddha’s Dharma, Discerns with wisdom what is not inverted,
Abandoning the causes of saṃsāric suffering and distress, They will gradually be able to cultivate the path to enlightenment.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is fundamentally pure, And the ultimate truth transcends verbal expression;
If upon hearing this one gives rise to a heart of joy and devotion, Know that such a person is a true child of the Buddha.
I speak these words based on the Tathāgata; all you gods, with one mind, should joyfully seek [this path].
If you can practice according to the principle and in accordance with the Dharma, you shall all ultimately attain the Buddha-way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the deep thoughts in the minds of the devaputras, emitted pure light from his mouth, which universally illuminated the entire assembly.
Having beheld this light, the Venerable Bhikṣu Aśvajit joined his palms with single-minded devotion and asked in verse:
“The Tathāgata now emits a brilliant light; Having seen it, the assembled multitude has conceived doubts.”
We pray that you will explain the cause for this, so that this great assembly may find peace of mind.
If the various devas have received their predictions, they shall all show respect and give rise to sympathetic joy;
those endowed with wisdom likewise aspire to always exert themselves with diligence within the Buddha-dharma.
These sons of heaven stand before the Buddha, all of them supreme vessels for merit;
we humbly hope that the Tathāgata will unfold his great compassion and graciously bestow his acceptance with the sound of Brahmā’s voice.
Hearing of the Buddha’s virtues, his heart was filled with joy; he thought, "I shall surely attain [enlightenment] without doubt.
If he receives the Tathāgata’s words of prophecy, he will practice with courageous diligence and never regress.
How great is the Unsurpassed Teacher of Gods and Men! He shatters heterodox arguments and leads them back to the True Principle.
The assembled multitude awaits his subtle and wondrous voice; May he swiftly proclaim the account of the prophecy granted by the gods.
