At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the Venerable Aśvajit:
“Aśvajit Bhikṣu, listen attentively As I proclaim the matter of the emission of light;
The devas and humans in this great assembly Desire to hear of the Tathāgata’s virtues.”
In this world there are base and ordinary persons who, upon hearing of the Buddha’s virtues, feel no joy;
harboring greed and anger that are ever-blazing, they engage in much strife throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.
If one gives rise to faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma, that person has practiced it through熏習 (xūnxí, perfuming/cultivation) in past kalpas;
with the power of great compassion and vows ever in accord, they shall attain such buddha-merits as these.
If one sees those in the world suffering from decline and misery, one should constantly give rise to a heart of compassion out of pity;
by praising the Buddha’s inconceivable and supreme virtues, one causes them to develop pure faith and joyful devotion.
The devas, who in the past cultivated vast roots of goodness under former Buddhas,
now hear of the Buddha’s inconceivable and wondrous virtues, receiving them upon their crowns like a garland of flowers.
That Yāma-deva, together with his retinue, has sought deliverance within my Dharma;
possessing pure wisdom and a heart of great compassion, he has grown weary of and detached from all worldly fetters of existence.
I have served and made offerings to all Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
I have accumulated boundless causes of supreme merit for the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi.
A lion among men appearing in the world, he is able to expound the boundless, pure Dharma;
for sentient beings submerged in the midst of afflictions, he rescues and delivers them with a heart of great compassion.
Observing that sentient beings are entangled in karma and delusion, he preaches for them the supreme Dharma of liberation;
having heard this Dharma, they engage in correct contemplation and realize that all phenomena are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature.
The faculties are tranquil and free from attachment; they understand that all phenomena are like illusions.
Each realizes that the fundamental nature of phenomena is empty, and thereby enters into the comprehension of the true mark.
Those sons of gods, having already performed vast offerings before me,
shall attain the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi in the future Star宿 Kalpa.
These Tathāgatas appeared in the world, filling forty-four koṭis of kalpas;
they liberated immeasurable suffering beings, causing them all to become pure and free from all delusions.
That Yāmāntaka deity received the prediction that he would become Buddhas named Mahārṣi-Daṇḍadhārin.
"Now, for the sake of Aśvajit, he has answered his doubts; all those gathered in the great assembly rejoice.
*The Sūtra of the Combined Collection of Father and Son*, Scroll Eight;
*The Sūtra of the Combined Collection of Father and Son*, Scroll Nine.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court-Scattered Official and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master of Xuanfan, the Imperially Ennobled Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Rìchēng, and others, by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Seventeen: The Prediction Bestowed upon the Gods of Tuṣita Heaven. At that time, within the assembly, there were eighty koṭis of gods from Tuṣita Heaven. Seeing all the asura kings, up to those of the Yāma Heaven, making various offerings to the World-Honored One, and further hearing the Tathāgata bestow upon them the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, their hearts were filled with great joy, attaining what they had never experienced before.
Then those devaputras had this thought:
"This dharma of bodhi is fundamentally without the mark of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise without marks."
Now, World-Honored One, by what dharma should you bestow a prediction of enlightenment?
Why is this so? Because form is fundamentally unarisen, and awakening (bodhi) is likewise unarisen; even up to consciousness being unarisen, awakening is likewise unarisen.
How can the non-arising of dharmas attain bodhi?
Thus, because form is without cessation, bodhi is also without cessation; likewise, up to consciousness being without cessation, bodhi is also without cessation.
How can a dharma that is without cessation attain bodhi?
Because form is quiescent, bodhi is also quiescent; likewise, because consciousness is quiescent, bodhi is also quiescent.
In this way, because form is non-dual, awakening is also non-dual; and so on, up to: because consciousness is non-dual, awakening is also non-dual.
In this way, because form is immovable, awakening is also immovable; and so on, up to: because consciousness is immovable, awakening is also immovable.
In this way, because form is invisible, awakening is also invisible; and so on, up to: because consciousness is invisible, awakening is also invisible.
Since that mark of bodhi is by nature devoid of self-essence, how can it further be described as neither arising nor ceasing, quiescent and non-dual, profoundly still and unmoving, and invisible?
Among all phenomena, what is called "form"?
Form is empty of intrinsic nature; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise all empty.
What is called "Buddha"?
What is called a bodhisattva?
What is called a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa)?

A Buddha is empty of the self-nature of a Buddha; a bodhisattva is empty of the self-nature of a bodhisattva; awakening (bodhi) is empty of the self-nature of awakening; and a prediction of enlightenment is empty of the self-nature of a prediction of enlightenment.

That which is called "Buddha" is merely based on worldly convention—a provisional name used for invocation, hope, and conceptual differentiation. Those who possess wisdom, upon hearing that all phenomena are empty, do not give rise to grasping or attachment; yet those foolish people, upon hearing it, become angry and are unable to enter into understanding.

For example, suppose a person, while in a dream, fully experiences the pleasures of the five desires; having awakened, they reflect that these were truly unattainable, and the wise one, understanding this, gives rise to no distress.

In this same way, those who are established in the Bodhisattva vehicle realize that the nature of bodhi is fundamentally empty and quiescent, such that there is truly nothing to be attained; they likewise give rise to no fear.
Why is this? Because they understand that all phenomena are like dreams.
Foolish worldlings have differing interpretations and give rise to attachment toward these delusive phenomena.
In this way, all these dharmas are unattainable.
An ordinary person is unattainable, and the dharmas of an ordinary person are also unattainable;
a śrāvaka is unattainable, and the dharmas of a śrāvaka are also unattainable.
Pratyekabuddhas cannot be apprehended, nor can the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas;
bodhisattvas cannot be apprehended, nor can the dharmas of bodhisattvas;
Buddhas cannot be apprehended, nor can the dharmas of the Buddhas.
“Awakening (bodhi) cannot be apprehended, nor can the phenomena of awakening be apprehended;
nirvāṇa cannot be apprehended, nor can the phenomena of nirvāṇa be apprehended.
When the devaputra of Tuṣita had spoken thus, he addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!

Now, regarding this ultimate truth, I have attained freedom from doubt and have given rise to a pure mind. I shall prepare various kinds of sublime offerings that surpass those of the Yāma Heaven and cannot be compared to them.”

Having made this offering, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and stood to one side. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he praised him in verse:
“If a person practices the teachings of the Tathāgata, They abide securely in the merits of the Buddha.
Regarding the three gates of liberation, They penetrate their profound meaning and flavor without hindrance.”
Within this, there is no form, nor feeling, nor perception; Nor are there formations, consciousness, mind, or objects.
To realize that these five aggregates are merely provisional names— Such a person is called a lion among those possessed of wisdom.
Such a supreme and most excellent man does not grasp even the slightest mark of enlightenment;
having realized the emptiness of the aggregates, he has attained noble benefit and harbors no doubt regarding the Buddha’s qualities.
Profoundly penetrating the meaning of the true nature of bodhi, Neither giving rise to hope nor engaging in disparagement,
With a mind free from longing and acting spontaneously— This is abiding well in the practice of bodhi.
If a person perceives the nature of phenomena with equanimity, they will have no fear regarding any phenomena;
such a son of the Buddha is able, within this world, to fully cultivate and realize supreme merit.
Thoroughly realizing that all forms and appearances are empty, they completely renounce all objects of desire;
observing the three realms of cyclic existence, they neither hope for nor take pleasure in them.
If a person clearly understands the phenomena of the five aggregates, that the Buddha, awakening,
and the prediction of enlightenment are all empty for both speaker and listener— through such realization and understanding, one is unimpeded.
The dharmas of the Buddha’s merit and the dharmas of ordinary beings— All these marks are fundamentally unarisen.
One who can thoroughly understand this gateway of the supreme dharma-nature Is truly called a son of the Buddha.
Furthermore, one thoroughly understands that these phenomena—the five aggregates, the sense bases, and the elements—are fundamentally without cessation;
that the Buddha, awakening, and the words of prophecy—all such dharmas are entirely equal.
The wise who penetrate and understand this Dharma-gate do not abandon the practice of bodhi;
because they realize that the nature of phenomena is without cessation, it is not difficult for them to attain the bodhi of the Buddha.
Furthermore, the aggregates, bases, and elements, as well as the Buddha and awakening, are all empty and quiescent;
if a person has no reliance or seeking regarding these, they are able to uphold the true Dharma of the Buddha.
All aggregates, sense bases, and elements are devoid of agency; the Buddha, awakening, and the prophecy—all these phenomena are entirely the same.
One who understands this is a child of the Buddha.
The aggregates, sense bases, and elements are empty of intrinsic nature;
the Buddha, awakening, and the prophecy—these the wise understand with certainty. Such a person is called a true son of the Buddha.
All aggregates, sense bases, and elements are entirely illusory;
so too are the Supreme Honored One among bipeds and the prophecy of enlightenment—those who understand this are the children of the Buddha.
This Dharma is neither detached nor non-detached; it is neither existent nor non-existent.
It is neither conditioned nor unconditioned—one who understands it thus is a child of the Buddha.
The Tathāgata has appeared in the world, having fully realized such subtle and wondrous meanings;
he is the supreme and most excellent of men, worthy of receiving the vast offerings of all the devas.
I now praise the merits of the Buddha; may the blessings and rewards obtained benefit all sentient beings.
Only the Tathāgata fully perceives and knows this; I dedicate it so that both myself and others may all attain Buddhahood.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the devaputras and their aspiration for the Tathāgata to bestow upon them the prediction of Buddhahood, immediately emitted pure light from within his seat.
At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit, having beheld this sign, joined his palms toward the Buddha and asked in verse:
“World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions, Do you manifest such an auspicious omen through the power of your supernormal faculties?”
I pray that you will explain the origins of this for the sake of the assembly, so that all the world may rejoice.
Beholding the pure light emitted from the Buddha’s mouth, the devas are all filled with doubt;
each gazes upon his compassionate countenance, single-mindedly wishing to hear what the Buddha shall speak.
Just as a sick person who encounters a skilled physician hopes only for rescue and the granting of a divine elixir,
so too do these assembled ones stand before the Buddha, thirsting with longing and hope in the same way.
The assembly of devas and humans gathered here, all possessing vast and pure wisdom,
listen with single-minded attention and without distraction, able to enter into understanding of what the Buddha has spoken.
The Tathāgata, with his ever-present heart of great compassion, is able to shatter all nets of doubt;
having heard this, they all uphold it, subduing all heterodox arguments and giving rise to right view.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣu Aśvajit:
“Aśvajit, you have now raised this question To bring benefit to the world and act as a lamp of illumination.
The wise are able to still all the doubts of the multitude; Therefore, they are revered by both humans and devas.”
The King of Tuṣita Heaven and his sons have attained the supreme Dharma, the flavor of nectar;
having performed great offerings and sublime adornments, I now bestow upon them this prediction of enlightenment.
With supreme wisdom he contemplates the world, Perceiving the nature of phenomena without attachment;
Skillfully attaining the three gates of liberation, He is beyond the reach of the ignorant.
In the presence of past Buddhas, he has already inquired about such meanings;
observing that the nature of all phenomena is ultimately empty, it is exactly as previously taught by those former Buddhas.
Now you have again offered worship to me— most supreme, most excellent, and peerless—
able to praise the Tathāgata through the meaning of emptiness, all for the sake of the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
All phenomena are entirely without arising; the Buddha, awakening, and the prophecy of attainment—even those who cultivate for awakening—are likewise equal in their nature of non-arising.
If a person thus realizes the nature of phenomena, they will certainly realize great enlightenment;
because those sons of gods previously heard and upheld [this teaching], they are able to proclaim the ultimate truth.
Able to discern with clear wisdom, they understand that the nature of phenomena is eternally without decrease;
those sons of the gods, free from all doubt, spontaneously achieve the teacherless wisdom.
The nature of phenomena is neither grasped nor sought; it is ultimately without support and free from conceptual discrimination.
While those sons of the gods are freed from all doubts, the minds of the foolish give rise to alarm and fear.
All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; Both awakening and that mind of awakening— Those sons of the gods understand them well: Primordially pure and free from attachment.
The gods and sons of the Tushita Heaven Kings, dwelling in steadfast wisdom without abiding anywhere,
shall before long attain the Bodhi of the Buddhas and fully perfect all-encompassing knowledge.
In that future Constellation Eon, they shall appear in succession within the world, delivering and liberating boundless sentient beings;
all shall be known by the same name, Buddha King of Resolute Wisdom.
The Tathāgata, knowing the thoughts in their minds, suddenly emitted pure light in response;
he proclaimed for them the prediction of their future buddhahood, causing those in the assembly to give rise to joy and celebration.

**Chapter 18: The Prediction for the Gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations** *The Compendium of Father and Son Sūtra, Chapter Eighteen: The Prediction for the Gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations.* At that time, the Lord of the Gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, together with a retinue of seventy koṭis of devaputras, saw all the asura kings and even the devaputras of the Tuṣita Heaven making offerings to the World-Honored One. They felt profound sympathetic joy and leaped for joy immeasurably. Furthermore, hearing that the Tathāgata had bestowed predictions upon them, these devaputras, having heard this teaching, became serene in body and mind; they attained abiding in the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality) and were freed from all doubt regarding the dharma of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
At that time, the Deva-king Nirmāṇarati rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, all dharmas are called the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); they are called the limitless limit, the unobstructed limit, the non-abiding limit, the inexhaustible limit, and the non-dual limit. That which is neither a limit nor a non-limit is designated as the limit of reality.
World-Honored One!
That which is called the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is so called because it is non-erroneous;
that which is the immeasurable limit is so called because it is without boundaries.
The limit of non-obstruction is because it is not a composite;
the limit of non-abiding is because it is free from intrinsic nature;
the limit of the immeasurable is because there is no arising.
That which has no duality of limits exists because it is of a single characteristic;
that which is not a limit exists because its essence is non-existent;
that which has no limit exists because it is fundamentally and infinitely so.
World-Honored One!

This dharma of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) pervades all places; it penetrates both the conditioned and the unconditioned without obstruction, for there is not a single dharma that is not the limit of reality. Even up to bodhi, it is likewise the limit of reality.
Furthermore, by what dharma is "bodhi" defined?
All these dharmas are themselves bodhi; even all five deeds of immediate retribution are likewise bodhi.
Why is this? Because that dharma of awakening is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*) are likewise devoid of intrinsic nature,
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, those five acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) are themselves the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder. Why is this?
Because the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of those phenomena is free from the characteristics of transgression; therefore, the acts of immediate retribution are called the realm of nirvāṇa.
“World-Honored One!

Those who dwell in saṃsāra may seek nirvāṇa; yet within that reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), there are no two distinct characteristics. There is no saṃsāra to be abandoned, and there is no nirvāṇa to be realized.”
Why is this? Because its intrinsic nature is detached.
World-Honored One!

I now have no doubt regarding this principle of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); if one attains freedom from doubt concerning this Dharma, it should be known that such a person has already received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.

At that time, having heard these words spoken by the Heavenly King, the Tathāgata, wishing to cause the great assembly to develop pure faith and understanding and to give rise to joy, immediately emitted a great radiance from within his seat.
Then the Venerable Aśvajit Bhikṣu asked in verse:
"O Compassionate Teacher and Tamer of the World, You have manifested this auspicious omen amidst the great assembly;
From your mouth you have suddenly emitted pure radiance— This sign cannot be without its cause."
Now that this great assembly has gathered, all have given rise to pure and respectful hearts;
we pray you will explain the causes and conditions for the emission of these rays of light, so as to eliminate all doubts and delusions.
If these hear what the Buddha has spoken, they shall listen with single-minded attention and accept it in faith;
all shall follow the Buddha’s teachings and be able to practice them, vowing to seek the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will quickly expound [the Dharma], to comfort the hearts of those sentient beings who thirst for it;
may the bodies and minds of all devas be at peace, so that they may know with certainty that they shall attain Buddhahood.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣu Aśvajit:
"Aśvajit now asks about the emission of light; The deeds of the Tathāgata are never without cause.
You should listen attentively without distraction, For I shall now bestow the prophecy of Buddhahood upon the devas."
The King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, together with his retinue, will gradually achieve all-knowledge;
amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, he shall let out a lion’s roar and crush all heterodox arguments.
Just as it is certain that no pearls are produced within any mountain caves,
so too these devas of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations shall definitely attain Buddhahood in the future.
Furthermore, just as when the sun sets in the world, one should know that before long the moon will appear;
so too, those sons of the gods who have realized the nature of phenomena know for themselves that they will certainly attain perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, just as in the world at midday, All forms and images are clearly perceived,
So too these sons of gods, having realized the nature of phenomena, Shall attain the all-knowing wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, just as in the world during the night, sentient beings all know that the sun does not appear;
so too, those sons of gods who have realized the nature of phenomena shall attain clear wisdom and illuminate all things with full understanding.
Just as all streams and springs in the world Flow downward and return to the ocean,
So too these sons of the Buddha, having realized the nature of phenomena, Will surely and swiftly realize great enlightenment.
Just as when a clod of earth is thrown into the air, it must inevitably fall to the ground once its momentum is spent;
so too, those sons of the Buddha who have realized the nature of phenomena will undoubtedly attain Buddhahood before long.
If a person thoroughly understands this nature of phenomena, entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and transcending conceptual proliferation,
they shall realize great merit and draw near to the site of enlightenment.
Even if twenty nayutas of evil Māras were to say, "You shall not become a Buddha," because I possess right view and have realized the nature of phenomena,
they could not cause me to retreat from or destroy my resolve for enlightenment.
Thus, those hosts of devaputras, having well understood the nature of phenomena with minds free from attachment, each hoped for words of prediction;
therefore, I praise and encourage them, bringing them joy and consolation.
These sons of the gods have long practiced cultivation; without relying on others for awakening, they are able to enter into understanding.
Knowing for themselves that they will certainly attain bodhi, all who possess wisdom rejoice in them.

Bhikṣu Aśvajit, you should understand this: those who seek unsurpassed bodhi should always delight in drawing near to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and contemplate the nature of all phenomena without obstruction.
Being able to enter into and understand the correct principle oneself, and further enabling others to achieve thorough mastery, one explains it to them according to their capacity;
such a person is the foremost practitioner of the Dharma.
Even if one were to practice asceticism for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, giving away one's own flesh and blood as alms,
to realize the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) in a single kṣaṇa brings forth merit far more vast than that.
All Buddhas of the past, those who now deliver sentient beings,
and all the World-Honored Ones yet to come— there are none who have not practiced in reliance upon this.
The King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, together with his retinue, now extends offerings before me;
having already planted the causes of merit in the past, they are thus able to comprehend the meaning of this profound Dharma.
All those in the world who possess wisdom should cultivate and realize samādhi;
if one can rely upon this supreme meditative concentration, that person shall reach the sphere of the Buddha’s activity.
The bhikṣu Aśvajit should understand that these sons of the Buddha have realized the nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
they are constantly able to sport within the realm of the Buddhas and subdue all heterodox disputants.
Therefore, by diligently cultivating pure deeds, one can remain far removed from all suffering and affliction;
by always joyfully drawing near to the Dharma-preacher, one shall attain the path of unsurpassed Bodhi.

Chapter Nineteen: The Prediction for the Gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*). In the *Sūtra of the Combined Collection of Father and Son*, Chapter Nineteen: The Prediction for the Gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Emanations. At that time, the King of the Gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Emanations, together with a retinue of eighty nayutas of devaputras, beheld all the asura kings up to those of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations making various offerings to the Tathāgata. Furthermore, hearing the Tathāgata bestow predictions upon them, they leaped for joy with unprecedented delight.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

This 'reality-limit' (bhūtakoṭi) spoken of by the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations—I now find that even 'reality' itself is unobtainable; how then can one further speak of there being a 'limit'?"
Why is this? World-Honored One!
If one who perceives reality were also to perceive a limit, it should be known that such a person dwells in two kinds of marks; how then could they enter into understanding and realize that bodhi?
One should know that what they say is the practice of non-path.
If a son of good family is free from these two characteristics, he is said to be well-established; abiding in non-abiding, there is then no verbal expression.
For one who seeks awakening, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be perceived by the mind, yet they are able to awaken to and attain that awakening.

Why is this? This reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) is neither existent nor non-existent; it is free from all marks; it is not of the past, not of the present, and not of the future; it is neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it is not known by consciousness (*vijñāna*), nor known by wisdom (*jñāna*); it is not an object of observation, nor is it a direct realization. There is not the slightest dharma that acts as an antidote, nor is there the slightest dharma that serves as the object to be remedied.
Why is this? Because phenomena are not defiled by afflictions, and because phenomena lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and are unapprehendable;
if those various phenomena were subject to antidotes, then some slight intrinsic nature of phenomena would be observable.
World-Honored One!

If form arises, that form is devoid of the characteristic of arising; if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness arise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise devoid of the characteristic of arising.
World-Honored One!
If form ceases, that form is because it is dissociated from the characteristic of cessation;
if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cease, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are because they are dissociated from the characteristic of cessation.
World-Honored One!
If it is the past, it is because it is free from the characteristics of the past;
if it is the future, it is because it is free from the characteristics of the future.
The present is so called because it is devoid of the characteristics of the present.
World-Honored One!
That which is conditioned is so called because it is devoid of the characteristics of the conditioned;
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is so called because it is free from the characteristics of the unconditioned.

Thus, all these phenomena—whether comprised within the five aggregates, comprised within the three time periods, comprised within the conditioned, or comprised within the unconditioned—are ultimately unapprehendable.
Because they are unapprehendable, those phenomena cannot be known, cannot be seen, cannot be described, cannot be explained, cannot be observed, and cannot be realized.
“World-Honored One!
If good sons or good daughters, seeking bodhi, thus resolve their minds and practice with determination,
they are all called those who are well-established in the Bodhisattva Vehicle.”

At that time, the devaputras of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, having all spoken thus of the Dharma they had realized, joined their palms toward the Buddha and praised him in verse:
“The Tathāgata has revealed the limit of saṃsāra, Which is beginningless, firm, and difficult to transcend.
The ignorant commoners of the world Delight in dwelling within the ocean of birth and death in the three realms of existence.”
The aggregates are empty of intrinsic nature from the very beginning; all sentient beings are unfindable.
There is not the slightest dharma that can serve as an antidote; one should know that all phenomena are signless.
The intrinsic nature of form is empty and fundamentally non-existent; it is neither cognition nor consciousness, nor is it observation;
it is neither vision nor realization, yet it is not non-existent either—one who relies on this correct principle understands it clearly.
Enlightenment is signless and unattainable; the factors of enlightenment are likewise so.
The Buddha, Bodhisattvas, and the Sangha are merely provisional names; apart from the mind’s grasping at signs, all are signless.
Fools, attached to desire, grasp at various signs; They claim for themselves that they have attained the bodhicitta.
Wandering within the realm of perversity, Their defiled wisdom makes it difficult to realize the principle of true permanence.
Those who are free from signs within the realm of the Buddha, These are the wise who practice in accordance with the Dharma;
They remain far removed from all signs as if signless, And are likewise detached from both emptiness and non-emptiness.
By practicing the conduct of enlightenment in reliance upon this, one attains the supreme, foremost bliss;
that which no outsiders can know, nor is it the sphere of training for śrāvakas,
nor yet for pratyekabuddhas— whose minds are well-liberated and free from defilement.
Nor can Arhats free from outflows enter into or understand this correct principle.
The signless bodhisattva practice of the Muni is known only by those of great wisdom;
if one relies on the authentic teaching to explain emptiness, it is not something possessed by those of the two vehicles.
Skillfully attaining the inconceivable true reality, one realizes that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature;
this bodhi cannot be known by those of shallow understanding, but those of superior faculties and keen wisdom comprehend it upon hearing it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the devas of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, immediately emitted pure radiance from within his seat.
Then the Venerable Aśvajit, having beheld this sign, joined his palms toward the Buddha and questioned him in verse:
"The Buddha knows the inclinations of the devas of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations; Suddenly he has emitted a vast, pure radiance."
This is known only through the Tathāgata’s self-realization; we pray that you will explain it in detail for the sake of this assembly.
All the devas harbor this thought: "The Buddha does not manifest this light without cause;
it must be for the benefit of all living beings, so as to inspire in them a sincere faith and a yearning thirst [for the Dharma]."
Now this great assembly harbors doubt because they have beheld such a rare cause as this:
that you have emitted this pure radiance from your mouth.
The Buddhas should bestow their prophecy upon these devas.
Having turned their backs on the path of saṃsāra, they seek to proceed toward the city of quiescent nirvāṇa;
standing here to hear the Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice, may he swiftly expound with unimpeded eloquence.
The assembly honors the Tathāgata’s teaching, Realizing the nature of all phenomena without doubt;
With firm minds of hearing, retention, faith, and understanding, They praise the ocean of virtues of the Muni.
The Tathāgata’s sublime teaching is inconceivable; it leads all sentient beings to the place of peace and security.
If one can practice and cultivate according to the principle, one will ultimately attain the unsurpassed path.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the Venerable Aśvajit:
“Excellent, great bhikṣu Aśvajit! Because you inquire for the benefit of all living beings, I now emit this pure light and bestow upon you the supreme prediction of bodhi.”

The Lord of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations and others, With firm resolve and sharp faculties, are all able to uphold the words of the Buddhas; They have long practiced the path to enlightenment.
One who can thoroughly understand the various deluded thoughts of the world, seeing them as like a mirage known to be unreal—
whereby the foolish take it for water and give rise to deluded minds— let those seeking Bodhi not be like them.
Those who cling to conceptualizations and views, lacking wisdom, instead fear the signless;
these deluded ones follow false paths through their妄想 (conceptual proliferations), yet by departing from these, one can attain great enlightenment.
Deluded thoughts and perverse reflections are the root of suffering; To give rise to conceptual discrimination is itself bondage.
The wise understand that all these are entirely empty, And thus attain the supreme *dhāraṇī* and the bliss of tranquility.
The deluded mind is uneven and will certainly cause one to fall into the various realms of existence;
for hundreds of thousands of lifetimes it serves as the condition for suffering—thus have the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time spoken in unison.
If a person clings to perceptions, they will be bound by the aggregates and elements;
one who observes well brings false conditions to rest, for all things are empty and devoid of marks.
Through the characteristics of conceptualization, one increases all afflictions, And further diminishes all meritorious deeds;
If one is free from doubt regarding the signless, One will swiftly realize the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi.
If a person seeks the noble path through conceptual discrimination, that seeking of the path through discrimination is itself a bond.
The wise one practices dhyāna while amidst desires; such a person skillfully cultivates the practice of signlessness.

All phenomena are without essence and ineffable; when one discerns that the nature of all phenomena is empty, those signless dharmas transcend conceptual thought, and thus awakening is not difficult to attain.
Hearing these words spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the assembly was freed from doubt and attained fearlessness;
as if receiving a garland of campaka flowers, they joyfully received them upon their heads.
The hearts of these hosts of devas have opened to awakening; now, before the Buddha, they extend their offerings.
Having realized that the nature of phenomena is originally empty, they shall all become Buddhas in future ages.
The Compendium of the Father and Son Sūtra, Volume Nine;
The Compendium of the Father and Son Sūtra, Volume Ten.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu.

Translated by the Imperial Decree by the *śramaṇa* of Purple Robes, the Great Master of Dharma (Fan-da-shi) Rìchēng, along with others, under the supervision of the Minister of State for Ceremonial (Hónglùqīng).

Chapter Twenty: The Prophecy Bestowed upon the Great Brahmā King. At that time, within the assembly, there were sixty *koṭis* of Brahmā devaputras. Having seen the various asura kings up to those of the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven making offerings to the World-Honored One, and further hearing the Tathāgata bestow prophecies upon them, they leaped for joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
These sons of the gods have, in the past, drawn near to and made offerings to various Tathāgatas;
they have accumulated roots of goodness, deeply cultivated meditative concentration, and transcended worldly dharmas.

Within the Buddha’s true teaching, each has attained the most supreme and profound joy of the Dharma, clearly understanding and penetrating it, being free from all conceptual proliferation, and having given rise to certainty.
Understanding that all phenomena are neither created nor uncreated, neither born nor unborn, neither attained nor unattained,
neither exhausted nor inexhaustible, neither separated nor not separated,
neither defiled nor free from defilement, neither deluded nor non-deluded, and neither wise nor unwise.
Wisdom is neither view nor non-view; it is neither grasping nor non-grasping;
it is neither empty nor non-empty; it is neither characterized nor uncharacterized; it is neither aspiration nor non-aspiration.

Having understood this, those sons of the gods were free from mental attachment; they remained far removed from all conceptualizations, having nothing upon which to rely or seek. They had no notion of manifold seeking, no notion of an agent, and no notion of the phenomena of an agent. They had no notion of ordinary beings, nor of the phenomena of ordinary beings; no notion of śrāvakas, nor of the phenomena of śrāvakas; no notion of pratyekabuddhas, nor of the phenomena of pratyekabuddhas; no notion of bodhisattvas, nor of the phenomena of bodhisattvas; no notion of Tathāgatas, nor of the phenomena of Tathāgatas; no notion of nirvāṇa, nor of the phenomena of nirvāṇa; and no notion of saṃsāra, nor of the phenomena of saṃsāra.

These sons of the gods thoroughly understood that the nature of phenomena is like empty space, free from defilement and attachment, and they were devoid of conceptual discrimination regarding the Buddha-dharma.
Then, the Brahma King joined his palms toward the Buddha and, with a tranquil mind, praised the Buddha in verse:
“The Tathāgata is fully endowed with impartial wisdom; Having cultivated the practice of tranquility, he has reached the further shore.”
Proclaiming the Dharma of tranquility to deliver all beings, they perceive all worlds as eternally quiescent.
Awakening is tranquil and fundamentally unstained; relying on the realm of tranquility, they remain undisturbed.
Constantly partaking of the nectar-flavor of tranquility, they attain complete penetration in all places.
This supreme path of ultimate tranquility brings sublime bliss to those who observe it well;
by long-term cultivation of the Eightfold Noble Path, one is able to sever the fetters of worldly afflictions.
Cultivating the dharma of tranquility to realize bodhi—this is what the Buddhas of the past have taught;
it will certainly lead to the city of nirvāṇa, no different from that of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
If a person relies upon the Buddha’s true teaching, Upholding, reciting, and diligently training in it,
Seeking to enter the gate of tranquil liberation, They shall be unsurpassed by anyone in all the world.
Having well cultivated the path of equanimity and tranquility, with the faculties ever joyful and pure,
and fully adorned with all merit and wisdom, he possesses great strength like that of Nārāyaṇa.
If one realizes the dharma of tranquil nectar, Then one can completely eliminate all marks of existence;
Observing that the world has nothing to rely upon— Such a person is the supreme son of the Tathāgata.
This person has long encountered the various Buddhas, Planting boundless and supreme roots of goodness;
Having attained this gate of tranquil samādhi, They extinguish all delusions and remain unstained.
By possessing the power of right mindfulness and diligence, Free from deceit, crookedness, and thoughts of indolence,
One realizes that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, Because one is able to leave behind all worldly signs.
The Buddhas appear in the world To proclaim the Dharma of peace and liberation;
The wise understand this without doubt, Forever emerging from the ocean of saṃsāra.
If a person seeks liberation within the aggregates, yet finds no delight in the dharma of tranquility,
perceiving only that the nature of the aggregates is insubstantial, they will give rise to terror toward the Buddha’s bodhi.
Having abandoned desire and purified the mind to seek liberation, one is able to discern well with clear wisdom;
yet for those fools who cling to desire and grasp at signs, the Buddha does not reveal [these truths].
If one grasps even at quiescent extinction, that too is bondage; one cannot achieve omniscience.
To not give rise to any mind of attachment—this is called being well-established in the practice of signlessness.
One can reach the nameless state of peace and security, attain the pure virtues of a Buddha,
cease all contentious disputes and subdue demonic enemies, and sever every bond of affliction.
With a mind of equanimity and tranquility, I praise the mass of merit of the Muni;
dedicating this to all sentient beings throughout the Dharmadhātu, may they together realize the fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King, knowing that the assembly of Brahmā devas had praised the Buddha’s virtues in verse, joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke this verse:
“The Muni has thoroughly understood the phenomena of the world;
He is certain that they are empty and false, like an empty fist, And like autumn clouds or a flash of lightning. The Buddha constantly reveals this to dispel all delusions.”
Just as a person in a dream, oppressed by hunger, Encounters and partakes of various exquisite and delicious meals,
Yet ultimately there is neither food nor a person— The Dharma realized by the Tathāgata is likewise so.

Furthermore, just as one who is parched with thirst in a dream May drink the sweet, cool water of ambrosia, One should know that both the thirst and the drinking are entirely non-existent; The Dharma realized by the Tathāgata is likewise so.
Just as one hears exquisite words within a dream, yet the characteristics of those words cannot be found in reality—
there being neither a speaker nor a listener— one who understands phenomena in this way is free from doubt.
Furthermore, just as a lute produces exquisite sounds, yet those sounds fundamentally lack intrinsic nature, so too does the wise contemplate the principle of the aggregates:
they know that the intrinsic nature of the aggregates cannot be found.

There is no agent, no recipient, and no sentient being; there is no action performed nor any retribution received, nor is there anyone who experiences that fruit of retribution—the Buddha is perfectly clear regarding this principle.
Just as a mani jewel is translucent and pure, Which changes its hue according to the cloth upon which it is placed,
So too the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is fundamentally free from defilement, Yet it becomes increasingly stained by following after conceptual discrimination.
Furthermore, as when a conch is blown and a great sound is produced, if one seeks the source from which that resonance arises, its inherent nature is found to be fundamentally empty;
the Buddha’s realization of all phenomena is likewise so.
Furthermore, just as worldly fragrant and delicious delicacies Are composed of a combination of various flavors,
And when one contemplates the nature of food, it is fundamentally empty, So too does the Buddha understand all phenomena.
Like the celestial king’s banner, exceedingly high and manifest, It displays all manner of forms without thought;
The inherent nature of that banner is originally empty— The Dharma realized by the Great Sage is likewise so.

Furthermore, just as the body is formed by depending on various conditions, and its essential nature cannot be found upon investigation, one should know that the aggregates are fundamentally like this; the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata is also thus.
Furthermore, just as the sound produced by striking a drum Can cause those who hear it to feel joy,
Yet that resonance is originally empty, So too is the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata.

Just as when a person strikes a drum with a mallet, one seeks from which direction its sound appears, and further investigates toward which direction it vanishes; so too is the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, just as the resonance of a drum has neither hatred nor love, and it rings forth only when separated from the conditions of moisture, so too is this body empty and false by nature; the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata is likewise.
Just as when a person strikes a drum and sound arises, that sound occurs spontaneously without being summoned;
realizing the body is like that, empty of intrinsic nature, the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata is also thus.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of Brahmās and Mahābrahmā, praised the Tathāgata with a tranquil mind. He then emitted a great radiance from his mouth, causing those present in the assembly to behold this light, whereby their right view was made firm and their pure wisdom was further increased.
Then the Venerable Aśvajit Bhikṣu asked in verse:
“The Tathāgata now manifests a wondrous sign, Radiating pure light most rare and marvelous.
Gods, humans, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits— Beholding this supernatural transformation, all harbor doubts.”
The Supreme Muni, the Tamer of Men, manifests this auspicious omen for no reason other than a cause;
we pray that the Buddha will explain the origin of this light, so that all those gathered here may have their hearts filled with joy.
With single-minded devotion we give rise to longing, gazing upon your compassionate countenance without ceasing for even a moment;
if we may hear the Buddha’s Brahma-voice, each and every one shall have their doubts dispelled and develop faith and understanding.
The Tathāgata manifests these supernatural feats; surely it is out of compassionate regard for all sentient beings.
For what reason do you emit this pure radiance? Now is the very time; we hope for your instruction.
By the power of skillful means of the Great Sage Muni, you have caused those suited to the occasion to give rise to the supreme resolve;
as this assembly stands before the Buddha with palms joined, we pray only that the Tathāgata will swiftly expound it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣu Aśvajit:
"Aśvajit, you behold this radiance, Which serves to bring all sentient beings to maturity.
If the assembly hears what I have spoken at this time, They shall never regress from bodhi."
The Great Brahma King, the Brahma hosts, and others, Thoroughly realized the nature of phenomena and eliminated all doubt;
Throughout nayuta eons, they have Cultivated boundless pure practices.
Untainted by attachment toward any sensory objects, their minds are like space, free from all hindrance;
they constantly delight in bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, yet do not realize the fruit of enlightenment for themselves.
Furthermore, in a future age, after the passing of immeasurable *koṭi* kalpas,
they will fully cultivate and realize the gates of liberation; having accomplished the power of infinite great patience,
they shall thereafter attain the unsurpassed path, known as the Tathāgata Mahākṣāntibalas.
Taming and gathering all living beings, he observes that all worlds are empty and quiescent.
That Buddha’s lifespan is exceedingly long, equal to the number of kalpas spent in former practice;
possessing great majesty, virtue, and renown, he is able to uproot the suffering of birth and death for sentient beings.
That Buddha-field is supremely adorned and pure, Its wealth, joy, and abundance are peerless;
Even were one to speak for *nayuta* eons, One could not exhaustively describe its merits.
That Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma is inconceivable; its self-nature is empty and quiescent, with nothing upon which to rely.
All sentient beings within that land bring their roots of goodness to maturity, without any diminution.
All have exhausted the limits of suffering within saṃsāra; not a single one shall again receive a future body.
Even the names of ghosts, animals, and hell-beings no longer exist; there remains only the suffering of conditioned formations in their constant flux.
Because they have realized that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, each has made a supreme vow to give rise to weary detachment;
therefore, all sentient beings in that land are forever able to be free from old age, sickness, and death.
Furthermore, those sentient beings practice well, no longer listening to other sounds,
but hearing only the dharmas of selflessness, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, quiescence, and signlessness.
Upholding the Buddha’s words with heedfulness, Always cultivating pure and authentic conduct,
One seeks the gateway to liberation, the nectar of immortality, The supreme and most excellent path to enlightenment.
All the stūpas and temples in that land, whether walls, enclosures, or groves of trees, all emit the pure and wondrous sound of the Dharma;
those who hear it shall all ascend to the stage of non-retrogression.
This is due to the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, Who utters these eight kinds of Brahma-sounds;
Having heard them, one abandons the flow of birth and death, Seeking to realize the tranquil, true, and eternal bliss.
All sentient beings within that land, who have already practiced for a long time over kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges for the sake of Bodhi, shall now, in due order, attain Buddhahood.
The Great Brahmā King and his retinue of Brahmā hosts, Through the constant cultivation and realization of the principle of quiescence,
At that time, those Buddhas and sentient beings Together partook of the nectar-flavor of quiescence.
Furthermore, observing that the realm of sentient beings is fundamentally empty, they never for a moment give rise to thoughts of weariness;
thus, they are able to enter universally into the nature of all phenomena, constantly practicing the tranquil conduct of signlessness.

**Chapter 21: The Prediction for the Gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven** *The Compendium of the Sūtra on Father and Son, Chapter Twenty-one: The Prediction for the Gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven* At that time, within the assembly, there were eighty koṭis of gods from the Ābhāsvara Heaven. Seeing the various asura kings, up to the Brahmā kings, each manifesting supernatural transformations before the World-Honored One to present offerings, and further hearing the Tathāgata bestow upon them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they leaped for joy with unprecedented delight.
At that time, the Lord of Devas rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet in respectful salutation, and stood before the Buddha.
He addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
There is a samādhi called "Illuminating All Dharmas.
If there is a bodhisattva who skillfully cultivates this samādhi, they will be able to penetrate and understand all dharmas;
furthermore, they will attain immeasurable eloquence, namely:

They possess unattached eloquence, empowered eloquence, skillful eloquence, exquisite eloquence, agreeable eloquence, unbound eloquence, secure eloquence, profound eloquence, subtle eloquence, and peerless eloquence, until they attain all the supreme eloquence of a Tathāgata.
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is it called the ‘Samādhi that Illuminates All Dharmas’?

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains this samādhi, they will have no discursive thought (*vitarka*) or sustained reflection (*vicāra*), nor any mental engagement (*manasikāra*) with respect to any dharma; if they are free from these, then there will be no doubt.”
If one eliminates doubt regarding all phenomena, one will attain unimpeded penetration in all places.

Why is this? Because those phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); if one realizes that the intrinsic nature of phenomena does not exist, that bodhisattva is then able to enter and understand the gateway of the meaning of the letter *A*.
That which is called *a* is non-action; *a* is omnipresent; *a* is not conditioned; *a* is not unconditioned;
*a* is that in which nothing is not accomplished; *a* has no basis of dependence;
*a* is not movement; *a* is not confusion; *a* is not conceptualization; *a* is not apart from conceptualization.
"A" is not ultimate; "A" is not disintegration; "A" is not form-color; "A" is not manifest color;
"A" is not sustenance; "A" is not fixed abiding; "A" is not cognition; "A" is not vision;
"A" is not verbal expression; "A" is not the departure from verbal expression.
"A" is not conceptual thought; "A" is not the departure from conceptual thought.
"A" is neither going nor coming; "A" is neither entering nor exiting. "A" is not manifest action; "A" is not non-manifest action.
"A" is not name; "A" is not sign. "A" is not antidote; "A" is not obscuration. "A"...
"A" is not exhaustion; "A" is not non-exhaustion; "A" is not duality; "A" is not non-duality;
"A" is not reality; "A" is not falsehood; "A" is not seeking; "A" is not free from seeking;
"A" is not purity; "A" is not free from purity; "A" is not grasping.
"A" is not the abandonment of grasping; "A" is non-arising, wherein there is nothing that does not arise, for there is not even the slightest dharma that can arise.
"A" is non-extinction, wherein there is nothing that does not extinguish, for there is not even the slightest dharma that can be extinguished.
"A" is not empty, wherein there is nothing that is not empty. "A" is signless, wherein there is nothing that is not signless. "A" is non-... [the text continues]
Aspiration is that which aspires to nothing.
Having understood it thus, one knows it is not frivolous conceptual proliferation; this is called entering the gateway of understanding the meaning of the letter A.
"World-Honored One!..."

Furthermore, all phenomena arise from the mind; by means of the syllable *a*, the syllable *da* is induced. If one can enter into and understand the gateway of the syllable *da*, then one can enter into and understand all teachings.

That is to say, the entry into and understanding of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), manifest phenomena (*vijñapti-dharma*), non-manifest phenomena (*avijñapti-dharma*), conventional phenomena (*saṃvṛti-dharma*), and ultimate phenomena (*paramārtha-dharma*).
World-Honored One!
"As for the ultimate dharma, it is solely true suchness (*tathatā*). By what means can it be understood through verbal expression?
World-Honored One!

It is like a person performing various activities within a dream; the dream objects are not real, existing only as provisional names. Upon awakening, one realizes that they were all created by the mind."
World-Honored One!
Just as an echo reverberates within an empty valley, its self-nature is without reality and arises from a combination of conditions.
World-Honored One!
It is like a person created by magical illusion performing various illusory feats; the deluded, failing to understand this, claim they truly exist.
World-Honored One!
It is also like a mirage that falsely gives rise to the perception of water; the wise understand that it has no inherent substance from the very beginning.
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, just as various forms and images appear within a mirror, giving rise to false conceptualization though they are in reality unobtainable;
so too is the nature of all phenomena empty.
It is only to please those foolish ladies that I speak thus; in reality, all phenomena are fundamentally quiescent from the very beginning.
World-Honored One!
In the past, I heard the Dharma of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as taught by previous Buddhas, and thereby attained the vision of reality.
When these sons of the gods had finished speaking thus, they were approved by the Buddha; bowing their heads in prostration, they praised the Buddha with this verse:
“The World-Honored One has thoroughly realized the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), And is therefore able to explain all dharmas in successive stages.
All those wise true sons of the Buddha Are able to sport within the ocean of the Buddha’s teachings.”
In this world, those of little wisdom and deluded people, due to their attachment to a self, cannot understand that "I" and "mine" are primordially empty;
even if one searches throughout the ten directions, they cannot be found.
Just as one sees a mirage that is fundamentally not water, yet the deluded person’s false imagination interprets it as water;
so too do they grasp at a self through such inversion—all arising from defiled wisdom that obscures true gnosis.
Because of the five desires, they give rise to craving and attachment, And thus undergo all the agonizing pains of birth and death.
The intrinsic nature of the aggregates is originally empty, Yet fools fall pointlessly into the various realms of existence.
Lacking right wisdom, their minds are deranged; they falsely perceive various states of suffering as happiness.
Constantly scorched by the fires of the three poisons, they never awaken or give rise to fear.
Fools do not weary of their various defilements and delusions, As if they were following a bandit as a close friend;
Upon hearing the Tathāgata teach the emptiness of ultimate truth, They instead give rise to alarm and fear, or even treat it with contempt.
Just as a person of timid nature in this world, though holding a sharp sword, feels anxiety and fear in his heart;
so too does the Tathāgata expound the gateway of the True Dharma, namely the single syllable "A," which is subtle and secret.
Giving birth to the most supreme and true wisdom, like a tall tree growing from level ground,
you are well able to subdue the armies of all Māras and swiftly realize the path of unsurpassed Bodhi.
The Muni has many eminent disciples who have thoroughly realized this ultimate truth;
having themselves extinguished and subdued the defilements of the three poisons, they bestow the medicine of the Dharma upon others who are afflicted by poison.
Using the great ship and raft of the Eightfold Noble Path, He carries all sentient beings across the ocean of existence,
Causing them to know that all phenomena are originally empty, And bringing to rest all heterodox arguments and false discriminations.
The wise person abandons error to return to the right path;
having cultivated those roots of goodness in former lives, they realize that the essential nature of all phenomena is originally empty. With a mind free from attachment, one attains liberation.
If one realizes the nature of phenomena, one is identical to the Buddha; this is called the Great Wisdom Nārāyaṇa.
All phenomena are empty by nature, yet there is nothing that is empty; likewise, there is neither bondage nor a binder.
True Suchness is quiescent and free from all marks; its essence is neither defiled nor pure.
Because it is by nature primordially thus, it is neither bound by afflictions nor subject to cessation.
One who thus understands the nature of all phenomena will before long attain enlightenment;
having attained liberation for themselves, they also benefit others, skillfully discoursing on the correct principle without seeking reward.
Sentient beings constantly give rise to false conceptions, Clinging to the marks of male and female within objects;
They increase their ignorance and defiled minds, Just like thirsty deer rushing toward a mirage.
Beings are born into various realms by means of their respective karmas; all such karma arises from conceptual construction.
When one realizes that the essential nature of karma is fundamentally empty, there is ultimately no agent whatsoever.
We understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught; he reveals this inconceivable and wondrous Dharma-door.
We take refuge in the Great Teacher, the Muni, whose faculties are tranquil and who is free from all attachment.
The Tathāgata is pure and free from all blemish, Having perfected an ocean of boundless merit;
He acts as a illuminator within the triple world, Worthy of receiving the sublime offerings of the devas.
Within this great assembly today, we extol the Great Sage, the mass of immense merit;
well done, O peerless Honored One among bipeds, who has fully realized the true nature and meaning of all phenomena.
By the power of these roots of goodness thus obtained, I dedicate them to all sentient beings within the three realms of existence;
may they all be able to achieve the fruit of Bodhi within the pure lands of the future.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the devaputras of the Ābhāsvara Heaven—who had attained clear and thorough penetration into the Buddha-dharma and were endowed with supreme, vast, and great eloquence—perceived their hope for the Tathāgata to grant them the prophecy of Buddhahood.
Immediately from his mouth, he emitted a great radiance.
When the Venerable Aśvajit Bhikṣu beheld this event, he joined his palms toward the Buddha and asked in verse:
"O Great Compassionate One who protects and saves the world, You who have perfected the accumulation of auspicious merit, [Please explain] why you emit such light from your mouth?"
By the power of skillful means, he stilled the multitude of doubts, emitting this most rare radiance.
If those in the assembly hear what the Buddha has spoken, their hearts will give rise to pure faith and certain understanding;
they will diligently cultivate sublime practices to advance toward Bodhi, transcending the ocean of saṃsāric birth and death.
All devas, humans, and asuras are oppressed by old age, sickness, and death;
the Tathāgata, with a mind of constant great compassion, rescues them and causes them to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path.
Through courageous and great diligence, with a profound mind firm and free from retreat,
they delight in cultivating such sublime Dharma-gates, vowing to realize bodhi and seek the Buddha-wisdom.
Now this assembly is free from all other thoughts, gazing with single-minded devotion upon the Buddha’s compassionate countenance;
they wish to hear the Tathāgata’s subtle and wondrous voice, so that their net of doubts may be decisively severed and joy may arise.
Beholding the Buddha manifesting this miraculous transformation, emitting such pure light from his mouth—
like a chronic patient meeting a skilled physician, or like an infant gazing upon its compassionate mother.
Who is it that inquires into the profound treasury of Dharma, Fulfills the power of vast compassion and vows,
And attains the supreme gateway of secrets, Moving the Buddha to manifest such a rare occurrence?
The entire assembly rejoiced greatly in their hearts, hoping to hear the Buddha explain the causes and conditions of the light;
each was able to bring their pure mind to fulfillment and cultivate this samādhi accordingly.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣu Aśvajit:
“Aśvajit, you possess wondrous eloquence; Able to respond to the minds of the multitude, you have raised this question.
Now is the very time to explain this cause; This is indeed the power of the Tathāgata’s spiritual transformations.”
This assembly of devaputras from the Ābhāsvara Heaven, having in the past made offerings to countless Buddhas,
observed the suffering beings of the world and vowed to seek the Buddha-way in order to deliver them.
Having already cultivated vast and true practices, you will certainly attain all-knowledge;
for those who are deeply attached to false views, you shall point the way so that they all return to the Right Path.
Having heard the Buddha’s true teaching, they enter deeply into its meaning and flavor and develop profound respect,
just as women in the world feel their hearts fulfilled upon joyfully giving birth to a son.
These sons of the gods possess pure minds, Resolutely seeking the unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment;
Throughout nayuta eons in the past, They have cultivated supreme practices for the benefit of others.
The sentient beings to be transformed are limitless in number, All of whom are able to give rise to the Mahayana mind;
Endowed with merit and wisdom, their bodies adorned with the marks, They shall all become Buddhas during the Constellation Eon.
When those sons of gods attain Buddhahood, their lands will number immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions;
vast, exquisite, and inconceivable, their various adornments shall be beyond compare.
The three evil realms and the eight states of no leisure are never heard of in those Buddha-fields;
nor are there any who seek realization through the two vehicles, for all have individually ascended to the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, within those various Buddha-fields, the lifespans of sentient beings are all equal, reaching a full ten billion Ganges-sands;
they are always able to serve and attend upon the Buddhas.
If one were to cause ten billion sentient beings to attain extinction by relying on the Dharma of the Two Vehicles,
it would not equal the merit of being able to transform a single person— whether male or female— to cultivate the Great Practice.
Compared to this, the former mass of merit does not equal even one-hundred-thousand-millionth part;
how much less so for those who encourage many others to abide securely in the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path.
Aśvajit, you should now listen attentively: the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is exceedingly rare;
it is like the udumbara flower, which is difficult to encounter even after the passing of boundless kalpas.
A Dharma teacher skilled in expedient means, who can reveal the true, unconditioned path—
those who aspire to seek the tranquility of bodhi should revere and constantly draw near to such a one.
Nayuta-s of devaputras scattered exquisite jeweled robes, descending from the sky;
they further praised the Tathāgata’s supreme merits with pure and wondrous gāthās.
The Buddha has preached the Dharma of tranquil nectar, Which can dispel the fever of afflictions for all sentient beings;
If one follows and practices according to the Tathāgata’s teaching, One will gradually attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
The Sutra of the Combined Collection of Father and Son, Volume Ten.
The Sutra of the Combined Collection of Father and Son, Volume Eleven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court-Dispersing Grandee.

Translated by the Imperial Decree by the Qianfandashi (Master of the Dharma-sounds) Shramana Risheng, a recipient of the purple robe, and others, serving as the Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.

Chapter Twenty-two: The Prediction for the Śubhakṛtsna Devas. At that time, within the assembly, there were twelve nayutas of Śubhakṛtsna devas. Seeing all the asura kings up to the Ābhāsvara devas making various offerings to the World-Honored One, and further hearing the Tathāgata bestow upon them the prediction of Buddhahood, their hearts were filled with joy at having attained what they had never experienced before.

These sons of the gods, who had already planted the roots of all virtues under immeasurable Buddhas in the past, who had entered into and understood the True Dharma, were replete with the wealth of the Dharma, possessed great supernormal powers, and moved with sovereign ease and without obstruction; they rose from their seats, prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads, and said:
"World-Honored One!

There is a samādhi called "Surpassing the Joy of All Dharmas. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains and realizes such a wondrous samādhi, all their activities will be free from all攀缘 (pān-yuán, objective attachments), they will attain the most supreme bliss, and no painful sensation will arise; there shall not be a single cause or condition that does not give rise to the perception of joy.
Even if they enter into the various hells and are subjected to the torments and coercion of diverse instruments of punishment,
by the power of this bodhisattva’s samādhi, all such suffering and affliction are transformed into bliss.

Just as those various sentient beings in the world who commit evil deeds and acts of non-restraint—plundering the wealth of others and being executed by royal law, having their ears and noses cut off, or their hands and feet severed, or being beaten with clubs, or bound with ropes, and being imprisoned in dungeons by wardens—even though they undergo such agonizing suffering, their minds feel no remorse; being shrouded by greed, they instead perceive it as pleasure.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who sustain themselves by selling their labor; they seek their livelihood through arduous toil, taking suffering for pleasure—such as those who tailor clothes, those who fashion wax candles, those who press sugarcane juice, those who perform music, those who prepare food and drink, those who provide wine for elephants, or those who light lamps of ghee or oil.

Regarding such various activities as these, whether they were performed improperly or with negligence and indolence, resulting in being scolded, rebuked, or dismissed by their masters and subjected to all manner of humiliation, they perceived them all as pleasure.

Furthermore, it is like the actors of this world who, in order to bring joy to others, change their own appearances to assume the faces of owls or lions; though they are beaten or bound, they instead conceive the notion of pleasure.
Why is this? Because those sentient beings have fixed their karmic actions, being driven by greed and having no remorse in their hearts.
It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:

For the benefit of sentient beings, they are able to practice various difficult and painful austerities throughout the long night of birth and death, aspiring for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; even to the point of saving beings from hunger and thirst by consuming their own flesh and blood, they always give rise to thoughts of joy.
Should they encounter a bodhisattva who reviles, beats, binds, or even takes their life, they give rise to a perception of joy despite experiencing such suffering and affliction.

Thus, being fully endowed with the power of vast vows, able to bestow various forms of happiness upon sentient beings, and practicing for a long duration without interruption, they will be able to attain that samādhi, remain undisturbed by evil māras, and further destroy all demonic activities; they shall then obtain these five kinds of mastery.
What are the five? First, mastery over lifespan;
second, mastery over rebirth; third, mastery over karmic retribution; fourth, mastery over investigation and analysis; and fifth, mastery over enjoyment.

If that bodhisattva seeks to attain equal and perfect enlightenment in a single lifetime, by attaining such a sublime samādhi, they will be able to fulfill their vow for bodhi according to their wish.

If one does not swiftly seek unexcelled bodhi, then one can dwell for immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya kalpas, benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields.

Why is this? Because from the moment they first resolve their minds toward enlightenment, those bodhisattvas universally seek to gather in and sustain all sentient beings; they do not fear the evil realms and take birth therein, causing all beings to practice and study the various bodhisattva deeds, master skillful means to penetrate all phenomena, and bring the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) to maturity.
This is what it means to be one who is well-established in the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva delights in cultivating such a samādhi, one should know that this person is sustained by the majestic spiritual power and merit of the Tathāgata; they will then certainly enter into and understand that the self-nature of all phenomena is fundamentally empty, without any doubt.”
When the Śubhakṛtsna devaputra had spoken these words, he joined his palms in homage and praised the Buddha with this verse:
“We Śubhakṛtsna devaputras, who are able to understand the Buddha’s True Dharma,
Bow our heads in reverent salutation to the Teacher of Men, Whose faculties are tranquil and who is free from all fear.”
The Tathāgata, by the power of his great wisdom, is able to utterly destroy all the armies of Māra;
I take refuge in the Most Supreme Muni, who guides all sentient beings to the further shore.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-existent, and they likewise ultimately have no place of abiding;
one thoroughly understands the攀緣 (pān-yuan) of false conceptualization, just as a magician clearly perceives his illusions.
Thus, all sentient beings of the six realms of existence arise from false causes and conditions;
like an echo, they have no intrinsic nature when sought, and the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata is likewise so.
The Lion of the Śākyas, supreme among men, observes that all delusive phenomena are entirely empty;
therein is neither the mark of a self nor a person, nor the notions of a sentient being or a life-span.
The Tathāgata’s great compassion is peerless; To deliver the deluded, he has appeared in the world.
He expounds the Dharma of the true mark, wondrous and inconceivable, Which none at all can fathom.
The Buddha contemplates the equality of the realm of sentient beings, Constantly giving rise to pure, unconditioned compassion;
Thus he is able to pity all the worlds, Yet ultimately perceives no mark of a sentient being.
Now, regarding the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom, my mind is free from defilement and all doubt;
through the gateway of pure compassion, I benefit sentient beings and am worthy of receiving the vast offerings of the devas.
The Tathāgata, the most supreme among gods of gods, Constantly gives rise to compassionate protection for all sentient beings;
Yet throughout the worlds of the ten directions, The nature of suffering cannot be found.
Since there are neither sentient beings nor suffering, the Tathāgata has no object of perception;
having already dispelled all grief and doubt, he has realized the bliss of true, eternal tranquility.
The Buddha perceives no suffering within the various realms of existence, nor is there any great enlightenment to be realized;
yet out of compassion for sentient beings, he causes them all to cast off the bonds of birth and death.
There is no suffering, no rescue, and no sentient beings; Nor is there any bodhi that can be attained.
The Buddha knows that the nature of phenomena is fundamentally thus; Therefore, I extend sublime offerings to the Buddha.
The Tathāgata appears in the world, benefiting sentient beings through the four immeasurables;
yet he perceives no mind of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, or equanimity, nor does he perceive the mark of a "sentient being.
He sees no one practicing negligence, nor does he see anyone cultivating the Noble Path.
Knowing such skillful means of the Buddha, I therefore offer worship to the Buddha.
The Muni constantly teaches the four foundations of mindfulness; he observes that the body is ultimately ungraspable.
Understanding the Buddha’s teaching in this way, I now obtain the opportunity to worship the Savior of the World.
The Buddha taught that feeling cannot be apprehended, Because feeling lacks any true inherent nature;
Even so it is with the feeler— Therefore, I offer worship to the Buddha.
The Buddha taught the contemplation of the mind and the contemplation of phenomena; seeking these two aspects, they cannot be found.
Nor does one see anything that is cultivated as mindfulness, nor anyone who abides in the foundations of mindfulness.
I now do not perceive any phenomena, nor do I perceive one who cultivates the Dharma;
the Buddha delivers sentient beings through the foundations of mindfulness, yet the intrinsic nature of that mindfulness is eternally empty and quiescent.
Furthermore, it is taught that mindfulness is conjoined with the Dharma; Those seeking liberation should cultivate this practice.
Thus have I understood the Buddha's teaching, And now I am able to make offerings to the Omniscient One.
Since even a single foundation of mindfulness cannot be found, how much less can there be two, three, or four?
Therefore, I now realize the Buddha’s intent: ultimately, there is no one who experiences suffering or pleasure.
The Tathāgata has always taught the four right efforts;
if there are bhikṣus who single-mindedly practice them, this can serve as the cause for liberation, enabling them to cross the ocean of saṃsāric birth and death.
Thus there is neither liberation nor bondage, Neither Buddha, nor Dharma, nor Bodhi;
Yet you do not destroy their conventional designations— Therefore, I prostrate in reverence to the Buddha.
The Buddha taught the four bases of psychic power that grant the wish-fulfilling mind; they are the most supreme, excellent, peaceful, and blissful.
For those whose faculties are tranquil and who have attained liberation, practicing these leads to the path of Nirvana.
Furthermore, regarding that *ṛddhi* and *abhijñā*, if one observes their essence with clarity, it cannot be seen;
it is neither moving nor still, neither active nor inactive—thus it manifests in a way that is difficult to conceive.
The sons of the gods in this present assembly do not harbor the notion of a "sentient being";
having correctly understood the Buddha's teaching, they are all able to remain far removed from every doubt.
This is the supreme offering of Dharma; only a Buddha is worthy of receiving such an offering.
Since the Tathāgata’s wondrous wisdom is peerless, I have offered praise from the depths of my heart.
Furthermore, the Muni has taught the five faculties;
This Dharma can attain the path to enlightenment, Giving rise to the two provisions of merit and wisdom; Those who observe well eliminate heedlessness.

Regarding what are called faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—seeing neither the one who practices nor that which is attained—I have no doubt concerning the Buddha’s Dharma; therefore, I shall now offer worship.
The Tathāgata has proclaimed the five powers, which can eliminate the crookedness of mind and false views,
quell all afflictions, destroy all Māras, and lead one toward the unconditioned path of tranquility.
Thus these powers cannot be overcome; there is nothing bound, nor any binder.
Having become free from all doubt regarding the Buddha’s Dharma, I shall now make offerings to the Tamer of Men.
The Great Sage reveals the seven factors of enlightenment, The most supreme and pure path to bodhi;
Sentient beings who skillfully practice them Shall realize the state of true, eternal peace.
The Muni further taught the Eightfold Noble Path, which ripens the roots of goodness in all sentient beings;
