by constantly cultivating noble wisdom that manifests before them, one can exhaust the limits of suffering and all its fetters.
Thus, noble wisdom and all afflictions are ultimately pure without exception;
the devas have attained freedom from doubt regarding this, and so I make offerings to the Sage among Men.
Having well cultivated śamatha, and likewise vipaśyanā,
the Tathāgata has fully perfected them throughout vast eons, and is thus able to sever all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies.
Thus, the associated cause and its fruit, as well as the observer, are all empty;
the gods have attained freedom from doubt regarding this, and therefore I make offering to the Lord Muni.
The Buddha taught the contemplation of impurity to eliminate lust, loving-kindness as the antidote to hatred, and wisdom to dispel delusion;
all this was spoken by the Buddha for the benefit of sentient beings.
They are all without action and without the mark of transgression; therefore, they are neither defiled nor pure.
The devas have attained freedom from doubt regarding this, and thus they make offerings to the Unsurpassed One.
Furthermore, the Buddha taught the ten unwholesome paths: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and double-tongued speech;
harsh words, frivolous talk, greed, anger, and delusion—these are called the ten courses of action.
Sentient beings do not exist, nor is there killing; the same principle applies to the other nine transgressions.
There is no distinction between good and evil, nor is there any remedy, for the nature of those offenses is fundamentally empty and quiescent.
This meaning is not devoid of the Buddha’s authentic teaching, yet it does not destroy the essential nature of phenomena.
Such is the supreme Dharma of the Muni, which proclaims and guides all deluded beings;
one should attend to it with correct mental application and right reflection.
"This is called being the most supreme true son of the Buddha.
At that time, after the sons of the gods from the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven had spoken these verses, they all remained silent, standing to one side.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the devaputras and their longing for the bestowal of a prophecy, suddenly emitted pure light from his mouth.
Having witnessed this event, the Venerable Aśvajit joined his palms toward the Buddha and asked him in verse:
“Excellent is the Great Holy Lord, the Tamer of Men; For the benefit of all beings, you have appeared in the world.”
Your profound wisdom is wondrous and inconceivable, Able to transform and subdue the hosts of devas.
O Savior who has exhausted all phenomena, This manifestation of auspicious signs is not without cause;
Since you can act as a guide for sentient beings, I pray only that the Benevolent One will expound it for us.
This multitude of Śubhakṛtsna devaputras joined their palms in praise of this most rare occurrence;
gazing up at the Tathāgata, the mountain of merit, they heard his words and received them with single-minded devotion upon the crowns of their heads.
The Buddha is the supreme teacher of gods and humans;
having thoroughly realized all phenomena without hindrance, may he take pity on all sentient beings and explain this miraculous manifestation of emitting light.
Whoever in this life gives rise to a pure mind and understands these subtle and wondrous nectar-like verses,
shall attain the all-encompassing, perfectly luminous omniscience throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Who, in future Buddha-fields, will benefit and gather in all deluded beings,
skillfully proclaim the unsurpassed, wondrous wheel of Dharma, and subdue the armies of Māra and heterodox disputants?
These sons of the gods have deeply entered the flavor of the meaning within the Buddha’s teaching, their minds firmly resolved;
we only pray that the Tathāgata will resound the Dharma-voice, causing all those gathered here to cast off the net of doubt.
The Unsurpassed One, adorned with a hundred blessings, With a heart of loving-kindness universally covering the world,
Possessing the eightfold qualities of Brahma’s voice— May all beings hear and uphold the Buddha’s instructions.
If there are sentient beings who, in the presence of the Buddha, delight in hearing the True Dharma and practice it with diligence,
and whose resolve for Bodhi is firm and non-retrogressive, they will gradually be able to accomplish all-knowledge.
The Tathāgata has well expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma, Which can exhaust the suffering of birth and death for sentient beings.
Sons of the Buddha, you should uphold it with a pure mind, So that the lineage of the Buddhas shall never be severed.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣu Aśvajit:
"Aśvajit, you have asked well concerning the emission of light; For the sake of the benefit and happiness of all devas and humans, The merit you have gained is inconceivable;
Even if one were to explain it through metaphors, it would never be exhausted."
Excellent! The Venerable One has responded to their capacities; the entire great assembly rejoices in their hearts.
These gods and humans of the Universal Purity Heaven have attained liberation within my Dharma.
In the past, they made offerings to billions of nayutas of Buddhas;
having realized the nature of all dharmas without doubt, each of them questioned those Buddhas regarding this very meaning.
Due to causes and conditions from the past, he praised the Buddha with sublime gāthās;
in this life, moreover, with a pure mind, he extolled all the Sugatas of the Bhadrakalpa.
In a future Udumbara kalpa, he shall attain Buddhahood under the name Nārāyaṇa;
he will teach and transform nayutas of sentient beings, causing them all to realize the bliss of unconditioned tranquility.
Appearing in the world within a single eon, all shall be named Dharmadhvaja, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones;
they shall deliver an equal number of sentient beings, and each, in succession, shall attain the Way of the Buddha.
When these Tathāgatas have completed their work of transformation, they distribute their remaining physical relics;
they establish immeasurable stūpas, as if scattering flowers to adorn the Buddha-fields.
All such classes of sentient beings, each making offerings to the śarīra,
shall all ascend the gate of tranquil nectar, as praised by all Tathāgatas.
If there are those who invoke the name of that Buddha, And give rise to pure faith and a joyful mind,
Know that by virtue of these wholesome causes and conditions, They shall encounter Maitreya Buddha in the future.
Because he was sustained by the compassionate World-Honored One, he applied himself with diligent vigor to sever all fetters;
delighting in the cultivation of tranquil śamatha, he gradually attained the fruit of arhatship.
Traveling from one buddha-field to another, making offerings and attending upon them without weariness or indolence,
they proclaim the supreme virtues of the Buddhas amidst the great assemblies of devas and humans.
Now these sons of the gods from the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, all endowed with majestic virtue and great renown,
having deeply penetrated the inconceivable wisdom of the Buddha, each prostrates at the feet of the Tathāgata.

Chapter 23: The Prediction for the Gods of the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) Heaven. The *Sūtra of the Combined Collection of Father and Son*, Chapter Twenty-Three: The Prediction for the Gods of the Vast Fruit Heaven. At that time, within the assembly, there were eighty million gods of the Vast Fruit Heaven who saw the various asura kings, up to and including the gods of the Universal Purity (*Śubhakṛtsna*) Heaven, making diverse arrangements and performing various offerings to the World-Honored One, presenting them to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, hearing that they were granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, their hearts were filled with great joy, experiencing what they had never known before.
These devaputras then thought to themselves:

"All dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata cannot be found when sought within the three periods of time; all faculties are ineffable. If one can enter into and understand that dharma-realm, then one will be able to penetrate all dharmas."

If one can thoroughly understand all phenomena, then one can realize the four truths as they truly are—namely, the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path. As the Blessed One has said, all phenomena are entirely empty and quiescent; they are without self, without person, without sentient being, without life-span, without perception, and without agency.
"We, O World-Honored One, have attained definitive understanding within this Dharma and no longer give rise to doubt or confusion.
Because all sentient beings are fundamentally quiescent, there is no suffering."
It should be understood in this way. Why is that?
Because sentient beings do not exist, the Truth of Suffering also does not exist.
Because suffering does not exist, the truth of the origin also does not exist. Why is this?
If this cause does not exist, then its effect cannot exist.
World-Honored One!
Because there is no origination, the truth of cessation also does not exist. Why is this?
If there were no Truth of Origination, there would be no abandonment of origination.
Because there is no cessation, the Truth of the Path would also not exist. Why is this?
"There is no such path as one that does not sever the accumulation [of karma].
World-Honored One!
Because those afflictions and karmas cannot be apprehended, the severing of afflictions and their cessation likewise cannot be apprehended."
Because cessation cannot be apprehended, the path likewise cannot be apprehended; as long as this path does not yet exist, its fruit cannot exist.
These Four Noble Truths are merely conventional designations established through conceptual differentiation.
Because they do not exist, they cannot be described as past, present, or future. Why is this?
The past has already ceased; the present does not abide; and the future has not yet arrived.
Within the three periods of time, [these] are all unobtainable.
According to conventional truth, there are various appearances;

yet if the three periods do not exist, then there is no arising and no cessation. There is no perception, no volitional action, no giving, no receiving, no speaking, and no listening. There is no dharma taught, and no one who realizes it, because those three times have never existed.

Whether phenomena or emptiness, all are ineffable; yet sentient beings, due to their inversions, are unable to enter into understanding them. They are without cause and without condition, without name and without mark, without anything to be expressed, and without any direction toward which they tend; because their intrinsic nature is detached, they are all unattainable.
That is neither obtainable nor unobtainable. Why is this? Because the realm of sentient beings is fundamentally non-existent.

If all those various phenomena are unobtainable, then there is neither defilement nor purity; there is no action and no realization; there is no stage of ordinary beings, no stage of śrāvakas, no stage of pratyekabuddhas, no stage of bodhisattvas, and no stage of Tathāgatas. It is neither a stage nor a non-stage; this is precisely suchness—quiescent and signless.

If one says that the Tathāgata is named as such because he possesses manifest action (*vijñapti*) and conditioned limitations (*saṃskṛta-pramāṇa*), this is spoken according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); it is not that a Tathāgata exists in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Why is this so?
Because phenomena are unattainable.

If that Tathāgata were to extensively proclaim the realm of form up to the realm of consciousness, and likewise the mental realm up to the realm of phenomena—if there were no realm of phenomena, there would be nothing upon which to rely, nor anything to be expressed;
there would be no Four Noble Truths, no five faculties, and no dependent origination, and so forth.
World-Honored One!
All those dharmas, according to their respective locations, are established and arranged with various names; yet they do not destroy the essential nature of that dharma-realm.
“World-Honored One!
Just as the element of earth is given various names according to its location, yet it does not destroy the intrinsic nature of that element of earth;
so too it is with the elements of water, fire, wind, and space—the establishment of different names for them is likewise.”
World-Honored One!

Furthermore, one who realizes and enters that dharmadhātu is able to penetrate and understand the twenty-two faculties, namely: the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, female faculty, male faculty, life faculty, suffering faculty, pleasure faculty, grief faculty, joy faculty, equanimity faculty, mind faculty, faith faculty, diligence faculty, mindfulness faculty, concentration faculty, wisdom faculty, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."
World-Honored One!
If the eye and the essence of the eye cannot be apprehended, and if the faculties and the essence of the faculties likewise cannot be apprehended—
for what reason is this so?

Because the eye is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and cannot be perceived, if a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it is not a functional entity (*bhāva*). Since it is not a functional entity, it cannot be produced; and since it cannot be produced, it does not arise.
If it does not arise, then it does not cease; because it is neither arising nor ceasing, it cannot be described as past, present, or future.
That which has no arising or ceasing within the three periods of time is neither the eye nor the faculty of sight;
how could there be any activity or conventional designation for it?
World-Honored One!
For example, an empty fist contains no object at all; it merely deceives ignorant children and exists as a mere conventional designation.
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), even the name established for an empty fist cannot be found.
In this manner, even the eye and the visual faculty do not exist within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
*Pitṛputrasamāgama-sūtra*, Scroll 11;
