Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Official, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master of Propagating the Dharma, the Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Rìchēng, et al., by Imperial Decree.
From the remainder of the "Chapter on the Prophecy of the Gods of the Vast Fruit Heaven": "World-Honored One!..."
Thus, the aggregate of form has no measure, nothing that sustains it, and is not an object of entry or comprehension. Why is this?
Because the intrinsic nature of form cannot be apprehended.
If all phenomena were not produced through conditioning, there would be no accumulation; it is because of this accumulation that they are called "aggregates" (*skandha*).

It is just as in the world, where houses, palaces, towers, windows, balconies, gardens, canals, and surrounding walls are constructed from a multitude of materials gathered together, and this collection is then called a "city."
One should know that those forms have never existed from the beginning; by what dharma, then, could they be called an accumulation?
Since there is no accumulation, there are likewise no aggregates (skandhas).
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
If one attains penetration and understanding regarding each of the aggregates, the created pure matter that sustains their intrinsic nature is found to be ungraspable;
one should know that the earth element and the nature of the earth element are ultimately pure, and likewise, up to the wind element and the nature of the wind element, they are all ultimately pure.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is devoid [of such characteristics].
Furthermore, why speak of the existence of marks such as arising and ceasing in the past, present, and future?
Therefore, the aggregate of form cannot be differentiated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise cannot be differentiated.
World-Honored One!

Furthermore, if the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the eye does not exist, being primordially pure and devoid of suffering, it is merely displayed through conventional designations; both that name and its substance are unobtainable.

Why is this? Because in reality there is not the slightest dharma that can be named "eye," nor is there the slightest dharma that can be named a "base" (*āyatana*). Likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and the bases of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and dharmas—all lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and are primordially pure. Both suffering and the name "suffering" are both unattainable.
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, that eye-element cannot be apprehended in the slightest degree. Why is this?
If the eye is separated from the nature of the eye, and if the elements (dhātu) are separated from the nature of the elements, and so on up to the dharma-element, it is likewise.

Because they are separated from their own-nature (svabhāva), they are not entities; because they are not entities, they are not produced; that which is not produced has no arising; that which has no arising also has no cessation; and that which is neither born nor ceasing has no establishment or designation of past, present, or future.

One should know that all phenomena are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature; if a phenomenon is devoid of intrinsic nature, it has no name or characteristic, no activity, nothing that can be spoken of, nothing to be praised, and no prediction of enlightenment.
When those sons of the gods had finished speaking thus, those in the assembly who heard it felt love and joy; they leaped for joy, having attained excellent benefit.
Then the Lord of the Gods rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!"

There is a samādhi named "Infinite Gateways of Meaning. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to cultivate this samādhi, they will obtain immeasurable eloquence, namely: continuous eloquence, corresponding eloquence, eloquence of correct exposition, unattached eloquence, infallible eloquence, subtle and secret eloquence, profound eloquence, skillful eloquence, exquisite eloquence, and eloquence of right discourse.
Having attained such sublime eloquence, they each enter and understand immeasurable Dharma-gates; being fully endowed with right view, they penetrate the nature of all phenomena;
they abandon objective clinging, extinguish the darkness of ignorance, and comprehend the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-dharma*).
They enter the gates of dhāraṇī, and they enter into the understanding of the aggregates (*skandha*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), and the elements (*dhātu*).

Regarding the faculties: entering into the understanding of the Four Noble Truths; entering into the understanding of dependent origination; entering into the understanding of sentient beings; entering into the understanding of the non-existence of sentient beings;

entering into the understanding of those with perception; entering into the understanding of those without perception; entering into the understanding of those with form; entering into the understanding of those without form;
entering into the understanding of self; entering into the understanding of non-self; entering into the understanding of emptiness; entering into the understanding of the non-empty...
He enters into the understanding of emptiness, enters into the understanding of signlessness, enters into the understanding of wishlessness,

enters into the understanding of renunciation, enters into the understanding of non-renunciation, enters into the understanding of the conditioned, and enters into the understanding of the unconditioned.
Within the teaching of the Tathāgata, it cannot be expressed; it is merely a provisional name, a conventional discrimination.

It is neither speech nor the absence of speech, neither thought nor the absence of thought, neither seeing nor the absence of seeing, neither hearing nor the absence of hearing, neither cognition nor the absence of cognition.
It is not knowledge, nor is it ignorance; it is not discernment, nor is it non-discernment; it is not awakening, nor is it non-awakening;
it is not attainment, nor is it non-attainment; it is not with opposition, nor is it without opposition;
it is not realization, nor is it non-realization; it is neither white nor black, neither light nor dark, neither shallow nor deep, and neither clear...
It is not turbid; it is neither tranquil nor moving; it is neither bound nor liberated; it is neither conformable nor contrary; it is neither defiled nor pure;
it neither goes nor comes; it neither arises nor ceases; it is neither wise nor foolish; it is neither formed nor destroyed;
it is neither the Path nor non-Path; it is neither grasping nor free from grasping; it is neither a sentient being nor...
There are no sentient beings; it is neither a life-span nor the absence of a life-span,
neither self nor non-self, neither existent nor non-existent, neither empty nor non-empty, neither with marks nor markless,
neither with vows nor vowless, neither renunciation nor non-renunciation, and not conditioned.
It is neither unconditioned nor conditioned; neither annihilated nor eternal; neither deviant nor correct;
neither true nor false; neither real nor illusory; neither abiding nor non-abiding; neither having a basis nor being without a basis;
neither liberation nor apart from liberation; neither observation nor realization; neither saṃsāra nor...

Nirvana is not the realm of ordinary beings, nor the realm of śrāvakas, nor the realm of pratyekabuddhas, nor the realm of bodhisattvas, nor the realm of buddhas; it is neither a realm nor a non-realm.
If one can thus enter into and understand the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), then one can enter into and understand dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda);

that is to say: ignorance conditions volitional formations (saṃskāra), volitional formations condition consciousness (vijñāna), and so on, until sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress constitute the great mass of suffering.
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, the nature of that ignorance cannot be apprehended. Why is this so?
Because they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

If a phenomenon is devoid of intrinsic nature, it is not a substantial entity; because it is not a substantial entity, it is ultimately pure. It is without arising or ceasing and is not subsumed within the three periods of time. It is without name, without marks, and cannot be demonstrated; furthermore, it is without description.

It is only for the sake of maturing foolish worldlings that these are provisionally established through conventional designations, giving rise to various conceptual proliferations; in the ultimate sense, however, they are truly unfindable.
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, if ignorance has no intrinsic nature, how could it give rise to the link of volitional formations?
Since ignorance does not exist, the link of volitional formations also does not exist;
and so on, until there is no birth-conditioned aging and death.
World-Honored One!
If dharmas are unarisen, how could there be aging?
If there is no aging, there would likewise be no illness or cessation.
The bodhi of all Buddhas of the three times is merely conventional, established through names and designations;
it is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Thus it is said: that which is called ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself bodhi, and all the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) are likewise bodhi.
To thus enter into and understand the twelvefold dependent origination is precisely to enter into and understand the true dharma-realm.
World-Honored One!
As the Tathāgata is unarisen, all dharmas are likewise unarisen.
Therefore, the dharma of non-arising is itself the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One,
the Tathāgata does not perish, and all dharmas likewise do not perish.
Therefore, the dharma that is non-extinguished is the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata is without marks, and all dharmas are also without marks; therefore, the dharma that is without marks is the Tathāgata.
To state the essentials: thus it is without name and without mark, neither defiled nor pure, neither loved nor hated; the dharma-realm cannot be cognized, nor can it be known.
World-Honored One!
True Suchness is the Tathāgata; all dharmas are True Suchness. Therefore, all dharmas are the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!
The reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) is the Tathāgata; all dharmas are the reality-limit; therefore, all dharmas are the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!
Whatever dharmas there may be are themselves the Tathāgata; within those dharmas, there are all dharmas. Therefore, all dharmas are themselves the Tathāgata.
"Bhagavān!
If someone were to say:
'The Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
"You should know that this person is one who clings to views.
Why is this? The Tathāgata is non-dual, and awakening (bodhi) is also non-dual; because they are non-dual, there is nothing to be attained."
"Bhagavān!
If someone were to say:
'The Tathāgata turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.'"
"You should know that such a person is one who clings to views.
Why is this? Because, in reality, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended as a Tathāgata, for the nature of all dharmas does not undergo transformation."
"Bhagavān!
If someone were to say:
'The Tathāgata has transformed and delivered immeasurable sentient beings.'"
"You should know that such a person is one who clings to views.
Why is this? In reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers."
"Bhagavān!
If someone were to say:
'The Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa because his conditions have been exhausted.'"
One should know that such a person is one who clings to views.
Why is this? Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is eternally abiding and is not subject to arising or ceasing.

If there are sentient beings who are able to believe and understand such essential teachings as I have spoken, you should know that these persons will attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
World-Honored One!

Even if the dharma-realm were subject to change, it would be impossible for a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has deep faith in this Dharma to ever regress from the Bodhi of the Buddha.

At that time, the devaputras of the Vast Fruit Heaven (Bṛhatphala), having spoken before the Tathāgata of the ultimate dharma they had realized, prostrated with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and with single-minded palms joined, praised the Buddha in verse:
"We take refuge in the Great Holy Lord, the Muni, Who is endowed with unsurpassed supreme wisdom;
Out of compassion for all sentient beings in the world, You constantly proclaim such the foremost truth."
Having accomplished an immeasurable mass of merit, you rescue and deliver beings from the causes of all suffering within saṃsāra;
having personally realized the nature of all phenomena, you are further able to reveal it to the multitude of living beings.
The intrinsic nature of the five aggregates is fundamentally non-existent; one should know that they merely deceive the foolish.
Like a monkey clinging to glue, those without wisdom remain in doubt and cannot escape.
When seeking the essence of the aggregates, it cannot be found; Having no place of dependence, it cuts off all攀緣 (pān-yuán, object-relations).
It is like adorning empty space with necklaces and ornaments; The wise attain liberation therein.
Furthermore, the Muni has declared that the intrinsic nature of all sense-bases is entirely non-existent;
they are like echoes transmitted through deep valleys—when one seeks those reverberations, what is there to be found?
Bound by these fetters, foolish worldlings do not understand the Dharma of True Reality;
they are like those who carry jewels and ornaments on the wind—the wise observe this and remain unattached.
The Omniscient One has declared: all elements are from the beginning eternally empty and quiescent;
they are like an empty fist shown to a child, which deceives and lures the ignorant, yet nothing real is obtained.
Ordinary fools, through deluded conceptualization, cling to things as existing;
because they cannot understand the ultimate truth, they wander in cyclic existence within the three realms, like merchants lost at sea.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has spoken thus: "The intrinsic nature of the sense faculties is eternally pure;
like reflections appearing in a mirror, when sought to their ultimate limit, they are fundamentally non-existent."
Lacking wisdom and beset by doubt, they cannot comprehend; deluded regarding the true Dharma, they give rise to false attachments.
Like fish fallen into a deep abyss and caught in a net, how can they be liberated from such entanglements?
Sentient beings are fundamentally empty, and phenomena are likewise empty; Relying on the supreme ultimate truth, nothing is to be apprehended.
Just as one perceives the form of a man painted upon a wall, The wise observe that there is no self therein.
Fools cling to things and give rise to attachment and delight; this is entirely due to their failure to comprehend the True Teaching.
Since causes and conditions have no inherent nature upon which to rely, they are like those born from eggs emerging from their shells.
Phenomena born of conditions exist for but a moment; arising briefly, they perish and lack solidity.
Like one experiencing the five desires within a dream, what joy can be found when seeking them upon waking?
Sentient beings, from time without beginning, have been bound by false discrimination to their objective realms;
if they can realize that the nature of phenomena is empty, they will be like birds escaping from a cage or net.
All phenomena are quiescent and beyond verbal expression; the Buddha was able to realize this very nature of phenomena.
All phenomena are quiescent and originally empty; the Buddha was thus able to enter parinirvāṇa.
All phenomena are quiescent and free from all marks; the Buddha can proclaim the ultimate truth.
The Buddha has no attachment within the three realms; it is for this reason that the Tathāgata appears in the world.
The Buddha is free from all fears regarding all phenomena, Because he does not give rise to the notions of self and other;
He extensively proclaims the True Teaching to shatter the delusions of the multitudes, And is thus called the One Who Skillfully Guides Sentient Beings.
The Buddha is free from conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena, yet he is able to assist in manifesting the ultimate truth;
this is solely the gateway of the Tathāgata’s skillful means, and is not the realm of ordinary beings.
Some sentient beings speak thus: "The Tathāgata has already realized great Bodhi";
some sentient beings speak thus: "The Tathāgata is able to turn the wondrous Wheel of Dharma";
some sentient beings speak thus: "The Tathāgata has already delivered as many beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."
Some people speak thus: "The Buddha has long been liberated from saṃsāra;
having already brought benefit to immeasurable sentient beings, he has entered the great nirvāṇa of tranquility."
All these are views clung to by ordinary beings, held by the factions of Māra;
they do not understand the Dharma of ultimate truth, and because they do not understand it, they do not know the Buddha.
If there are those who penetrate this True Dharma, these people will certainly attain Bodhi;
they will be able to extensively rescue and deliver all worlds, fully endowed with the most supreme collection of merit.
Such is this auspicious and quiescent Dharma, Its essence being True Suchness (tathatā) without change;
Only the Muni is able to realize and know it, And I have well attained the meaning of the true nature of reality (dharmatā).
Now these sons of the gods from the Vast Fruit Heaven, their minds fully resolved regarding the profound Dharma,
stand before the Buddha with palms joined in reverence and undistracted focus, proclaiming it extensively.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that those sons of the gods from the Vast Fruit Heaven had ultimately realized the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and could also increase the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) of the assembly, immediately emitted a great radiance from his mouth.
At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit, having observed this sign, joined his palms toward the Buddha and asked in verse:
“O Unsurpassed One, endowed with merit and wisdom, By what cause do you manifest this sign of supernatural power?”
I have heard from the Buddha in the past that if he emits pure light for the sake of great benefit,
the Tathāgata manifests this wondrous sign, which enables the assembly to find peace of mind;
may all devas, humans, and asuras alike wish to personally hear what the Buddha speaks.
For what reason does the Muni now suddenly emit this cool light from his mouth?
The great assembly stands before the Buddha with palms joined, gazing upon his venerable countenance without ceasing for even a moment.

The Buddha is the unsurpassed teacher of gods and humans; we pray that you will swiftly expound these rare signs, so that all sentient beings in every world may have their doubts dispelled upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching.
Now these hosts of devas from the Vast Fruit Heaven each know for themselves the matter of attaining Buddhahood;
therein there is nothing realized and nothing cultivated—what person could have acted, and what could be attained?
The Tathāgata’s eightfold Brahma-voice, once heard by sentient beings, brings them all joy;
they follow the correct principle and act according to the Dharma, and are all able to protect and uphold the Buddha’s teachings.
We, this great assembly, give rise to longing, hoping to hear it directly from the Buddha;
if we are granted the teaching on the causes cultivated in past lives, the various merits of humans and devas will increase.
Those sons of the gods have long planted the roots; they are certain to achieve all-knowledge.
They shall deliver immeasurable suffering beings, causing them to awaken to the true nature of reality, the self-nature of dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣu Aśvajit:
“Excellent, Aśvajit, that you have raised this question; I shall explain it to you in detail.
For the benefit of the devas and humans of the Bṛhatphala heaven, this auspicious sign has been manifested within the great assembly.”
The Tathāgata, endowed with all-encompassing wisdom, emits rays of light for three reasons;
observing those receptive capacities in accordance with their conditions, he manifests these auspicious and miraculous deeds.
Some delight in dwelling in nirvāṇa; with limited wisdom, they seek the vehicle of the śrāvakas.
Some cherish and delight in silence; their resolve is to seek the fruit of pratyekabuddha enlightenment.
Others delight in being great teachers of the world; they seek the bodhi of a Buddha to benefit all sentient beings.
Therefore, I observe those roots of goodness and provide them with teachings according to their inclinations.
For those who seek deliverance as Śrāvakas, I emit an inferior grade of light for them;
for those who seek liberation as Pratyekabuddhas, I emit a medium grade of light to save them.
Aśvajit, you should know that the Most Supreme Light has bestowed the prophecy of Buddhahood upon the sons of the gods.
According to their respective orders—lower, middle, and upper—he reveals the attainment of the fruits of the three vehicles.
If he emits light for the sake of śrāvakas, the light, having issued forth, disappears into his feet;
if he emits pure light for the sake of pratyekabuddhas, it appears and then vanishes into his navel;
if he emits it for those seeking the unsurpassed path, the light enters through the crown of the Buddha’s head.
According to their superior or inferior capacities, there are various manifestations; now I bestow upon the devas the prediction of the fruit of Buddhahood.
Bhikṣu Aśvajit, you should understand this: I shall now further explain the signs of the light.
If the light gradually increases and expands, winding through the air and turning to the right—
Equal in measure to the Buddha’s body, they are universally adorned, Resplendent like a mass of molten gold;
such manifestations of pure light Should be known as the prophetic declarations concerning the Buddha-fields.
If, once the light has issued forth, it is like a canopy, completely covering the Tathāgata’s body from above;
or if there is light like a flower abiding in mid-air, brilliantly manifesting his majestic and dignified marks;
or if the light circles three times and enters the Buddha’s body—these are all predictions of the Buddha’s lifespan.
You should know that the marks manifested by the Tathāgata skillfully respond to the minds of sentient beings who possess faith and joy.
These sons of the gods from the Vast Fruit Heaven, numbering eighty koṭis in total,
have for many nayutas of kalpas served and made offerings to the various Buddhas.
Always delighting in preaching this Dharma of ultimate truth, Transforming and benefiting sentient beings without weariness,
Vowing to seek the unsurpassed Great Bodhi, One practices with courageous diligence, never retreating.
Having passed through thirty-six koṭis of kalpas, Fully cultivating merit and wisdom and planting roots of goodness,
He delivers infinite sentient beings, Causing them all to leave suffering behind and attain peace and security.
Thereafter, they shall all attain Buddhahood, sharing the same name, Nārāyaṇa;
that kalpa shall be called Supreme Golden Banner, and each shall achieve perfect enlightenment in a different land.
Each and every Tathāgata appears in the world, Their lands are pure and wondrously adorned;
The Buddha’s body is like the disk of the pure sun, A mass of merit endowed with the light of wisdom.
The lifespans of those Tathāgatas are long and far-reaching;
they abide in the world for more than nayuta eons, each one transforming and delivering śrāvakas in numbers so vast they are immeasurable.
Even if calculators and their disciples were to employ metaphors and calculations, they could not know [the number];
the assembly of transformed bodhisattvas is likewise boundless, equal in number to that of the śrāvakas.
Thus, this assembly of bodhisattvas, practicing in unison with the former Buddhas,
shall all achieve omniscience by means of this firm resolve for enlightenment.
When those Tathāgatas have completed their work of transformation, the True Dharma shall long abide in the world;
for twelve nayutas of kalpas, it will be constantly guarded by the sons of the Buddha.
When the True Dharma flows widely, there shall be those who give rise to the great mind of Bodhicitta,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each diligently practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva.
Thus, after that Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa, all those śrāvakas who have attained realization will likewise seek to enter nirvāṇa,
just as a fire is extinguished when its fuel is exhausted.
Now that the great assembly has heard what the Buddha has spoken, they have all given rise to pure minds and attained faith and understanding;
with joy, they stand before the Buddha and with single-minded devotion prostrate at the Tathāgata’s feet.
With peerless and wondrous offerings, they present them to the Tamer, the Teacher of Gods and Men;
all resolve upon firm, courageous, and diligent effort, seeking liberation as if their very heads were on fire.
Diligently cultivate the supreme perfection of wisdom, And always delight in drawing near to teachers who preach the Dharma.
This is the most excellent and true gateway; O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves well therein.
The Compendium of Father and Son Sūtra, Volume Twelve;
The Compendium of Father and Son Sūtra, Volume Thirteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu.
Translated by the Imperial Envoy, Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master of Dharma, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject, Rìchēng, et al., by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Twenty-Four: The Gods of the Pure Abodes Speak Verses in Praise of the Buddha. At that time, within the assembly, there were countless gods of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) and immeasurable sentient beings who, regarding the Buddha’s Dharma, attained awakening in their minds, became free from all doubt and confusion, and gave rise to profound love and joy. Elated and leaping for joy, they experienced what they had never known before. With single-minded devotion, they joined their palms and stood before the Buddha, each praising him with *gāthā* verses.
At that time, the Devaputra Sudatta spoke these verses:
“In the past, the Buddha relinquished his body and life, His kingdom, as well as his wife and children;
Having brought those acts of giving to perfection, I therefore prostrate in homage.”
At that time, the Devaputra Śīlavant spoke in verse:
“Firmly maintaining pure precepts, Free from all defilements,
Able to cross to the further shore— I prostrate to the one endowed with virtue.”
At that time, the Devaputra Kṣānti spoke in verse:
“The Buddha extensively cultivated the practice of patience;
Though others severed his limbs and joints, he gave rise to no heart of resentment, And thus attained unsurpassed wisdom.”
At that time, the Devaputra Vīrya spoke in verse:
“O Great Hero, World-Honored One, You have cast off the heavy burden of birth and death;
Through diligent practice without retreat, You have swiftly reached Bodhi.”
At that time, the Devaputra Śamatha spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgata of great majestic power Dwells perpetually in meditative concentration;
Unattached to that worldly realm, He is entirely equal throughout the three periods of time."
At that time, the Devaputra Jñānavat said in verse:
“The Tathāgata’s power of supreme wisdom knows the various actions of sentient beings;
according to their karma they receive retribution, flowing and wandering through the realms of existence.”
At that time, the devaputra Puṇyakarmaprabhāsa spoke in verse:
"If one cultivates those meritorious deeds, The supreme retribution constantly manifests before one.
Others cannot understand this; It is solely the domain of the Buddha."
At that time, the Devaputra Realizing the Nature of Offenses spoke in verse:
"Sentient beings, due to delusion and karma, Constantly crave and seek after external things;
If they awaken within their own minds, They will fully comprehend all things."
At that time, the Devaputra Skillful Wisdom spoke in verse:
“If a person, regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, Reflects upon it with skillful discernment And constantly remembers it as their own possession, Enlightenment will not be difficult to attain.”
At that time, the devaputra Skillful Practice spoke in verse:
"If various afflictions and karmas arise, And the inner mind is not subject to conceptualization,
To realize that the nature of offenses is fundamentally empty— This is what it means to be one who realizes the Dharma."
At that time, the Devaputra Sarvatragāminīcaryā spoke in verse:
“If a person creates various formations (*saṃskāra*), they flow along with the currents of good and evil, receiving retributions of the beautiful and the ugly;
the Buddha’s eye perceives and knows them all.”
At that time, the Devaputra Vigatapratyaya spoke in verse:
"If one can thoroughly understand the conditions (*pratyaya*) regarding the retribution one receives,
then even while being born within the various realms of existence, one will always proceed in accordance with wisdom."
At that time, the Devaputra Anukūlakauśalya spoke in verse:
"If one commits various evils, Or practices manifold virtues, It is all due to prior karma;
One receives the fruits according to what has been produced."
At that time, the Devaputra Karmakauśalya spoke in verse:
“Having understood the karmic actions of the three times, One severs the old and does not create the new;
The fool, lacking right wisdom, Flows along with evil.”
At that time, the devaputra Skillful in Fruits spoke in verse:
“Because of a small cause there may be a great fruit; because of a great cause there may be a small fruit.
Those who do not understand this are foolish non-Buddhists.”
At that time, the Devaputra Jñānakarmānta spoke these verses:
"Virtuous causes lead to superior realms; Evil karma causes one to fall into perilous difficulties.
According to the conduct of sentient beings, The Tathāgata fully understands them all."
At that time, the devaputra Drṣṭadharmananda spoke these verses:
"If a person receives the retribution of merit, yet does not understand wholesome dharmas, they are deceiving themselves; before long, they shall fall."
At that time, the devaputra Sujāta spoke in verse:
“If one performs various superior karmas, And receives their retribution in the subsequent birth, Only the Buddha knows this correctly; The world cannot understand it.”
At that time, the devaputra named Susaṃmata spoke in verse:
“If karma has passed through many lifetimes, Or even through the count of koṭis of eons,
And has been transmitted down to this present body, The Buddha is able to fully comprehend its ripening retribution.”
At that time, the Devaputra Ripakavipāka spoke in verse:
“If these karmas converge, And those sentient beings take birth,
The Tathāgata fully understands That all arise from past causes and conditions.”
At that time, the devaputra Unripened Faculties spoke in verse:
"Those whose faculties are unripened Delight in performing unwholesome deeds;
They remain far removed from the Honored One among Bipeds, And have no aspiration for liberation."
At that time, the Devaputra Susaṃparipācita spoke in verse:
"If karma has already matured, or is yet to mature,
the nature of karma is originally empty, being produced according to the mind."
At that time, the Devaputra Niścita spoke these verses:
"Whatever karma sentient beings perform, Whether heavy or light and subtle, The Tathāgata fully realizes and knows it; The retribution received is without error."
At that time, the Devaputra Vijñātakarmasvarūpa spoke in verse:
"If one commits various evil deeds, One shall fall into the evil realms;
Yet if one encounters favorable conditions externally, The heavy may be transformed into light retribution."
At that time, the Devaputra Karmavipākaprajña spoke in verse:
“Accumulating all manner of evils, Bound and entangled by them,
They do not fear future suffering— These are the heretics of wrong views.”
At that time, the Devaputra Sunetravicintin spoke in verse:
"One who is able to discern and practice wholesome deeds, though their goodness be small, will attract a supreme reward;
it is like placing a single drop of water into the ocean, which never diminishes."
At that time, the Devaputra Comprehending All Dharmas spoke in verse:
“If a person can forever exhaust The outflows and the karma of conceptualization, They shall realize the fruit of no-more-learning; This is what the Tathāgata has taught.”
At that time, the devaputra Sākṣādbuddhajñāna spoke in verse:
"The Buddha-eye perceives with complete clarity The karmic fruits of all three times;
With no seeds or habitual tendencies left behind— I pay homage to the All-Knowing One."
At that time, the devaputra Karmanirdeśa spoke these verses:
“Among all sentient beings in the world, Some are born here and some perish there;
But the Tathāgata has forever exhausted [all such states], And thus he is called the One Who Has Attained Fearlessness.”
At that time, the Devaputra Vigatapratyayagati spoke in verse:
"The practices undertaken by sentient beings Lead only toward birth and extinction;
Their karmic fruits are like dreams and illusions— This is what the Tathāgata has taught."
At that time, the Devaputra Subduer of All Defilements spoke in verse:
"Those who are foolish and attached to desire Are like the thirsty who drink salt water;
Therefore, the Teacher of Men and Gods Views them as mere dream-visions."
At that time, the Devaputra Free from Conceptualization spoke in verse:
"Due to the faults of greed and delusion, One gives rise to conceptual attachment;
The wise understand this well: What pleasure can there be even in a dream?"
At that time, the Devaputra Śāntamithyātva spoke in verse:
"To speak of dream-events within a dream arises from perversion;
As for the instructions of the Tathāgata, One should seek the Dharma of tranquility."
At that time, the Devaputra Avalokita-kṣīṇāsrava spoke these verses:
"Just as a person in a dream Sees the heavens raining down in torrents,
And realizes the dream-body is fundamentally non-existent— So should one know that the outflows (āsravas) do not exist."
At that time, the Devaputra Realizing the Dream Realm spoke in verse:
"The dream realm is fundamentally provisional; When has it ever been seen as outflowing?
Successive deluded thoughts arise, And one forms the conception of outflows."
At that time, the Devaputra Satyavimala spoke in verse:
"Just as when a maiden of the world dreams that she has given birth to a son,
and having been born, he dies young— how could there be the suffering of separation?"
Then, the deity Svapnāntara spoke these verses:
"Just as when a person in a dream has their own head severed by another, that consciousness fundamentally has no object of attainment; who, then, is the one who severs it?"
At that time, the Devaputra Samyag-vipaśyin spoke these verses:
“That wisdom which realizes all phenomena To be like a composite dream-scene— Without joy and without separation; This is the true ultimate truth.”
At that time, the devaputra Jñānacitta spoke these verses:
"Having heard the True Dharma from the Buddha, The mind is realized to be like empty space.
Seeking the cause of a dream within a dream— Such is the fundamental nature of phenomena."
At that time, the Devaputra Manojña spoke these verses:
“You gods and humans, always delight in meditative concentration;
Thoroughly understand that world to be like a reflection in a mirror.”
At that time, the Devaputra Sunetra spoke these verses:
“The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata Is like the sound produced by a lute;
It benefits all devas and humans, Therefore I praise and pay homage to him.”
At that time, the Devaputra Vijñātamāyā spoke these verses:
"A phantom person performs phantom deeds, Which the foolish cannot comprehend;
That which the wise understand Is that all things are like phantoms."
At that time, the Transformation Devaputra within meditative concentration spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata appears in the world like a phantom seen in a dream;
those who thoroughly understand the principle of the Buddha have no doubt regarding this.”
At that time, the Devaputra Māyā-nirmita spoke in verse:
“The illusionist knows the nature of illusion, And is able to manifest transformations through illusion;
Because he understands that illusion, He perceives the true nature of all phenomena.”
At that time, the Devaputra Prajñāvicaya spoke these verses:
"You observe the Buddha in the world, Arising from conceptualization and discrimination;
Seeing the Buddha’s body within a dream— What could he possibly say regarding the Dharma?"
At that time, the Devaputra Vimatisamudghātin spoke in verse:
"No thing arises without craving; Through craving, one accumulates.
Where there is no thought, there is no craving; Seeing the Buddha is likewise so."
At that time, the Devaputra Samyagjñāna spoke in verse:
"In a deep valley there is originally no sound, Nor is there anyone there to hear it;
Thus realizing the principle of the Buddha, One has no attachment to the world."
At that time, the Devaputra Well-Spoken uttered these verses:
"Just as a person hears an echo, That sound cannot be apprehended;
Yet the fool, failing to understand this, Falsely clings to it as real."
At that time, the Devaputra Pratyekāvatāra spoke these verses:
"Ordinary fools are attached [to appearances] and do not comprehend the ultimate Dharma;
if one realizes the nature of phenomena, there will be no doubt regarding self or others."
At that time, the devaputra Arthasiddhi spoke in verse:
"The supreme dharma of ultimate truth is equal and without distinction among all Buddhas;
there is neither speaker nor listener, nor is there anyone who attains realization."
At that time, the Devaputra Praviṣṭadharmajñāna spoke these verses:
“Having severed all defilements of affliction, And having abandoned both the conceptualizer and the conceptualized, One attains purity through freedom from passion; Such is what the Muni has taught.”
At that time, the Devaputra Sucintita spoke in verse:
"Regarding the names and categories of all phenomena, Who has severed the outflows and afflictions,
Whose mind is pure and free from blemish— Such a one is called a true son of the Buddha."
At that time, the Devaputra Anāśrita spoke these verses:
"Your mind is equal to space, Unattached to the three realms;
You give generously without seeking reward, Tranquil and fearless one."
At that time, the Devaputra Vimala spoke these verses:
"Free from all craving for the realm of desire, And likewise for the realms of form and formlessness,
The Muni’s mind is equanimous, Unobstructed like space."
At that time, the Devaputra Nirāśa spoke these verses:
"Having no desire for the realm of desire, nor likewise for the realms of form or formlessness,
Free from conjunction and association, I take refuge in the Unsurpassed King."
At that time, the devaputra Utpannarāga spoke these verses:
"By severing the defilement of craving, And extracting the poisonous arrows of the three realms,
I pay homage to the Teacher, the Tamer, Who has forever transcended to the further shore."
At that time, the Devaputra Subduer of Attachment spoke in verse:
"Arousing the most supreme diligence, Subduing and eliminating worldly craving and attachment,
Constantly giving rise to the mind of great compassion— Such a one is the Savior of the World."
At that time, the devaputra Virāgānurāga spoke these verses:
"Having abandoned the craving associated with passion, I shall no longer undergo saṃsāra.
I take refuge in the Unsurpassed Honored One, Like a lotus rising above turbid water."
At that time, the Devaputra Dharmatāpratilabdha spoke these verses:
"I take refuge in the one who has transcended bondage, Who has thoroughly realized the meaning of the true nature of reality,
Who clearly understands the nature of all phenomena, And whose mind is free from fear."
At that time, the devaputra Transcender of the Mire of Desire spoke in verse:
“Craving is like the mud; The valiant one is able to transcend it.
I pay homage to the Honored Muni, Who will no longer be born within the three realms of existence.”
At that time, the Devaputra Abandoning Precious Ornaments spoke these verses:
"If a person distances themselves from pursuit, They will be able to leave all evils behind;
Having no greed for precious ornaments, Their mind’s purity exceeds even that."
At that time, the Devaputra Vigataśoka spoke in verse:
"If a person, regarding the objects of desire, Does not give rise to heedlessness in the mind, Then they can transcend the net of Māra; Such a one is a person of great wisdom."
At that time, the Devaputra Abhayadatta spoke in verse:
"When self and others cultivate right practice, They leave behind sorrow, fear, and the fever of affliction.
Through unimpeded eloquence, the Buddha Causes all sentient beings to awaken to understanding."
At that time, the devaputra Kīrtidhara spoke in verse:
"If one hears the Buddha’s teaching And reflects upon it with skillful discernment,
That person, within this world, Will be able to reach the end of all suffering."
At that time, the Devaputra Abhayamkara spoke these verses:
"O Savior, Lion of the Śākyas, Ocean of wisdom vast and boundless,
You have definitively realized all dharmas And are able to give rise to the path of remedy."
At that time, the devaputra Vigatabhaya spoke in verse:
"Homage to the Honored One among gods, Stainless and unattached,
Who has skillfully extracted the arrows of affliction And is able to leave all fears behind."
At that time, the devaputra Asaṅga spoke in verse:
“If all the devas, Māras, and Brahmās Entreat the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma,
Amidst this great assembly, Only the Buddha attains fearlessness.”
At that time, the Devaputra Siṃhavikrāmin spoke in verse:
“You have excellently taught all dharmas and accomplished all-knowledge;
I pay homage to the Lion of the Śākyas, who is peerless throughout the three realms.”
At that time, the Devaputra Removing Fear spoke in verse:
"The lion relies upon the mountain valleys; His mind is always free from all fears.
Roaring amidst the forests and thickets, He causes the other small beasts to scatter."
"The Holy Lord has appeared in the world; his wisdom is inconceivable.
He expounds the Dharma to terrify the various Māras and subdues all those of external paths.
At that time, the Devaputra Subduer-of-Māra-Enemies spoke this verse:
“The Dharma you have come to realize, and that which you have attained, is peerless in the world;
therefore, I prostrate in homage to you, the most holy among the holy.
At that time, the Devaputra Siṃhamati spoke this verse:
"Homage to the Lord of Munis, the Teacher of all sages,
who has accomplished omniscience and mastered boundless dharmas.
Then, the Devaputra Born Following the Buddha spoke this verse:
“The Tathāgata has realized all dharmas, yet there is none who can pose a question;
born according to the Buddha’s own realization, please proclaim the profound and wondrous meaning.
At that time, the Devaputra Dharaṇīdhara spoke in verse:
“The Buddha upholds the treasury of the true Dharma And fearlessly proclaims it well;
He causes hundreds of billions of sentient beings To all give rise to awakening.
Then the Devaputra Anudharmagati spoke these verses:
"Practicing all deeds in accordance with the Dharma, One can give rise to the bodhicitta;
A hero within the world, Such a one is the supreme among great men.
Then, the Devaputra Raticandra spoke these verses:
“Those beings of great resolve, by hearing the Buddha’s teaching,
practice and train according to the Dharma, and thus attain the unsurpassed fruit.
At that time, the Devaputra Viśuddhacitta spoke this verse:
"The Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice, upon hearing which the mind becomes pure—
though there are myriad types of capacities and conditions, none are able to pose a question.
At that time, the Devaputra Śuddhaparivāra spoke these verses:
“Throughout the long night, the Buddha practiced all deeds according to reality;
possessing the radiance of the marks and signs of excellence, he has attained a perfect retinue.
At that time, the Devaputra Anāsravadharma spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata has exhausted all outflows;
therefore he can roar the lion’s roar, regarding the unprecedented dharmas, discerning them to eliminate doubt.
At that time, the Devaputra Arthaviniścita spoke these verses:
“With the great power of wisdom, the Tathāgata has thoroughly realized the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
among all devas and worldlings, there is none who equals the Buddha.
At that time, the devaputra Kṣīṇāsrava spoke this verse:
“The most supreme Great Śramaṇa, who has utterly exhausted all outflows—
within this great assembly today, none are able to pose a challenging question.
At that time, the Devaputra Nityavīra spoke these verses:
“The Great Hero of great power and wisdom, There is no dharma he does not see;
Delusion and karma are exhausted without remainder, He is undisturbed by difficult questions.
At that time, the Devaputra Śāntamati spoke in verse:
"Forever free from the affliction of greed, and likewise from hatred and delusion, you do not give rise to the intention for evil karma; I pay homage to the one who is tranquil.
Then, the devaputra Saṃprayuktacārin spoke this verse:
“I take refuge in the Sugata, the Teacher, who has forever exhausted all karma and delusions;
through constant union with right practice, he has reached the state of omniscience.
At that time, the devaputra Saṃprayuktajñāna spoke these verses:
"Boundless corresponding practices are the sphere of the Buddhas' activity;
when seeds, manifestations, and habitual tendencies are all eliminated, one attains omniscience.
At that time, the Devaputra Saṃprayuktamati spoke these verses:
“The Buddha, through wisdom in accord with reality, acts as a lamp for the world;
the root causes of all afflictions are forever and utterly severed.
At that time, the devaputra Śāntavedanin spoke these verses:
"Having forever severed all delusions, with a profound mind always tranquil, the Buddha’s sons are well-advanced in diligence; what fear could they possibly have?
Then, the devaputra Jñānābhimukha spoke these verses:
“The Buddha has exhausted all afflictions—both those of the seeds and those manifesting simultaneously;
he has shattered the ignorance of sentient beings, and his great compassion is peerless.
At that time, the Devaputra Aparakleśahara spoke this verse:
“The Sage, the God among Gods, through wisdom has awakened;
he has severed the secondary afflictions along with their intensities, and has eliminated all remaining habitual tendencies.
At that time, the Devaputra Suyāma spoke this verse:
“The Sage of Benevolence has appeared in the world;
having severed all causes of outflows, he manifests birth from a mother for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
At that time, the Devaputra Free from All Defilements spoke this verse:
“The Teacher and Tamer of Gods and Humans, Free from the terrors of affliction,
Has incinerated the sprouts of the roots of suffering, Leaving no further seeds behind.
At that time, the Devaputra Elimination-of-Falsity spoke these verses:
“The Buddha, by means of all-encompassing wisdom, has forever cast off the defilement of ignorance;
relying upon pure conduct, he is called ‘Well-Subdued.
— *The Compendium of Father and Son*, Scroll 13.
The Compendium of the Sūtra on Father and Son, Volume Fourteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Great Master Xuanfan,
who was bestowed with the purple robe and held the rank of Chao San Da Fu and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.

Translated by the Śramaṇa Subject Rìchēng and others, by Imperial Decree. Chapter Two: The Praise of the Buddha in Verses Spoken by the Devaputra Sunirmita. At that time, the Devaputra Sunirmita spoke in verse:
“The Buddha has transcended the ocean of the three realms of existence; He is able to transform those who are difficult to transform.
Therefore, within this world, He is entitled to the name ‘One Possessed of Fearlessness.’”
At that time, the Devaputra Satyadarśin spoke these verses:
“Having accomplished all-knowledge, And having extinguished all afflictions and karma,
Causing them to be exhausted without remainder— This is called Great Tranquility.”
At that time, the Devaputra Dharmadhvaja spoke these verses:
“Having raised the high and victorious banner of Dharma, He has crushed the firm and solid pride of self.
With immeasurable power and valor, He shows the right path to all sentient beings.”
At that time, the Devaputra Dharmasāgara spoke in verse:
“The Muni has taught all dharmas as a great treasury of Dharma jewels;
He guides those who are deluded, leading them to the place of peace and security.”
At that time, the Devaputra Dharmakāya spoke in verse:
"The Son of the Buddha abides in the Great Dharma; His mind knows no satiety.
Peacefully enduring and free from all fears, He is thus able to roar the lion’s roar."
At that time, the Devaputra Dharmārthaparigaveṣin spoke these verses:
“O Son of the Buddha, understand this well: You should diligently seek the True Dharma;
Having heard it, practice according to the teaching, And you shall swiftly attain the path of Bodhi.”
At that time, the Devaputra Thirsting for the Dharma spoke in verse:
“Countless hundreds of thousands, And koṭis of sentient beings,
Longing to hear the Buddha’s voice, Maintain firm resolve and constant diligence.”
At that time, the Devaputra Vīradharma spoke in verse:
“Possessing vast eloquence, He crushes all heterodox arguments;
Delighting in the cultivation of sublime practices, He attains the most supreme enlightenment.”
At that time, the Devaputra Dharmadhara spoke these verses:
“The Buddha has taught the foremost Dharma, Profound and exceedingly difficult to comprehend;
Sealing all with the emptiness of ultimate truth, It causes one to attain the path of tranquility.”
At that time, the Devaputra Rativikrāmin spoke in verse:
“The Son of the Buddha practices giving well, Relinquishing even his own body and life;
By reason of these causes and conditions, He attains the state of Supreme Perfect Enlightenment.”
At that time, the devaputra Virajamatī spoke these verses:
“Firmly upholding the pure precepts, his mind is free from fear;
hearing the Buddha’s voice of the True Dharma, he receives it upon the crown of his head without forgetting.”
At that time, the Devaputra Ananyamanas spoke in verse:
"The Holy Lord, King of the Dharma, Skillfully expounds all phenomena;
Seeking not the fruits of the two vehicles, He diligently cultivates the unsurpassed path."
At that time, the Devaputra Upasthita spoke in verse:
"The Hero of the World, the Honored One among bipeds, Appears for the sake of sentient beings;
He distinguishes and explains the three vehicles, Yet the ultimate is only the Buddha-wisdom."
At that time, the Devaputra Accomplished Eloquence spoke in verse:
“The Buddha’s name pervades the ten directions, His eloquence is without limit or obstruction;
With hearts entirely pure, All rejoice in what has been taught.”
At that time, the Devaputra named Each Accomplishing Eloquence spoke in verse:
"If a person lacks eloquence, And seeks a vow from the Buddha,
To preach the Dharma and eliminate all fears, Such that those who hear it do not disparage it."
At that time, the Devaputra Nityapramudita spoke in verse:
"The Son of the Buddha abides in the power of patience; Though reviled and abused, he harbors no anger.
Resolutely seeking Great Enlightenment, He is ever joyful and free from cowardice."
At that time, the Devaputra Free from the Two Vehicles spoke in verse:
“As the eldest son of the Tathāgata, He takes no delight in inferior vehicles;
If he hears the voice of the Buddha, He seeks only the unsurpassed path.”
At that time, the Devaputra Ajita spoke in verse:
"Brave and of great diligence, Unafraid of any afflictions,
Having renounced the paths of Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, He vows to seek unsurpassed wisdom."
At that time, the devaputra Saṃtati-kuśala-dharma spoke in verse:
"Delighting in the cultivation of pure dharmas, Without any interruption—
The Great Guide, the Muni, Knows the basis upon which they rest."
At that time, the devaputra Subhāṣitadharma spoke in verse:
"Upholding that True Dharma, which is the seal of approval of the Tathāgata,
Abiding in firm diligence, like the full moon, it does not wane."
At that time, the devaputra Dharmasvabhāvaśuddha spoke these verses:
“The nature of phenomena is pure, Yet it is obscured by adventitious dust;
This arises entirely from the defiled mind— The Tathāgata is able to realize this through direct manifestation.”
At that time, the Devaputra Prāptanyāya spoke these verses:
“The nature of phenomena is fundamentally unstained; Black and white do not coexist.
This is what accords with correct principle, As taught by the Tathāgata.”
At that time, the devaputra Vibhajyakuśala spoke in verse:
"All unwholesome dharmas can be crushed and extinguished by the power of goodness;
if unwholesome dharmas increase, they will oppose and damage pure karma."
Then the devaputra Praviṣṭasamyagbodhi spoke in verse:
"Due to those defiled actions, The white dharmas do not increase;
They certainly serve as conditions for harm— This is what the Tathāgata has taught."
At that time, the Devaputra Seeking Liberation spoke in verse:
"The power of defilements is so strong and fierce That the mind does not aspire for liberation;
It obscures all-encompassing wisdom— Regarding this, one must exercise skillful discernment."
At that time, the Devaputra Mind-Clarified spoke in verse:
“If the mind is liberated from all desires, Evil karma will no longer arise.
The Tathāgata is able to realize this; He expounds it for the sake of sentient beings.”
At that time, the Devaputra Dṛṣṭikleśa spoke these verses:
"If one does not understand the True Dharma, And does not know defiled conduct,
Constantly contravening the words of the Buddha, One remains ever further from the Noble Path."
At that time, the devaputra Drṣṭāpattika spoke this verse:
"If one does not commit various evils, Then wholesome karma will increase.
Therefore, those wise people Delight in liberation and peace."
At that time, the Devaputra Śraddhābala spoke in verse:
"By practicing the abandonment of greed, hatred, and delusion, One is able to transcend the evil realms.
The Tathāgata, appearing in the world, Constantly instructs in this manner."
At that time, the Devaputra Jñānakalyāṇa spoke these verses:
"If one cannot distinguish between defiled and pure phenomena with the mind,
the Buddha says such a person is one who is utterly deluded."
At that time, the devaputra Vimukticaryā spoke in verse:
"Following the Buddha’s instructions, Abandoning all that is unwholesome—
Such a person will, regarding the Noble Path, Certainly attain accomplishment."
At that time, the devaputra Vimuktipratyupasthita spoke these verses:
“If one abandons all unwholesome dharmas, Pure karma will manifest before them.
If they practice with diligence and without regression, The evil Māra shall find no opportunity.”
At that time, the Devaputra Anulomaviniścaya spoke these verses:
“The Dharma taught by all Buddhas brings benefit and joy to all living beings;
it causes them to distance themselves from improper states and not to follow the entreaties of others.”
At that time, the Devaputra Śrī-Abhaya spoke these verses:
"The contemplation of impurity remedies greed; It constitutes the practice of correct application.
Once that greed has been eliminated, One shall cause the obstacles to recede far away."
At that time, the Devaputra Abhyudgata-viśeṣa-mati spoke these verses:
“Observing with a mind of loving-kindness cures hatred; Through that, one attains liberation from hatred.
Even if one should encounter a deep-seated enemy, Not even the slightest fear will arise.”
At that time, the Devaputra Viśuddhacakṣus spoke these verses:
"Pure wisdom cuts through delusion and confusion; This is the dharma that serves as the remedy.
Once that delusion has been dispelled, One no longer follows the instructions of others."
Then the Devaputra Dispeller of Doubt spoke in verse:
"Abiding in right mindfulness and reflection, One can leave behind all doubts and delusions;
Even if one encounters false teachers or friends, One may skillfully subdue them by relying on the Dharma."
At that time, the Devaputra Nirabhimāna spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata has taught the Dharma of emptiness; Abiding well within emptiness, he has realized the true principle.
Having reached this correct understanding, he does not rely on others for his awakening.”
At that time, the devaputra Mānāpanuda spoke these verses:
"Having understood the *māna* (conceit) regarding self and others, what is there to be gained by arrogance?
By being in accord with right practice, one causes all such [conceits] to be completely severed."
At that time, the Devaputra Śāntamati spoke in verse:
“Having forever severed all doubts and delusions, With a profound mind ever tranquil, Afflictions no longer arise;
One attains liberation in peace and security.”
At that time, the Devaputra Avalokita spoke in verse:
"Thoroughly understanding the path and what is not the path, Relying on purity and remaining free from defilement,
Following the words of all Buddhas, One eliminates fear and attains liberation."
At that time, the devaputra Liao shisu (Lokavyavahāra) spoke in verse:
"Worldly convention is merely a provisional name, yet it can give rise to the path of antidotes;
one should know that even the World-Honored One is likewise a provisional designation."
At that time, the Devaputra Śarīra-vinaya spoke in verse:
"With wisdom as the precursor, The physical karma follows the practice of the Dharma;
Bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, One attains the realization of omniscience."
At that time, the Devaputra Pure Physical Action spoke in verse:
“The Buddha’s physical action is pure; In all he does, there is no error.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, I now take refuge and pay homage.”
At that time, the Devaputra Karmaviniścaya spoke these verses:
"Whose physical actions are well-discriminated, Who benefits all beings through skillful means—
I pay homage with faith to the Teacher, the Tamer, The illuminator of the world."
At that time, the Devaputra Well-Contemplating Body spoke in verse:
“Having well observed bodily action, Possessing the marks and signs of purity,
He is the unsurpassed Great Being, Able to bestow happiness upon all.”
At that time, the Devaputra Accomplished in Vocal Action spoke this verse:
"Avoiding those evil words, Possessing exquisite and wondrous virtues,
Abiding in right mindfulness and reflection— This is what the Tathāgata has taught."
At that time, the Devaputra Vyakta spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice is revered by all the world;
skillfully examining the timing and circumstances of others, he speaks nothing that is not meaningful and beneficial.”
At that time, the Devaputra Arthasiddhi spoke in verse:
"Avoiding what is unbeneficial, Being endowed with peace and happiness,
And not destroying the ripening of karmic results— This was taught by the Buddhas of the past."
Then the devaputra Aviruddha spoke in verse:
"Never did he live by wrong livelihood, nor speak falsely for the sake of gain;
therefore the Buddha’s great fame cannot be destroyed by the world."
At that time, the Devaputra Satyavādin spoke in verse:
“The Buddha has appeared in the world; All that he speaks is true and real.
Therefore, all devas and humans Delight in hearing the wondrous Dharma.”
At that time, the Devaputra Realizing Ultimate Reality spoke in verse:
"Because the Buddha speaks with truthful words, He has attained the most perfect enlightenment;
Having realized all phenomena born of conditions, He is named the Truly All-Knowing One."
At that time, the devaputra Ati-saṃskāra spoke these verses:
"Whatever conditioned phenomena there may be, And the true nature of all phenomena—
The Muni, King of Dharma, Knows and perceives them all according to reality."
At that time, the Devaputra Niścayacārin spoke these verses:
"Regarding the deeds performed by oneself and others— The actions of body, speech, and mind— The Buddha,
with his pure wisdom, Is able to discern and explain them all."
At that time, the Devaputra Samāhita-mati spoke in verse:
"With a pure mind, the Buddha surveys all sentient beings six times;
I take refuge in the World-Savior, whose great compassion is peerless."
At that time, the Devaputra Suvicāraṇa spoke in verse:
"Whatever the Tathāgata does, his deportment is without deficiency;
Compassion and wisdom are ever in accord, as he takes pity upon the three realms of existence."
At that time, the Devaputra Bodhyartha spoke in verse:
“The sphere of the Buddha’s mental focus, His body and speech are entirely harmonious and gentle;
Amidst the great assembly, He has never committed any error.”
At that time, the Devaputra Vimalamati spoke in verse:
“The Buddha takes the mind as his ground; With great compassion, he observes all sentient beings.
Knowing that the intrinsic nature of phenomena is empty, He employs skillful means to bring them to awakening.”
At that time, the Devaputra Skillful of the Past spoke in verse:
"If there are various deeds practiced by a person in the past—
Generosity, morality, patience, diligence, and meditation— The Tathāgata understands them all with complete clarity."
At that time, the Devaputra Observing the Past spoke in verse:
"Having planted the roots of all virtues in the past, And having served many billions of Buddhas,
Now fulfilling those former aspirations, He has attained the fruit of Bodhi."
At that time, the Devaputra Endowed with Perfect Practice spoke in verse:
“For immeasurable eons, the Buddha cultivated sublime practices wherever he was;
He was always in perfect accord with right mindfulness, Because he never abandoned bodhi.”
At that time, he addressed the Devaputra Pūrvacintin with these verses:
"By drawing near to all Tathāgatas, Cultivating practice, and making skillful inquiries,
One delights in dwelling in samādhi And gives birth to manifold dharmas."
At that time, the Devaputra Corresponding to Original Practice spoke in verse:
"In the presence of the Buddhas of the past, I asked about practicing according to the teachings;
Regarding the gateways of samādhi, I observed them without weariness."
At that time, the Devaputra Jātismara spoke in verse:
“Birth and death abound with faults; What should be done and what should not be done— The Tathāgata, having fully understood this, Has preached the Dharma of liberation.”
At that time, the Devaputra Observing Previous Karmic Actions spoke in verse:
"In the past we together committed various evils; Our defiled karmas were similar.
Sometimes we devoured one another, And sometimes we played together."
At that time, the Devaputra Pūrvāntajña spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata has appeared in the world; By the power of his meditative concentration and wisdom, He is able to know the past lives Without obstruction across all realms of existence.”
At that time, the Devaputra Knowing the Future spoke in verse:
“The Buddha knows future ages, His wisdom is without obstruction;
From passing away here to being born there— The retribution of karma is likewise so.”
At that time, the Devaputra Jñānapaścimakoṭigocara spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata knows the future limit; The power of his wisdom is infinite and unobstructed.
Regarding the conduct practiced by sentient beings, They receive their retribution according to their karma.”
At that time, the Devaputra Free from Saṃsāra spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata, of great heroism, Has accomplished unsurpassed wisdom;
Unattached to the three realms of existence, He abides in the most supreme state.”
At that time, the Devaputra Lokavidita spoke in verse:
“The destination to which sentient beings resort, The various thoughts and perceptions they give rise to— These are merely provisional names; This is what the Tathāgata has taught.”
At that time, the Devaputra Observing the Present spoke in verse:
“The Honored One, valiant in the present, possesses wisdom-power that none can destroy;
throughout as many Buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, he discerns them all without limit or hindrance.”
At that time, the Devaputra Abiding in Fearlessness spoke these verses:
"The Holy Lord, King of Dharma, Illuminates the equality of the three times;
All phenomena lack intrinsic nature, Yet the foolish cannot comprehend this."
At that time, the Devaputra Jñānāsaṅga spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata is well-subdued; He dwells nowhere throughout the three times.
Since all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, Nothing whatsoever can be apprehended.”
At that time, the Devaputra Wisdom of the Three Times spoke these verses:
"Understanding that the past and future have no intrinsic substance, That the arising of the aggregates swiftly returns to extinction—
Such is the nature of saṃsāra, As taught by the Muni."
At that time, the Devaputra Anāsakta spoke these verses:
"All phenomena are like illusions, Like mirages and echoes from valleys;
Sentient beings and the world— Their intrinsic nature is not real."
At that time, the Devaputra Joy of the Three Times spoke in verse:
"The wisdom of the Tathāgata is peerless; He fully understands the three times.
The self-nature of all faculties is empty; All things are like illusions."
At that time, the devaputra Abhirati-caryā spoke in verse:
“At midnight, the Tathāgata manifested the attainment of perfect enlightenment;
He exerted diligent vigor and joyful aspiration, Never once did he falter or diminish.”
At that time, the devaputra Chanda-pravartaka spoke in verse:
“The Buddha is the light of the world; His diligence never diminishes.
By means of that great valor, He transcends and attains perfect enlightenment.”
At that time, the devaputra Transcender of Desire-Thoughts spoke in verse:
“The Buddha has appeared in the world, Utterly courageous and diligent;
He is able to transcend the mire of desire, Like a lotus unsullied by water.”
At that time, the Devaputra *Abhilāṣa-vimukti* spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgata has appeared in the world, Proclaiming the equality of the dharma-realm;
It is of a single nature, without a second— Therefore, I praise and pay homage."
At that time, the Devaputra Arising Diligence spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata of great majestic power Is able to awaken all classes of beings;
By practicing diligently without indolence, The celestial Māras cannot destroy him.”
At that time, the Devaputra Samyaksmṛti spoke in verse:
“The Buddha, in all places, Always gives rise to that right mindfulness;
Therefore, having attained the Way, He has obtained mindfulness that never diminishes.”
At that time, the Devaputra Dwelling in Meditative Equilibrium spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata is ever in samādhi, Knowing the dispositions and desires of sentient beings;
According to their respective practices, He expounds the various dharmas for them.”
At that time, the Devaputra Respecting Right Wisdom spoke in verse:
“The World-Honored One is a great ocean of wisdom, Its limits are boundless and immeasurable;
Even if one were to spend a hundred thousand kalpas Explaining it, one could never exhaust it.”
At that time, the devaputra Vimuktaruci spoke in verse:
"The invincible Great Man delights in supreme liberation;
Because he has realized liberation, he is unattached to the three realms of existence."
At that time, the Devaputra Saṃyuktavimukta spoke in verse:
“The Great Sage, the Supreme Lord, Possessing the knowledge and vision of liberation,
Delivers inexhaustible sentient beings, While his true wisdom never diminishes.”
At that time, the Devaputra Avalokitapūrvacaryā spoke in verse:
"In the past, under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, He realized the practice of the dharma of ultimate truth;
Through diligent cultivation without regression, He attained great awakening."
At that time, the devaputra Profound Practice spoke in verse:
“The Buddha has long been free from all evils, unlike other sentient beings;
Knowing the self-nature of phenomena to be empty, he is unimpeded throughout the three periods of time.”
At that time, the Devaputra Viśālamati spoke in verse:
"The Buddha, regarding all-knowledge, Gives rise to no doubt or uncertainty in his mind;
Right mindfulness is ever present before him, Like one holding a bowl filled to the brim with oil."
At that time, the Devaputra Asaṃkṣobhya spoke in verse:
"The Buddha-mind is ever serene, Never subject to distraction;
The nature of phenomena is fundamentally unstained, Yet sentient beings cannot comprehend it."
At that time, the Devaputra Anwuzhizhi (Anuruddha-jñāna) spoke in verse:
“The unique qualities of the Tathāgata Are profound and inconceivable;
Toward all sentient beings, He has never failed to discern and act with equanimity.”
At that time, the devaputra Transcending All Existences spoke in verse:
“The Buddha is the seer among gods; In the three realms, there is none to equal him.
He has thoroughly realized all phenomena; His supreme wisdom is unsurpassed.”
At that time, the Devaputra Dṛḍhāvivartya spoke these verses:
"The most supreme and steadfast Hero is fearless regarding all phenomena;
he awakens all sentient beings, his mind being entirely impartial."
