Chapter Twenty-five: The Prophecy Given to the Non-Buddhist Brahmin. At that time, there was a non-Buddhist Brahmin in the assembly named Parivrājaka, who, together with a retinue of sixty thousand, beheld the various Asura kings, Garuḍa kings, and great Nāga kings.
The yakṣas,
gandharvas, and others, as well as the gods adorned with necklaces and the gods of the Four Great Kings.
The Heaven of the Thirty-three,
the Yāma Heaven,
and the Tuṣita Heaven.
The Heaven of Delighting in Emanations,
the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations, and the Heaven of the Brahma Assembly.
The Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven,

the Bṛhatphala Heaven, and others, having made their offerings, received the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment; they also heard the assembly of devaputras from the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens proclaiming verses in praise of the Buddha with wondrous voices, and they leaped for joy at this unprecedented occurrence.
Then that non-Buddhist rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"When I heard the Gautama preach the Dharma of non-self, my heart found no joy; instead, doubt arose within me. I find no pleasure in staying here, nor do I have a home to which I can return."
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
If there were no self, why would this body arise from causes and conditions?
I observe that Gautama’s supernormal physical marks are the foremost among gods and humans; he is fully endowed with vast majesty and virtue, causing all who behold him to give rise to joy."
Furthermore, you once preached to the devas of the Vast Fruit Heaven that all dharmas are themselves the Tathāgata.
Why, then, do you now say that there is no self?
Śramaṇa Gautama!

I pray that you will analyze this for the sake of the assembly according to reality; I shall listen and receive it. Only the Tathāgata can know the minds of others; please cause me to understand and sever the net of doubt.
The Buddha said, "Excellent,
non-Buddhist!
Even if you were to pose hundreds of thousands of difficult questions, I would be able to answer them all without finding it difficult.
I shall instead question you; answer according to your own understanding.
O outsider!
"How do sentient beings first undergo conception and enter the mother's womb; do you know this?
The non-Buddhist replied, "According to what our school teaches, there are three causes: the father, the mother, and their union; in this way, the embryo is formed."
The Buddha said,
"O outsider! Does that embryo arise from the father's craving?"
He replied, “No. The Buddha said:
“O outsider!
Does that embryo arise from the mother’s thoughts?
He replied:
"No," the Buddha said, "O outsider!"
"Does that embryo descend from the heavenly realms and enter the mother's womb?
The non-Buddhist replied, "I do not know."
“O outsider! Does that embryo pass away from among human beings before entering the mother’s womb?
He replied:
“I do not know. “Outsider!
Did that fetus pass away from among the asuras, or from among the hell-beings, or from among the animals, or from among the hungry ghosts before entering the mother’s womb?”
The non-Buddhists replied, "We do not know.
The Buddha said:
“O non-Buddhist!
What do you think?
Does that embryo arise from form and enter the mother’s womb?”
He replied, "I do not know.
The Buddha said:
“O non-Buddhist!
What do you think?
Does that embryo arise from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and enter the mother’s womb?”
He replied, "I do not know.
Having said this, the Buddha immediately addressed him:
“O non-Buddhists!

This Dharma is profound, subtle, and difficult to know; it cannot be understood through your dialectical speculations or measurements. Only those who possess right view and cultivate their practice with single-minded devotion can truly comprehend this principle.”

For example, O outsiders, it is as if there were a person afflicted with a disease of the visual faculty who, upon encountering a skilled physician, has his eyes cured; by virtue of this cause, he once again perceives various forms.
O outsiders!

If one can draw near to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), that person will immediately attain the purity of the eye of wisdom (prajñācakṣus); by means of this eye of wisdom, they shall behold the profound Dharma.
It is impossible for one who does not possess the five faculties, such as faith and the rest, to enter into and understand the profound Dharma.

Therefore, you followers of various non-Buddhist paths, within the long night of past birth and death, have been deceived and deluded by those false doctrines; you have given rise to divergent views, clinging to them tenaciously and refusing to let go;
you have taken what is not the True Dharma to be the True Dharma, clung to what is not liberation as liberation, and regarded what is not renunciation as renunciation.
Your teacher has ruined himself and has likewise ruined you all,
O outsiders!
It is like a man who is himself blind yet acts as a guide for those who are blind.
You should know that such persons will certainly fall into perilous difficulties.

These śramaṇas and brahmins are deluded; they are not truly enlightened ones who claim to be enlightened, they abide in what is not the Path yet declare it to be the Path, they are themselves unsubdued yet say they are subdued, they rely on wrong mindfulness yet claim it to be right mindfulness, they are not saviors yet claim to be able to save, and though they themselves do not know the way of transcendence, they claim, "I am one who knows the way of transcendence."
The Buddha said, “O non-Buddhist!

It is like a cowherd leading his ox across a river; unable to first discern the shallow parts of the water, he mistakenly enters a deep abyss where the current swirls and eddies. That ox abandons him before reaching the other shore, drowning in midstream, distressed and without rescue.”
Why is this? Because the cowherds are unable to lead them.
O outsiders!
"Just as you and your like are not true guides yet claim to be guides, causing those who receive your instruction to instead encounter distress and calamity,
so it is with this. The Buddha said, "O outsider!"
I am called the Teacher, truly well-tamed, who brings about definitive peace within the True Dharma;
I am the Perfectly Awakened One, who has awakened to reality as it is, causing all sentient beings to attain true awakening;
I always maintain right mindfulness without forgetfulness, and likewise cause all sentient beings to be free from all distraction.
I have skillfully attained renunciation and am forever liberated from saṃsāra, enabling those to be transformed to reach the end of suffering;
I demonstrate the true path, which is certain and without deviation, enabling those to be transformed to reach the other shore.
"O outsider!

If you now wish to seek the Dharma of liberation, you should give rise to pure aspiration, respect it with single-minded devotion, and practice with diligent application. Regarding the essential points of the Dharma for transcendence that you have not heard before, you should engender pure faith so as to lead you to understanding."

The treatises of your own school that you have previously studied should be abandoned and no longer pursued; instead, you must cause yourself to enter and master the treasury of the True Dharma, which you have not yet attained, so as to achieve unimpeded penetration.
The Buddha said,
“Outsider! Within my Dharma,
it is taught that there are three factors that must come together in conjunction for one to enter the womb.”
What is called the father is the cause of past karma;
what is called the mother is the condition of past karma;
[it refers to] the stage of the *kalala* at the initial moment of conception.
Karma summons that consciousness, which takes refuge within the mother’s womb; because this karma has matured, one undergoes birth therein, appearing according to the mind, like a city of Gandharvas.
Once consciousness has taken its seat in the womb, it gradually grows and expands, just as the medicinal herbs and forests of the world grow and flourish by depending upon the great earth.
"O outsider!
Thus, once that consciousness has entered the mother's womb, it gradually develops until the limbs of the body are fully formed.
As the time for birth approaches, the physical parts manifest; through the harmony of causes and conditions, the continuity remains unbroken."
"O outsider!

Such distinctions in the stages of the initial conception within the womb can only be truly and thoroughly understood by the Tathāgata, who possesses all-knowledge and is called the Perfectly All-Knowing One; ignorant fools cannot comprehend them."
The Buddha said:
“O non-Buddhist!
If those sentient beings pass away from the hells and are reborn in the human realm, entering the mother’s womb and being born into the world, they will possess these signs:”
Their voices are hoarse and raspy, their speech is indistinct, and when they speak, people do not trust them.
They are suddenly anxious and terrified, frequently forgetting matters, their minds constantly filled with fear, and the hair on their bodies bristles in trembling agitation.

While dreaming, one sees a great fire blazing fiercely and cauldrons boiling; one runs about seeking refuge, but the rākṣasa jailers chase one away with clubs. Or one sees oneself bound and pinned to a pillar or stake, being beaten with clubs, unable to escape.

Or they may be seen pursued by mad elephants and venomous serpents, fleeing in all directions without knowing where to go, held in contempt by others and viewed like thieves or heretics; this is because they come from hell and possess these residual habits.
The wise understand this, but the foolish do not.
The Buddha said,
“O non-Buddhist!
If that sentient being passes away from the animal realm and is reborn in the human destiny, entering the mother’s womb and being born into the world, there will be these signs:”

They are dull-witted and obtuse, lazy, and prone to excessive sleep; they delight in eating earth and chewing grasses and trees; they associate with foolish people and constantly dwell in darkness and the mire.

Whether sitting or standing, they dig at the ground with their toes; their heads emit a foul odor, attracting flies and insects that swarm and feed upon them. They move about incessantly, unable to remain still for even a moment, and are constantly tormented by hunger and thirst. Should they obtain even meager or impure food and drink, they immediately feel satisfied and content.
They are mostly deceitful and fraudulent, falsely claiming what they have seen or heard.
Sometimes, in their dreams, their bodies fall into filth;
or in the fields, they consume water and grass.
Or one may dream that amidst mountains, valleys, and dense forests, one’s body is entwined by a great python, experiencing great terror with no one to provide protection.
O outsider!
This is because they have these residual habits carried over from their time as animals, such that even if one were to speak for an entire kalpa, one could not exhaust them;
the wise understand this, while the foolish do not.
The Buddha said,
"O non-Buddhist!
If those sentient beings pass away from the realm of hungry ghosts, they may be reborn in the human realm."
Upon entering the mother’s womb and being born into this world, he shall possess these characteristics:
his hair will be yellowish-red; he will glare with angry eyes; he will constantly suffer from hunger and thirst; and his nature will be solely one of stinginess and envy.
They crave great wealth and profit, their minds never knowing contentment; seeing the possessions of others, they conceive the thought that they belong to themselves.
Regarding the fine things of others, they long to steal them; they eat impure and leftover food without any sense of shame.
When seeing the gardens, groves, flowers, and fruits belonging to others, they have a strong desire to pluck them and thereby destroy them.
O outsider!
This is a residual habit carried over from having come from the realm of hungry ghosts.
"The wise understand this, while the foolish do not.
The Buddha said,
"O non-Buddhists, if those sentient beings pass away from the asura realm and are reborn in the human realm, they enter the mother's womb and are born into the world."
They will possess these characteristics:

they will constantly harbor anger, be arrogant and conceited, delight in contention and strife, harbor grudges without relinquishing them, be bold and physically powerful, take pleasure in combat, rely excessively on their eloquence, and treat others with contempt.
Furthermore, there is the power of intellectual skill and the power of ignorance by which they defeat the arguments of others to sustain their own livelihoods.
O outsider!
This is a residual habit remaining from having come from the asuras.
"This is what the wise know, which the foolish do not understand.
The Buddha said,
"O non-Buddhist!"
If that sentient being passes away from the human realm and is reborn again in the human realm, entering the mother’s womb and being born into the world, there will be these signs:

this person is upright and honest; they delight in associating with the worthy and good while distancing themselves from and abandoning the wicked; they are sincere in faith and steadfast in their integrity, cherishing their reputation for virtue.
By nature he delighted in craftsmanship, was constantly mindful of shame and modesty, and took pleasure in practicing generosity.
Toward virtuous persons, his mind was free from opposition.
He observed carefully before acting, and his speech was free from negligence or error; he was skilled in witty eloquence and capable of successfully carrying out diplomatic missions.
They retain all instructions without forgetting them and are able to discern between what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.
O outsider!
This is the remaining habituation from having come from the human realm.
"This is what the wise know, but the foolish do not understand.
The Buddha said,
"O non-Buddhist!"
If that sentient being passes away from the celestial realm and attains birth in the human destiny,
entering the mother’s womb and being born into the world,
there will be these signs:

He is upright in character and always delights in cleanliness; he enjoys wearing flower garlands, perfumes, and ointments, and bathes his body, loathing dust and grime. Regarding the five desires—song, dance, and music—he selects only the most excellent and sublime, never indulging in licentiousness, and he constantly forms bonds of friendship with virtuous people.
He delighted in ascending towers, pavilions, and magnificent halls; his nature was solely characterized by compassion and forbearance, bringing joy to others.
He constantly adorned his body with fine garments and necklaces, maintaining dignified deportment in all movements without a moment of indolence in his mind.
"O outsider!
This is a residual habit remaining from having come from among the devas;
it is known by the wise, but not understood by the foolish."
The Buddha said, “O non-Buddhists!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family approaches, reveres, makes offerings to, and prostrates before a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), delights in hearing the true Dharma, and applies their attention according to reality, they will immediately transcend all those evil forms and appearances previously described.”
“O non-Buddhists!
You should know this:

if those who have come from the hells are reborn among humans, because they previously committed many acts of anger that harmed sentient beings, they fell into the hells and underwent various sufferings; now that they have obtained human form, they still harbor anger and affliction. When they encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who explains for them the wholesome dharmas corresponding to the antidotes, they are led to give rise to a mind of loving-kindness (maitrī), and are gradually caused to practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).”
“O non-Buddhists!
You should know this:

if a being from the animal realm is born into the human world, because they previously accumulated ignorance and repeatedly committed those impure deeds, even now that they have attained human form they remain prone to excessive lust. When they encounter a virtuous friend who explains to them the practice of contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination as an antidote to ignorance, it causes them to awaken and give rise to pure wisdom, gradually leading them to cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*.
“O non-Buddhists!
You should know this:

if those from the realm of hungry ghosts are reborn among humans, it is because they previously cultivated stinginess, greed, and envy for a long time without interruption. Having now obtained a human body, their nature is mostly base and parsimonious; yet, when they encounter a virtuous friend who explains to them the wholesome dharmas associated with giving as an antidote to that stinginess, they will gradually be led to practice the perfection of generosity.”
“O non-Buddhists!
You should know this:

if one who has come from among the asuras is born into the human realm, it is because they previously performed vast meritorious deeds while constantly giving rise to pride and looking down upon others. Now born among humans, their nature is largely haughty. When they encounter a virtuous friend who explains for them the Dharma-gate of the six sense bases and emptiness to counteract their pride, they will gradually be led to practice the perfection of patience.”
“O non-Buddhists!
You should know this:

if a person comes from among the realms of beings to be born in the human world, it is because of the power of their habitual practice of the ten paths of wholesome action in the past that they delight in associating with virtuous friends and dwell together with them in gentleness.”
By contemplating correct principles, one awakens to the dharma of impermanence, becomes weary of the suffering of birth and death, and rejoices in true, eternal bliss.
By gradually practicing the six *pāramitās*, one is able to give rise to the aspiration for unsurpassed bodhi and shall attain the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes.
“O non-Buddhists!
You should know this:

if one comes from the heavenly realms to be born among humans, it is because in their previous lives they practiced giving and morality without being able to forget the signs [of those acts], and all sought after karmic rewards. By these conditions, they were able to be born in the heavens and long enjoyed celestial pleasures. Having subsequently fallen back to be born in the human world, it is due to the power of their past merit and wisdom that they remember their former karma; realizing they must fall from heaven, they apply themselves with diligent vigor toward this present body.”

One should be exhorted to practice giving without hoping for a reward; if one dwells upon signs, it becomes a fault and affliction, so one should dwell in signlessness to obtain immeasurable merit. One should be exhorted to maintain pure precepts without hoping for a reward.
If one grasps at signs, this constitutes a flaw and a defilement; one should instead be purely clean, free from all taints.
By maintaining the precepts in this manner, one attains immeasurable merit and achieves non-retrogression toward the Bodhi of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, O non-Buddhists!

Those who emerge from the hells and attain birth in the human realm should draw near to virtuous friends, delight in hearing the Dharma taught by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and dwell in *āraṇya* to cultivate pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) with single-minded devotion. They should practice with diligent effort, their minds free from weariness or indolence; they should be skillful in posing questions and discerning the underlying meanings. Having realized that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they should, through their understanding of the Dharma, joyfully expound it to others."

Or, within villages and cities, he transforms bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as well as upāsakas and upāsikās, preaching and proclaiming the True Dharma so that they may cause both themselves and others to sever evil and cultivate goodness, gradually practicing until they attain the Unsurpassed Way.
"Furthermore, O non-Buddhists!

Having been liberated from the animal realm and attained birth in the human destiny, one should associate with virtuous friends and favorable conditions to hear the True Dharma. By abandoning delusion and through the power of virtuous friends and the cultivation of extensive learning, one contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena and becomes free from all fetters. Regarding one's own body as having no inherent existence, one feels no fear amidst the great assembly; naturally realizing the nature of equality and understanding that all phenomena are fundamentally devoid of self-nature, one is swiftly able to attain the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, O non-Buddhists!

Those who have been liberated from the realm of hungry ghosts and are reborn in the human realm should rely upon virtuous friends and spiritual mentors to first practice generosity, thereby eliminating their stinginess and greed."

By virtue of practicing generosity, one gives rise to wholesome wisdom, seeks liberation with joy, and cultivates pure conduct; yet, one does not grasp at the merit thus cultivated, understanding that all phenomena of the three times are equal, being of but a single characteristic—namely, signlessness—and through gradual cultivation, attains omniscience.
"Furthermore, O non-Buddhists!
Those who come from among the asuras to be born in the human realm should first resolve their minds to rely upon virtuous friends and engage in battle against the māra of afflictions."
The māra of afflictions refers to what is called self-conceit (*asmimāna*).
One should reflect: "What is this conceit?"
Who gives rise to this conceit?
Who experiences this conceit?
Nor does one perceive anyone who abandons this conceit.

By attending to, contemplating, and examining in this way, the characteristic of the conceit "I am" is found to be utterly unobtainable; since self-deception within one's own person has no real nature at all, one is then able to thoroughly comprehend that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it is not a thing; if it is not a thing, it cannot be established.
If it is not established, it neither arises nor ceases;
if there is no arising or ceasing, it cannot be conceptually differentiated.
If there is no conceptual differentiation, then there is no past, future, or present;
if these three time periods cannot be apprehended, one should know that those phenomena are indestructible.
The Buddha said, “O non-Buddhist!
Such a dharma-nature is unchanging and undifferentiated; its essence is true suchness (tathatā), and it is named the Tathāgata.”

One should know that the mark of a self (*ātman*) is truly unattainable; it is due to the arising of the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*) that one is born among the asuras, or as a human or a deva, and wanders through the various realms of existence.

Therefore, by observing the mark of this conceit of "I," one sees that it is fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature and that self and others are equal; thus, by severing residual habits, the mind attains purity.
“O non-Buddhists!
This is called the perfection of skillful means for abandoning the conceit of ‘I’ and ‘mine. You should diligently practice and study within this.

At that time, sixty thousand non-Buddhists in the assembly, having heard this teaching, attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). They rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined their palms with single-minded devotion, and praised the Buddha in verse:
“The World-Honored One’s power of wisdom is peerless;
He fully understands the conduct of sentient beings, And likewise knows the destination of all phenomena, As clearly as observing an amra fruit in the palm of his hand.”
Behold the various evil karmas of that world, Like clouds and mist shrouding the void;
Fools, failing to understand, remain perpetually submerged, Just like the blind who have lost their way.
Some say the world is impermanent; others say the world is not impermanent;
yet others say it is neither permanent nor impermanent—like a mad elephant bound by its tether.
Some say the world is finite; others say the world is not infinite;
still others say it is neither finite nor infinite—just like a bird caught within a cage.
Some say that the body itself is taken as the self, while others claim there is a self distinct from the body;
all these are deluded by false views, like a beast caught in a net whose mind is filled with distress.
Some say they were created by Maheśvara; others claim they were not born from causes.
Such evil views shroud sentient beings, like clouds obscuring the moon in the water.
Just as a bird confined within a cage, Gazes through the bars of its enclosure, longing for escape,
Know that the ignorant followers of external paths Are likewise devoid of liberation.
Some take refuge in Mahābrahmā, Nārāyaṇa, or the god of Great Learning;
like a person dwelling in darkness who is assailed by thieves, they lack liberation and are constantly born in fear.
Foolish outsiders cling to false views; their minds seek liberation but find no refuge.
Like prisoners bound within a jail, they are ever like the destitute, begging for alms.
If one can abandon the deviant and cultivate right practice, the Tathāgata will arouse a mind of loving-kindness toward them,
swiftly causing them to escape the cycle of saṃsāra, just as a king grants amnesty and clears away all offenses.
The Tathāgata fully practiced all manner of ascetic austerities Before realizing the supreme Buddha-enlightenment;
To deliver those of ignorance and false views, He has brought them all to liberation from the bonds of nescience.
The Lion among Men, the Honored One among bipeds, who has attained mastery over all phenomena,
out of compassion for those submerged in the ocean of suffering, delivers them by means of his power of skillful expedients.
If I am graced by the Tathāgata’s great power of wisdom, May all demonic adversaries be subdued without remainder;
May I attain the state of the World-Honored One, And let out the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly.
The Tathāgata can shake the trichiliocosm, Emitting immeasurable light that shines everywhere, Bringing all sentient beings to maturity;
I pray only that you grant me the prediction of enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the deep faith and understanding of the various non-Buddhists, emitted pure light from his mouth.
Then the Venerable Aśvajit asked in verse:
“The Tathāgata’s majestic virtue is peerless, Causing all these non-Buddhists to give rise to faith.”
Now, amidst this great assembly of devas and humans, you emit a vast, inconceivable radiance.
Beholding the Buddha’s pure light issuing from your mouth, like the full moon in an autumn sky, all the devas and humans harbor doubts;
we pray to hear the cause from which this Buddha-light arises.
Who has offered sublime worship to the Buddha? Who has pleased the heart of the Tathāgata?
Who dwells within the Buddha’s merits, such that they have moved the Tathāgata to manifest this auspicious omen?
Now that the non-Buddhists have heard the Buddha’s prophecy, all sentient beings have likewise resolved their minds;
the Tathāgata has appeared in the world to gather them in and bring them to subdual.
Excellent, O Sage, Great Holy Lord! You are able to sever all doubts and delusions.
Now this entire assembly joyfully desires to hear, as they conceive a deep love for the Buddha’s Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣu Aśvajit:
"Aśvajit, bhikṣu, you should know: Now is precisely the time to pose this question.
Desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, You have requested instruction from the Tathāgata regarding the matter of emitting light."
I shall now explain this for you in detail; listen attentively without distraction.
The deeds of the Tathāgata do not occur without cause; you should give rise to joy and abide in right mindfulness.
All these non-Buddhists have been fully subdued; having abandoned false views, they have attained right view.
By entering the True Dharma and giving rise to its remedies, they are thus able to abide securely on the path to enlightenment.
Having realized the stainless and quiescent Dharma, and having become weary of the mind that clings to views,
upon hearing these words of prophecy from the Buddha, he knew with certainty that he would become a Buddha.
In the past, you have already practiced the correct conduct and encountered twenty koṭis of Buddhas;
you made offerings and served them without weariness, for the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi.
Extensively practicing generosity with a heart free from stinginess, Firmly upholding pure precepts and abiding in the power of patience,
Diligently cultivating the gateways of dhāraṇī, And relying on samādhi to give rise to pure wisdom.
Fully endowed with the merits of the six perfections, they advance in every thought-moment without regression;
they crush all heterodox arguments and abandon false schools, skillfully discerning hundreds of thousands of difficult questions.
Formerly, due to associating with evil friends and relying upon various heterodox and divergent views,
I encountered the Tathāgata, the Great Guide, and immediately abandoned the practices of the false teachings I had cultivated.
In that future Constellation Eon, they shall all become Buddhas of one and the same name;
each appearing in the world, they shall be known as Universal Supreme Renown.
That Buddha-land is exceedingly pure and adorned with various kinds of rare jewels;
its sentient beings have escaped all false views and together rely on the Buddha’s teaching to give rise to clear wisdom.
In that land, there are no three evil realms, nor any affliction from the eight difficulties;
the lifespans of the Buddhas are exceedingly long, equaling eighty-four thousand years.
If anyone hears these names of the Buddhas, they will all be able to abandon and leave behind desire;
women shall attain the transformation of their female forms into male ones—this is due to the power of hearing the merits of the Buddhas.
The Tathāgata, who has skillfully subdued the enmity of Māra, bestows the prophecy of Buddhahood upon all non-Buddhists;
having heard this, they all give rise to hearts of joy, and shall all attain the realization of omniscience.

Translated by the Court Gentleman for Ceremonial Affairs (Shì Hónglùqíng), the Great Master of Dharma (Xuánfàn Dàshī), the Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa (Cí zǐ shāmén) Rìchēng, and others, in accordance with the Imperial Edict.

Chapter Twenty-Six: The Differentiation of the Six Elements (Liùjiè Chābié Pǐn), Part One. At that time, King Śuddhodana, together with his retinue and kinsmen, saw the various asura kings and even the heterodox brahmins receive the Buddha’s prophecy. They conceived a sense of rare wonder and marveled at this unprecedented event, exclaiming:
"The World-Honored One’s voice is exquisite, beautiful, pure, and penetrating; all those in the world who hear it are filled with joy."
At that time, when King Śuddhodana first beheld the Tathāgata, his heart was filled with deep affection and earnest longing.
Then the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of his royal father, addressed him, saying:
"Great King!..."

The Dharma I teach is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its meaning is subtle and exquisite, its single characteristic is pure, and it is the perfection of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
What I am now correctly teaching is the Dharma-gate that analyzes the distinctions and stages of the six elements.
"O King, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!
At that time, King Śuddhodana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We wish to hear it with joy; please proclaim it for us, that we may remember, uphold, believe, and accept it.”
The Buddha said:
"Great King!
Thus, these six elements, the six bases of contact, and the eighteen mental investigations arise conditioned by this *puruṣa*."
What are the six elements?
They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
What are the six bases of contact?

That is to say: through the sense-base of eye-contact one sees forms; through the sense-base of ear-contact one hears sounds; through the sense-base of nose-contact one smells odors; through the sense-base of tongue-contact one tastes all flavors; through the sense-base of body-contact one directly experiences tangibles; and through the sense-base of mind-contact one cognizes mental phenomena.
What are the eighteen mental investigations? This refers to when, after seeing a form with the eye, one experiences pleasure, or experiences distress, or abides in equanimity;
likewise, each of the six sense faculties encounters these three—pleasure and so forth—and this is called the eighteen mental investigations.
Great King!
What is the internal earth element?
It refers to that which is hard and rough within the body, namely: hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, and bones.
If the internal earth element does not arise and there is no cessation, then there is no process of accumulation.
Great King!

When a woman internally conceives of that *puruṣa* as she has contemplated him, and that *puruṣa* likewise gives rise to affection and desire, through the union of these two, the *kalala* is produced.
Furthermore, it is impossible that birth could occur through a similar conjunction;
it is impossible for two women [to produce a child],
and it is likewise impossible for two puruṣas [to produce a child].
If it were produced through various modes of conceptualization, that too would be impossible;
for its own essence is unreal and lacks any corresponding reality.
How, then, can this be described as having solidity?
"O Great King!
This body stands upon a semblance of solidity and hardness, yet it will ultimately rot, decay, and disintegrate; its only destination is the burial mound."
"From where does that solidity and hardness come?
Nor does it go away toward the four directions, above, or below.
Great King!"
This internal earth element should be understood in this way:
"Great King!
What is the external earth element characterized by solidity and hardness? It is like those palaces inhabited by Brahmā when the world was first established, composed of great jewels."
Furthermore, they are reborn among the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), where the palaces they inhabit are all composed of the seven treasures.
Great King!
If there were no earth element, from what would that quality of solidity and hardness arise?
It further formed the great earth, eighty-four thousand yojanas in thickness and sixty thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
it further produced the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains, which were firm and securely established as one with vajra;
it further produced Mount Sumeru, Mount Yugandhara, Mount Īṣādhara, Mount Nimindhara, and so on, up to the Black Mountains (Kṛṣṇagiri).
In this way, once this trichiliocosm has been successively formed, it remains firm and stable.
If there were no earth element, from where would that solidity and hardness arise?
"Great King!

Furthermore, when this earth element is about to be destroyed, it may be consumed by fire, swept away by water, or blown apart by wind; it is like burning ghee or oil, whose flames blaze so intensely that even the ashes and embers can no longer be seen."
If it were carried away by water, it would dissolve in an instant, like salt cast into the water.
If it were blown by the fierce winds of Vairambha, at that time the trichiliocosm would be completely shattered and destroyed, leaving nothing behind but total purity.
"Great King!
Furthermore, this earth element is empty when it arises and empty when it ceases; because its intrinsic nature is empty, it possesses neither male characteristics nor female characteristics;
it is merely that which is displayed through conventional designations."
In this way, both the earth element and the nature of the earth element are unattainable; only the Buddha’s correct wisdom can fully comprehend them.
"Great King!
What is the internal water element?

That which is within this body, consisting of all that is appropriated and characterized by moisture and so forth— namely, saliva, spittle, fat, marrow, pus, blood, excrement, and urine— is the internal water element, Great King!

If at some time one suddenly sees beloved persons and tears flow from the eyes; or if tears flow because one is oppressed by suffering; or if tears flow out of faith and reverence upon hearing the profound Dharma; or if tears flow because one is struck by a cold wind.
From where does this water element come?
When its watery nature dries up, where does it go?

Furthermore, when this world-system is destroyed, great black clouds arise in thirty-two tiers, completely covering the trichiliocosm. They pour down torrential rain, with drops as large as elephants, streaming day and night in an unceasing succession.
Thus, after fifty kalpas had passed, the water accumulated until it filled [the world] and reached as far as the Brahma-world.
Great King!
From where did this external water element come?
Furthermore, when this world is about to be destroyed, two suns appear; once these two suns have appeared, all small rivers, springs, and streams completely dry up.
When three suns appear, even the four great rivers that flow from Lake Anavatapta likewise become parched and exhausted.

When four suns appear, the waters of the great ocean decrease by one *yojana*, or two, or three; gradually decreasing to ten *yojanas* or twenty *yojanas*, they successively dry up until they reach eighty *yojanas*.
There remains some water, either deep as one *tāla* tree, or deep as the chest, or deep as a cow’s footprint, down to even a small amount of water the size of a finger’s surface.
At that time, the waters of the great ocean will all be completely dried up, purified, and exhausted without remainder.
Great King!

This characteristic of the water element comes from nowhere when it arises and goes nowhere when it ceases. When it arises, it is fundamentally empty; when it ceases, it is likewise empty. Because its intrinsic nature is empty, there is neither the mark of male nor the mark of female; it is merely that which is displayed through verbal expression.
In this way, both the water element and the nature of the water element are ungraspable; only the Buddha’s correct wisdom can fully comprehend them.
"Great King, what is the fire element within the body?

Whatever is appropriated within this body—namely, that which provides warmth and heat, chews and digests food and drink, brings about maturation and transformation, and maintains equilibrium—that which belongs to the category of heat is called the fire element (*tejodhātu*).
What is the external fire element?
It refers to that which is not appropriated and arises as the characteristic of heat.
Furthermore, if a person seeks the conditions for fire in a wilderness, whether by means of mugwort or wormwood, or cow dung fragments, or cotton down, and having thus produced fire;
It may burn grass, wood, forests, mountains, villages, and all other locations;

yet, Great King, this nature of the fire element arises without coming from anywhere and ceases without going anywhere. When it arises, it is fundamentally empty; when it ceases, it is also empty. Because its self-nature is empty, it is merely that which is manifested through verbal expression.
In this way, both the fire element and the nature of the fire element are ungraspable; only the Buddha’s correct wisdom can fully comprehend them.
"Great King!
What are the characteristics of lightness, movement, and so forth within the internal wind element?"

That is to say, this internal wind sometimes moves upward, sometimes moves downward, or remains in the abdomen, the flanks, or the back; it may cause itching or eruptions, or coalesce into lumps, or feel like being sliced by a knife, or like being pricked by needles; the inhalation and exhalation, and so forth, pervade all the limbs and members of the body.
What is the external wind element?

It refers to when winds come from the four directions, whether arising violently to uproot and break trees, or to topple and split mountain peaks; or when they arise subtly to flutter one’s robes and move the *tāla* trees—this is called the external wind element.
"O Great King!

This wind-element arises without coming from anywhere and ceases without going anywhere. When it arises, it is fundamentally empty; when it ceases, it is likewise empty. Because its self-nature is empty, it possesses neither male characteristics nor female characteristics; it is merely that which is manifested through conventional designations."
In this way, both the wind element and the nature of the wind element are unapprehendable; only the Buddha’s correct wisdom can fully comprehend them.
"Great King, what is the internal space element?"
If the skin, flesh, blood, and so forth within this body manifest and increase, they are devoid of the nature of material obstruction.
That is to say, the cavities of the eyes, the orifices of the ears, the mouth, and the throat—the essences of food and drink drawn in by swallowing—pass through the intestines and stomach and emerge.

When the six sense bases are drawn forth by the conditions of karma, and once these bases have arisen, they encompass the space-element; this is said to be included within the category of the internal space-element.
But from where does that space-element come?
Furthermore, that which manifests externally in various locations, being devoid of the nature of substantial obstruction, is called the external space-element (*bāhya-ākāśa-dhātu*).
Great King!
If form undergoes transformation and disintegration, all of it is empty.
Why is this? Because this realm of empty space is fundamentally inexhaustible; it is tranquil and immovable, like nirvana, pervading all places without obstruction.
"Great King!
It is as if there were a person who were to dig a pond or a well in a high plateau.
What do you think?"
"From where does this mark of emptiness within the pond and the well come?
The king replied,
"It comes from nowhere."
The Buddha said,
“Great King!
Suppose that person were then to fill it with earth.”
"What do you think?
Where does emptiness go?
The King replied:
“Emptiness has nowhere to go. Why is this?
Because this realm of empty space has neither coming nor going; it does not abide in the mark of male, nor is it the mark of female.”
“Great King!

The external realm of space is fundamentally without movement, for its intrinsic nature is free from it; it is merely that which is indicated by words, and can be fully understood only through the Buddha’s correct wisdom.”
“Great King! What is the element of consciousness?
It refers to that which, with the eye faculty as its primary basis, takes those forms and those intangible manifestations as its object; this is called the element of eye-consciousness.”
If the other five faculties each establish themselves by taking their respective objects as conditions, they are called the five consciousness-elements (*vijñāna-dhātu*).
Furthermore, these consciousness-elements do not adhere to the faculties, nor do they abide in the objects; they are neither internal, nor external, nor in between the two.

However, O Great King, this element of consciousness, having individually cognized its respective objects, immediately ceases and passes away; it comes from nowhere when it arises, and goes nowhere when it ceases.
O Great King!

When consciousness arises, it is empty; when it ceases, it is also empty. Because its intrinsic nature is devoid [of self], it does not abide in the mark of male nor in the mark of female, but is merely displayed by means of verbal expression.
In this way, both the element of consciousness and the nature of the element of consciousness are ungraspable; they are to be understood through the correct wisdom of a Buddha.
"Great King, what is the sense-base of the eye?"
It refers to the translucent matter derived from the four great elements—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
If the earth element is pure, then the eye-base is pure;
if the water, fire, and wind elements are pure, then the eye-base is pure.
Why is this? Because the sense-base of the eye arises through the purity of the earth element, yet within it not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended.
Thus, up to the sense-base of the eye arising through the purity of the wind element, within it not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended.
Why is this? Because it is without a sovereign and without agency;
it is like nirvāṇa, which is pure by its very nature.
Great King!
Thus, when each of these sense bases of the eye is sought individually, none can be found. Why is this?
Because the earth element is empty, the earth element is pure; likewise, because the wind element is empty, the wind element is pure.
If the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is fundamentally empty, then how could those elements possess purity?
Furthermore, there is neither anger nor contention.
Since both purity and contention are unattainable, what form could possibly be seen?

One should know that because the sense base of the eye is ultimately empty, its intrinsic nature is also empty; it is unattainable in the past or the future, and that which is produced in the future is likewise unattainable.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is detached.
If intrinsic nature does not exist, then there is neither the mark of male nor the mark of female; how, then, could there be attachment or delight?
If one gives rise to craving and attachment, this is the realm of Māra; if there is no craving or attachment, this is the realm of the Buddha. Why is this?
Because if there is no craving or attachment, one is able to remain far removed from all phenomena.
"Great King!
What is the ear-base?
It refers to translucent matter derived from the four great elements, whose mode of activity is as previously described."
"Great King!
The liberation of all phenomena is definitively manifest; like the emptiness of the dharma-realm, it cannot be conceptually established.
Great King!"

The various faculties each delight in and become attached to their respective objects; when the eye encounters forms, it gives rise to craving and pleasure. For this reason, form is said to be the objective domain of the eye.
Furthermore, when this faculty of the eye encounters the object of form, there are three aspects:
seeing a desirable form, one gives rise to thoughts of greed.
Unpleasant forms give rise to the perception of aversion;
those that are neither pleasant nor unpleasant give rise to the perception of equanimity.

In this manner, even when the mind is attached to the sphere of mental objects as its domain, if that mental faculty conditions pleasant forms and gives rise to extreme fondness, it will be drawn away by them and give rise to the activity of greed.
Unpleasant forms give rise to the activity of aversion;
pleasant and unpleasant forms give rise to the activity of delusion.
In this way, the three types of objects—such as sounds—and their characteristics, such as reception, should be explained according to the preceding [analysis].
“Great King!
The sense faculties are like illusions and their objects are like dreams. It is, for example, as if a man were to enjoy himself with various court ladies within a dream.”
"Great King!
What do you think?
Once that person has awakened from the dream, does the pleasure they recall actually exist?"
The King said, "No! The Buddha said:
“Great King!
Would a person who takes what was dreamed to be real be considered wise? “No, indeed!”
World-Honored One!

Why is this? Within a dream, a court lady ultimately does not exist; how much less could one engage in mutual enjoyment with her? You should know that such a person merely exhausts themselves by recollecting the objects of the dream, which can no longer be obtained.
The Buddha said,
“Great King! So it is, so it is!”

When foolish sentient beings see forms with their eyes, they give rise to love and delight in their minds; further, they give rise to craving and attachment, being led astray by them to perform actions born of greed: three types of bodily action, four types of vocal action, and three types of mental action.

When an action is first performed, it perishes in a single moment; this karma does not abide in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, below, or in between. At the limit of death, when the life-faculty ceases, the karmic retribution corresponding to that very action manifests before one, just as one awakens from a dream and recollects the events within that dream.
"Great King!

Consciousness is its master and karma is its object-condition; with these two factors acting as causes, the initial consciousness arises, leading either to the hells, or falling among the animals, the realm of Yama, or the asuras, whether as humans or devas."

Once the initial consciousness has arisen, each receives its respective retribution; the mental factors of the homogeneous class continue in succession and evolve. The final cessation of consciousness is termed the "skandha of death," and the arising of the initial consciousness is termed the "skandha of birth."
"Great King!
There is not even the slightest dharma that passes from this world to another world. Why is this so?"
"Because its nature is subject to arising and ceasing, Great King!
When body-consciousness arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere."
When that karma arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere.
When the initial consciousness arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is detached.

Thus one understands that body-consciousness is empty of body-consciousness, karma is empty of karma, initial consciousness is empty of initial consciousness; whether it is cessation, it is empty of cessation, and whether it is arising, it is empty of arising. One understands that the transformation of karma has no agent and no experiencer, being manifested merely through names, signs, and conceptual discrimination.
“Great King!
Suppose, for example, there were a person who, while dreaming, engaged in battle with various enemies.
What do you think?”
"After that person has awakened, do they remember the fighting and other such events from the dream as being real?
The King replied, "No!"
The Buddha said,
“Great King!
Would a person who takes what was seen in a dream to be real be considered wise?”
The King said:
“No, World-Honored One!”
Why is this? In a dream, there is ultimately no such thing as an adversary, much less engaging in combat with one.
One should know that such a person merely brings distress upon themselves; it is entirely without reality.
The Buddha said:
“Great King! So it is, so it is!”
When foolish ordinary beings see unpleasant forms with their eyes, they immediately give rise to vexation, aversion, and a desire for destruction;

they revile faults and perform actions born of hatred. These consist of three types of bodily action, four types of vocal action, and three types of mental action. Created at the very beginning, they perish in a single moment. This karma does not abide in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, below, or in between. At the limit of death, when the life-faculty ceases, the retribution of one’s own karma manifests entirely, just as one recalls events from a dream upon waking.
"Great King!

Consciousness is its master and karma is its object-condition; with these two factors acting as causes, the initial consciousness arises, leading either to the hells, or to rebirth among animals, in the realm of Yama, or among the asuras, whether as humans or devas."

Once the initial consciousness has arisen, each receives its respective retribution; the mental states of the homogeneous class continue in succession, and the final cessation of consciousness is termed the "aggregates of death," while the arising of the initial consciousness is termed the "aggregates of birth."
Great King!
There is not even the slightest dharma that passes from this world to another world. Why is this?
Because their nature is subject to arising and ceasing,
Great King,
when body-consciousness arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere.
When that karma arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere.
When the initial consciousness arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere. Why is this?

Because its intrinsic nature is detached, one thus understands that body-consciousness is empty of body-consciousness, karma is empty of karma, the initial consciousness is empty of the initial consciousness, cessation is empty of cessation, and arising is empty of arising. One understands that the turning of karma has no agent and no experiencer, but is merely a manifestation of names, signs, and conceptual discrimination.
"Great King!
It is as if there were a person who, while dreaming, was harassed by a piśāca; his mind gave rise to fear, and he became deluded and fainted."
"Great King!
What do you think?
When that person has awakened and recalls being tormented by a ghost in his dream, is it real or not?"
The King said, “No! The Buddha said:
"Great King!
Would a wise person consider what this man dreamed to be real?
The King replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because..."
In a dream, there is ultimately no demon to cause affliction; why then speak further of being deluded, bewildered, or fainting?
You should know that such a person merely exhausts themselves in vain, for there is nothing real whatsoever.
The Buddha said:
“Great King! So it is, so it is!”
When foolish ordinary beings see these forms with their eyes, they are deluded and lack understanding, thereby creating the karmic actions of ignorance.

These consist of three types of bodily karma, four types of vocal karma, and three types of mental karma. Created at the very beginning, they perish in a single instant. Once this karma has perished, it does not abide in the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, below, or in between. At the final limit, when the life-faculty ceases, the retribution of one's own karma manifests entirely, just as one who has awakened from a dream recalls the events within that dream.
"Great King!

Consciousness is its master and karma is its object-condition; these two factors mutually cause one another for the initial consciousness to arise, whether it proceeds to hell, or falls among the animals, the realm of Yama, or the asuras, or among humans or devas."

Once the initial consciousness has arisen, each receives its respective retribution; the mental factors of the homogeneous class continue in succession. The cessation of the final consciousness is termed the "aggregates of death," and the arising of the initial consciousness is termed the "aggregates of birth."
"Great King!
There is not even the slightest dharma that can pass from this world to another world. Why is this so?"
"Because its nature is subject to arising and ceasing, Great King!
When body-consciousness arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere."
When that karma arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere.
When the initial consciousness arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere. Why is this?
Because its intrinsic nature is detached,

one thus understands that body-consciousness is empty of body-consciousness, karma is empty of karma, initial consciousness is empty of initial consciousness, cessation is empty of cessation, and arising is empty of arising.
"Know that the turning of karma has no agent and no experiencer; it is merely displayed through names, signs, and conceptual discrimination.
'Great King!
You should know that the sense faculties are like illusions and their objects are like dreams; all phenomena are entirely empty and quiescent—this is called the gate of liberation of emptiness.'"
Emptiness that is devoid of the characteristic of emptiness is called the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*);
if there are no signs, there is no aspiration or seeking, which is called the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).
These three dharmas proceed together with emptiness as the preliminary path to nirvāṇa; one should train in this manner.

When body-consciousness arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere.

After waking up, does that person remember the events of the dream as being real?
The King replied:

The King replied, "No!"
World-Honored One!
Why is this? Within a dream, beloved ones ultimately do not exist; how much less, then, could there be the occurrence of separation from them?
"You should know that this person merely exhausts himself in vain; there is no reality whatsoever.
The Buddha said, "Great King!"

"So it is, so it is! When foolish worldlings hear that evil sound, they give rise to distress and affliction, conceiving a mind of anger and performing karmic actions of anger—namely, the three types of bodily karma, the four types of vocal karma, and the three types of mental karma. Having performed those actions, they perish and pass away in an instant."

Great King!
When the ear hears a sound of equanimity, it gives rise to the perception of equanimity, just as a person in a dream hears another reciting words of incomplete meaning."
"What do you think?
Once that person has awakened, does he still remember the sound he heard in the dream as being something real?
The King replied:

The King replied, "No!"
World-Honored One!
Why is this? Within a dream, there is ultimately no sound at all, let alone any further phrases of incomplete meaning.
"You should know that this person merely exhausts himself in vain; there is no reality whatsoever.
The Buddha said, "Great King!"
So it is, so it is! When foolish worldlings hear the sound of "renunciation," they do not comprehend its meaning; they treat it with contempt and disparage it, thereby creating the karma of delusion.
The three types of bodily action, the four types of vocal action, and the three types of mental action perish as soon as they are first performed.

Once these actions have perished, they do not abide in the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, below, or in between. There is no agent and no recipient; they are merely displayed through names, signs, and conceptual discrimination.
"Great King!
The sense faculties are like illusions and their objects are like dreams; all phenomena are entirely empty and quiescent—this is called the gate of liberation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha).
That which is empty lacks even the mark of emptiness—this is called the gate of liberation of signlessness (animitta-vimokṣamukha)."
If there is no sign, then there is no aspiration; this is called the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).
If one can thoroughly understand these three gates of liberation, they proceed together with emptiness as the preliminary path to bodhi—vast as the *dharmadhātu* and ultimate like space.
Regarding this analogy, you should understand it in this way:
"Furthermore, Great King!

It is as if there were a person who, while in a dream, saw himself drinking wine and becoming intoxicated, such that he did not recognize wholesome dharmas or various evil deeds, and was entirely unaware of virtues or faults."
"Once this person has awakened, do they think of the events in the dream as being real?
The King replied, "No!"
The Buddha said:
"Great King,
what do you think?"
“Would this person who clings to their dream as being real be considered wise?
The King replied, “No!”
World-Honored One!
Why is this? In a dream, there is ultimately no one who drinks alcohol, much less anyone who becomes intoxicated.
"You should know that this person merely exhausts himself in vain; there is no reality whatsoever in it.
The Buddha said, "Great King!"

It is so, it is so! Foolish, ignorant, and unlearned ordinary worldlings fixate their minds upon various phenomena; they give rise to a mind of craving and attachment and perform these deluded karmas—the three types of bodily karma, the four types of vocal karma, and the three types of mental karma. Having performed those karmas, they pass away moment by moment.

Once this karma has ceased, it does not abide in the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, below, or in between; yet at the time of death, the retribution for one's own previously performed karma appears within the mind, just as a person, upon waking from a dream, recalls the events of that dream.
"Great King!

Consciousness is its master and karma is its objective condition; these two factors act as mutual causes for the initial arising of consciousness. The performance of actions and the experiencing of their retribution are never lost or destroyed—whether one proceeds to hell, or falls among the animals, the realm of Yama, or the asuras, or among humans or devas."

Each receives its own retribution; as the mental states of a similar kind continue in succession, the final consciousness that ceases is called the "aggregate of death," and the initial consciousness that arises is called the "aggregate of birth."
"Great King!
When body-consciousness arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere.
Its conditions, when they arise, come from nowhere; when they cease, they go nowhere."
When that karma arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere.
Great King!
There is not even the slightest dharma that can pass from this world to another world.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is empty.

Thus one understands that the initial consciousness is empty of initial consciousness, karma is empty of karma, body-consciousness is empty of body-consciousness; if there is cessation, it is empty of cessation; if there is arising, it is empty of arising; saṃsāra is empty of saṃsāra, and nirvāṇa is empty of nirvāṇa—all are empty of intrinsic nature. There is no agent and no recipient; whether it be karma or its retribution, all are unobtainable, being manifested merely through names, signs, and conceptual discrimination.
“Great King!
The sense faculties are like illusions and their objects are like dreams; all phenomena are by nature empty and quiescent—this is called the gate of liberation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha).
That emptiness is devoid of the characteristic of emptiness is called the gate of liberation of signlessness (animitta-vimokṣamukha).”
If there is no sign, then there is no aspiration; this is called the liberation door of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).
If one can thoroughly understand these three liberation doors, they proceed together with emptiness as the preliminary path to bodhi—vast as the dharma-realm and ultimate as space.
"In this parable, one should understand it thus.
