Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Official, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, and Great Master of the Propagation of the Dharma, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Rìchēng and others, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Twenty-Seven: King Śuddhodana’s Faith and Understanding. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
“Great King!
Regarding the Dharma-gate of liberation as explained above, you should bind your own mind to it, observe with right mindfulness, and practice with courageous diligence and resolute determination.”

The Buddhas of the past, future, and present have, by relying upon this, realized unsurpassed bodhi; it can summon all worldly wealth and happiness, can eliminate all worldly thirst and craving, can subdue all worldly pride, can shatter all worldly false views, and can extinguish all the evils of sentient beings.
May all ordinary beings who have not yet ascended to the first bhūmi realize the nature of equality of all phenomena.
Such a Dharma essential is not the sphere of practice for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; it is that which is cultivated solely by bodhisattvas.
"Great King!
You should form this thought:
'How may I become an eye for those among gods and humans?'"
May you become a source of illumination throughout the long night;
may you become a raft upon the river of craving;
and may you become a guide in places of peril and difficulty.
To act as a sovereign for those who are without refuge;
having attained liberation oneself, one is further able to liberate others;
having attained deliverance oneself, one causes others to attain deliverance.
"I have attained peace for myself and bring peace to others;
I have realized nirvana for myself and lead others to its realization.
"Great King! [he said.]

One should not regard the wealth, pleasures, and mastery over the five desires experienced in this present world as real; for the sense faculties are like illusions and their objects are like dreams. Thus, one gives rise to craving and attachment toward the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, never reaching a time of satisfaction.
"Great King!

In the past, immeasurable *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas ago, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Anantayaśas (Boundless Renown). He was wealthy, sovereign, and possessed of great majesty; he had elephants, horses, chariots, and various precious litters. His most excellent wheel-treasure was indestructible by any. Having already drawn near to immeasurable Buddhas, he planted many roots of goodness under those Buddhas, such that whatever he intended in his mind was accomplished accordingly."
"Great King!
At one time, King Anantayaśas suddenly had this thought:

'I shall personally test the power of my merit; by virtue of my merit, may all the trees, flowers, and fruits throughout the four continents flourish and grow so that they may be enjoyed without end.'"
Having formed this thought, all the flowers and fruits throughout those four continents flourished and bloomed.
Great King!
That King Anantayaśas reflected thus:
"I shall now further test the power of my own roots of goodness, so that all the people throughout the four continents may have whatever they desire fulfilled according to their wishes without fail.
Having formed this thought, all the hopes and requests of the people within those four continents were granted exactly as they desired.
"Great King!
That King Anantayaśas further reflected:
'By the power of all my roots of goodness, may the four heavenly kings pour down fragrant water.'"
Having formed this thought, he caused fragrant water to rain down everywhere throughout the four continents.
Great King!
That King Anantayaśas further reflected:
"By the power of all my roots of goodness, may exquisite flowers rain down everywhere throughout the four continents.
Having formed this thought, various kinds of sublime celestial flowers rained down upon the four continents.
"Great King!
That King Anantayaśas further reflected:
'By the power of all my roots of goodness, may the four continents rain down exquisite precious garments.'"
Having formed this thought, he caused a rain of precious garments to fall throughout the four continents.
Great King!
That King Anantayaśas further reflected:
"By the power of all my roots of goodness, may silver rain down everywhere throughout the four continents.
Having formed this thought, silver rained down across all four continents.
"Great King!
That King Anantayaśas further reflected:
'By the power of my own roots of goodness, may the four great kings cause golden rain to fall.'"
Having formed this thought, it rained down pure gold throughout the four continents. Why was this?
It was obtained entirely through the wholesome karma cultivated in the past by King Anantayaśas together with all sentient beings.
"Great King!

This great earth of Jambudvīpa measures eighteen thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Furthermore, there are sixty koṭis of great cities within it; among them is a city named Ratnavyūha, twelve yojanas in both length and breadth, perfectly level on all four sides and exquisitely constructed. Outside its walls stand rows of tāla trees, seven tiers deep and composed of the four precious substances—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—adorned and embellished so as to be most delightful."
As for those gold trees, their leaves, flowers, and fruits are all silver;
as for those silver trees, their leaves, flowers, and fruits are all gold;
and as for the vaidūrya trees, their leaves, flowers, and fruits are all crystal (sphāṭika).
The leaves, flowers, and fruits of those vaidūrya trees are all made of lapis lazuli.

The city has seven tiers, covered above by nets and bells of precious gems and various exquisite jewels; outside the city, there are further seven tiers of jeweled moats, all composed of the seven treasures combined.
Each jeweled moat was half a yojana deep and one yojana wide.
The bottom was strewn with golden sand, and it was filled to the brim with the eight qualities of pure water, crystal clear and serene.
Various birds with exquisite voices soar and gather therein, while *utpala*, *kumuda*, *padma*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers bloom everywhere.
The surrounding steps and thresholds were composed of the four jewels:
golden steps with silver thresholds, silver steps with golden thresholds,
lapis lazuli steps with crystal thresholds, and crystal steps with lapis lazuli thresholds.
The steps were made of crystal and the thresholds of lapis lazuli.
Each flight of stairs was composed of the seven precious gems, and alongside them grew golden plantains.
Furthermore, at the head of each path were placed various jeweled seats, exquisitely crafted and most delightful.
Such manifold riches, pleasures, and various adornments were all obtained through the power of the vast roots of goodness and merit accumulated by King Anantayaśas.

Furthermore, surrounding that City of Jewel Adornments were eighty-four thousand pure groves. Within each grove were eight great ponds, each half a yojana in width. The banks of each pond featured four stairways composed of the four jewels, exquisitely and skillfully adorned; they were filled with water possessing the eight virtues, and various colored lotuses bloomed and spread throughout them.
Upon the banks of that pond there were further various flowers:
*atimuktaka* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *vārṣikī* flowers, *sumana* flowers, *aśoka* flowers, and *vāsika* flowers—such diverse and wondrously fragrant flowers.
King Anantayaśas, together with his ministers and subjects, dwelt within the garden and enjoyed themselves there.
Great King!

That royal palace city was lofty, vast, and magnificent; rows of precious tāla trees were planted above it, and precious nets covered it entirely. Precious bells chimed in harmony, producing exquisite sounds like those of the five musical instruments.
At that time, the people there, relying on the king’s virtuous transformation, dwelt in wealth, joy, sovereignty, and peace.
"Great King! At another time, King Anantayaśas thought to himself thus:"
"I should now go to Pūrvavideha.
Having formed this thought, the king, leading his fourfold army, ascended into the air together and immediately arrived at that place.
All those minor kings came to welcome him, each offering his own realm with sincere devotion; the king resided there for hundreds of thousands of millions of years, O Great King!
King Anantayaśas further reflected to himself:
"I shall now proceed to the western continent of Aparagoyānī.
Having formed this thought, he led his fourfold army and, traveling together through the air, arrived at that place immediately.
All those minor kings came to welcome him, each offering his own kingdom with sincere devotion; the king resided there for hundreds of thousands of millions of years, O Great King!
King Anantayaśas further reflected to himself:
"I shall now go to Uttarakuru.
Having formed this thought, he led his fourfold army and, traveling together through the air, arrived immediately at that place.
Those people joyfully submitted to his rule, and the king resided there for hundreds of thousands of millions of years.
Great King!
That King Anantayaśas then reflected to himself:
"I have heard in the past that there are the Thirty-three Heavens dwelling upon the summit of Mount Sumeru; I shall go there now.
Having formed this thought, he immediately mounted a dragon-elephant and, together with his fourfold army, soared through the air and ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru.
At that time, King Anantayaśas asked his minister,
"What did you see of Mount Sumeru, the great ocean, and the four continents?
The minister replied:
"I see its form rotating and shifting without rest, like a potter's wheel.
The king said to his charioteer,
"What you see is that this great king of nāga-elephants has not yet ceased its great stride."
The king proceeded forward again and asked his charioteer,
"What are the characteristics of those things you see that resemble Mount Sumeru?
The charioteer replied:
"I now see that Mount Sumeru and the great ocean are all trembling.
The king said to his minister, "We are now approaching the summit of Mount Sumeru; this king of naga-elephants has not yet finished urinating."
The king proceeded further and asked his charioteer,
"What are the characteristics of those things you see that are equal to Mount Sumeru?
The charioteer replied:
"I now see that Mount Sumeru and the great ocean are neither moving nor shifting.
The king said to his minister,
"This king of dragon-elephants has now reached the summit of Mount Sumeru."
At that time, when King Anantayaśas and his fourfold army had reached Mount Sumeru, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saw King Anantayaśas from afar and came forward to welcome him with joy, saying:
"Welcome! Welcome!"
"Great King!
he said, and immediately divided his seat in half, inviting the king to sit upon it.
Thereupon, King Anantayaśas took his seat and dwelt in the heavens for immeasurable years, ruling in joint authority with that lord of the devas, sharing half of his domain.
After a long time had passed, he thought to himself:
"I shall displace that deva and become the sole ruler.
Having formed this thought, the king and his military host immediately fell away from the city of Ratnavyūha and the garden of Ratnapuṭa.
At that time, the park keeper, having witnessed this event, informed the people of the city, making this proclamation:
"Now a celestial being has passed away here."

At that time, the king, whose name was Karuṇākarin (Maker of Love), having heard this account, quickly prepared his carriage and went to that garden. Seeing the events as described above, he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

He immediately ordered the preparation of various kinds of incense, flowers, powdered incense, and unguents, and proceeded to the king’s presence. There, he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and after offering words of comfort and greeting, addressed the king, saying:
"The Holy Deva has arrived here; who might this be?"
He replied: "Have you ever heard before of a wheel-turning monarch named Anantayaśas? King Kāma said:
"I have heard from the elders:

'In the past, there was a king named Anantayaśas, whose majestic virtue was sovereign and who ruled over the four continents. Together with his fourfold army, he ascended into the air and proceeded to the Heaven of the Thirty-three.'"
“Is the one you heard of anyone else?
It was none other than myself.
At that time, King Anantayaśas, having descended from the heavens, was unable to endure the scent and flavor of human food and drink at first; it was as if clarified butter were poured onto hot sand.
At that time, King Priyarāma, seeing that he was suddenly in such distress and unable to remain, asked:
"What virtuous teaching is there?
What shall I proclaim for future generations?"
Then King Anantayaśas said to King Kāmakāra:
"Since ancient times, I have been a wealthy, noble, and sovereign king over the four continents, obtaining everything I required exactly as I wished."

"He ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and shared a seat with Śakra, the Lord of Devas; yet because of his insatiable greed, he fell from that celestial realm. All such matters should be recounted in this manner.
Having spoken these words, he immediately passed away.
The Buddha said,
"Great King! As for the King Anantayaśas of old, could he have been anyone else?"
"I am that very person now.
Therefore, you should know that the sense faculties are like illusions and their objects are like dreams; fix your mind in right contemplation and do not give rise to doubt.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Seeking the wealth of the True Dharma with joy, With a pure mind always upright and honest, The five desires are not solid; The wise should keep far from them.
If one has clear understanding of the Dharma, One will grow weary of the pleasures of the five desires."
He has well subdued his mind and is able to destroy all afflictions.
Because he has severed the afflictions, he does not undergo rebirth in the evil realms.
Having departed from those paths of karma, he is revered by the world.
Free from the defilement of sensual desire, he reveals the faults of craving;
with a mind that delights in benefiting all beings, he is hailed as the most supreme in the world.
Hearing of the perils of the five desires, one can swiftly give rise to weary detachment.
Purifying the mind through wisdom, he dwells in the world without superior; The most supreme Great Being,
able to extinguish the evils of sentient beings and cause them to leave behind greedy conduct, dwells in the world without superior.
The most supreme Great Being, who can extinguish the evils of sentient beings and cause them to leave behind ways of anger, is unsurpassed in the world.
The most supreme Great Being, who can extinguish the evils of sentient beings...
"May they be freed from that delusion and pride, becoming pure and wise ones.
When the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, he further expounded the essentials of the Dharma for King Śuddhodana.
The Buddha said, "Great King!

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a wheel-turning king named Jyotīṣprabha (Earth-Born). He ruled the world with the Dharma and was fully endowed with the seven treasures, namely: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the military treasure, the woman treasure, and the minister-treasurer treasure."
The king had a crown prince named Dharanindara, who succeeded his father, the Wheel-Turning King, and was consecrated by the ministers and high officials as a consecrated Kṣatriya Holy King.
On the fifteenth day, when the moon was full, he washed his hair and bathed to cleanse his body of impurities, and donned fresh, clean garments.
Adorning his body with various flower garlands, mani-jewel crowns, and diverse necklaces, he ascended a high terrace surrounded by female attendants.
Then, in the eastern direction, there appeared the precious golden wheel, complete with a thousand spokes and a perfect hub and rim, its radiance shining forth over an extent of seven cubits.
At that time, King Mahīdeva, having witnessed this event, thought:
"In the past, I heard what the elders said:"
"If a kṣatriya, upon receiving the consecration, has a golden wheel appear as previously described, it should be known that he will certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin).
I should now test this for myself."
Then the Heavenly King of the Earth rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the wheel, and spoke these words:
"This precious golden wheel shall descend to the earth."
Having thus offered his prayer, he stood before the king.
The king used exquisite incense and superior garments to wipe the wheel-treasure and placed it in his right palm, then addressed the wheel, saying:
"I now wish to go to the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha."
The Golden Wheel ascended into the air and immediately arrived at that place where the Holy King of the Earth-Gods appeared.

That ground was level and even, strewn with various precious flowers; by the sovereign power of the King, the entire earth shook, and the places where wells, springs, rivers, and ponds had run dry were all filled with water of eight virtues—namely, light, clear, sweet, smooth, non-turbid, odorless, such that those who drink it never tire of it, and which causes no pain to the belly.
All the trees and forests were in full bloom with flowers and fruit, and those that had been withered and parched became lush once more.

As the King traveled, a wheel led the way before him; in whatever lands he visited, the great and small kings there each took golden platters filled with silver grain, or silver platters filled with golden grain, and came forth to welcome him, offering greetings and inquiries:
"Welcome! Welcome!"
"Sage King!
This land is peaceful and secure; we pray that you will dwell here to govern and transform the people, and we shall all serve as your attendants.
The king then spoke, saying:

"I have no need now for kingdoms or treasures; you should instead follow my instructions: stay far away from killing and taking what is not given, stay far away from sexual misconduct and do not speak falsely, and so on, up to wrong views and the ten unwholesome courses of action.
You should abide yourselves in the ten wholesome courses of action, and also teach others to abide in the ten wholesome courses of action."
“Filially support your parents, serve your teachers and elders, do not commit unrighteous acts, cultivate wholesome deeds, and likewise exhort others to diligently practice all manner of goodness.

At that time, the Heavenly King of the Earth, together with his fourfold army, departed from Pūrvavideha, passed beyond the entire human realm, gradually crossed the great ocean, and reached Aparagoyānī and Uttarakuru, proclaiming the king’s virtuous transformation.
Having completely subdued them, the king and the wheel-treasure returned to Jambudvīpa and remained suspended in the air above the palace gate.

At that time, the four continents were transformed into the seven precious jewels; all suffering in the three evil realms, as well as the sounds of unwholesomeness in the eight difficult states, were entirely extinguished—let alone those who would commit evil deeds.
Why is this so? It is entirely due to the power of the original vows of the Earth-Heaven Universal Monarch.

Furthermore, as that Wheel-Treasure travels through and circles the four continents in the midst of space, natural fragrant rice grows everywhere; it requires no planting and is pure, free from husks and chaff.
Furthermore, as that wheel-treasure circulates throughout the world, various kalpavṛkṣa trees produce divine precious garments, which all sentient beings enjoy according to their wishes.
Moreover, as that wheel-treasure circulates throughout the world, all those with serious illnesses are healed; there remain only three types of illness:
first, those of mental disposition.
Second is edible food; third is aging.
Those sentient beings have a lifespan of a thousand years, and should they experience even the slightest suffering, it naturally vanishes away.
Countless and boundless such rare phenomena appeared simultaneously.
At that time, the Heavenly King of the Earth suddenly had this thought:
"I now possess such wealth, nobility, and sovereignty; could there perhaps be another place superior to this?"
He further reflected to himself:
"I have heard in the past that on the summit of Mount Sumeru there are the Thirty-three Heavens, whose bliss is beyond compare; I should go there now."
Accompanied by his fourfold army, he went immediately to that place.

Upon seeing the Heavenly King of the Earth approaching from afar, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, rose to welcome him, greeted him with kind words, offered him half of his seat, and invited him to rule together with him.
After a long time had passed, the Heavenly King Bhūmipati, wishing to retire from his position so that Śakra alone might rule as Lord of the Devas,
made this thought and, together with his military host, descended into the city of Mathurā in Jambudvīpa.
That King of the Earth Devas had long dwelt in his celestial palace, enjoying supreme and wondrous pleasures; yet suddenly falling into the human realm, he could find no moment of peace.
He was like clarified butter placed upon hot sand: his body and mind were instantly impaired, and he was utterly incapable of enduring it.
Then the Heavenly King Earth spoke in verse:
“The king is called ‘sovereign,’ yet he cannot sever craving;
it is like adding dry wood to a fire. Therefore, one should distance oneself from it.”
Just as one who drinks salt water in thirst only increases their thirst,
know that for those attached to desire, there is likewise no satiety.
Just as the various rivers flow into the sea, they never reach a time of fulfillment.
One should know that for those attached to desire, there is likewise no satiety.
Just as a mirror reflects a form, its manifestation is never fixed;
one should know that for those attached to form, there is likewise no satiety.
Just as one hears the echo in a valley, responding without ceasing, you should know that those who are attached to sound are likewise never satiated.
It is like a vessel filled with incense; it never tires of receiving the fragrance.
One should know that for one who is attached to fragrance, there is likewise no satiety.
Like a ladle that stirs fine delicacies, it distributes them evenly but has no time of its own use;
one should know that for one who is attached to flavor, there is likewise no satiety.
Just as the wind moves through space, its shifting never fixed,
you should know that for one who clings to touch, there is likewise no satiety.
Just as drinking water in a dream cannot dispel the thought of thirst, so it is with sensory contact.
Those whose minds are attached to various phenomena are likewise never satiated.
If one delights in and clings to various desires, the fire of greed will blaze ever more fiercely;
one must therefore extinguish it with the water of pure wisdom, leaving nothing behind.
"Then, after the Cakravartin King Bhūmideva had spoken this verse, he immediately passed away.
The Buddha said,
"Great King!"
"Was the King of the Earth and Heaven anyone else?
It was I myself.

The Buddha said: "Great King!

I shall now speak further. In ages past, there was a universal monarch named Mandhātṛ, possessed of great majesty and endowed with vast merit and virtue, who was born from the crown of his father the king's head."

In previous lives, they have long cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya) and have encountered immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas, planting the roots of all virtues in the presence of those Buddhas.
He succeeded his father-king to the position of consecration, ruling over the four continents with sovereign wealth and power.
Appearing in Jambudvīpa to govern and transform the world, he enjoyed the five sensual pleasures, which were supreme and unsurpassed.
It was peaceful and prosperous, with a flourishing population.
Villages and cities were so close that a rooster could fly from one to another. The great earth was free of tiles, rubble, and thorns; even its hills and mounds yielded much gold and treasure.
Gardens, groves, springs, and ponds adorned the realm; the capital city was named Ayodhyā.
The city measured twelve yojanas from east to west and seven yojanas in both breadth and length from north to south, with nets of jewels and jeweled bells covering it entirely.
The king was surrounded by a great retinue who paid him respectful homage, like Śakra in the Great City of Sudarśana.
That King Mandhātṛ constructed three seasonal palaces:
the first was named Moonlight (*Candraprabha*), which the king occupied during the hot season.
The second is the Vaiḍūryagarbha, wherein the king resides during the rainy season.
The third is called Sūryaprabha, wherein the king resides during the cold season.
When the king enters that Candraprabhā palace, he, together with his queens, concubines, and retinue surrounding him before and behind, finds his body cooled and refreshed.

Just as if his body were anointed with the fragrance of gośīrṣa-candana, so too was the King’s person peaceful and harmonious; he was like Śakra, together with the devaputras, enjoying supreme and exquisite delights in the Vaijayanta Palace.

During the rainy season, when the king enters the lapis lazuli palace with his retinue, his mind experiences such delight as if his body were anointed with the fragrance of tamālapatra. It is just so for the king’s mental satisfaction.
During the cold season, when the king and his retinue enter the Sunlight Palace, they anoint their bodies with aloeswood incense; the warmth of the king’s body is likewise of such a nature.
"Great King!

According to the seasons, in whatever palace King Mandhātṛ went, there arose sensations of pleasure: sometimes a cool breeze would blow, sometimes fragrant rain would fall, and sometimes musical instruments would play; in all these matters, he obtained his every wish."
"Great King!

That King Mandhātṛ suddenly had a rain of various gold and jewels fall from within his palace for seven days. When the seven days were complete, the king marveled at this rarity, saying, 'Such is the retribution for pure meritorious karma.'"
The king resided there, governing and transforming the realm for immeasurable years.
At that time, King Mandhātā thought to himself:
"I have heard that to the west lies the great continent of Goḍānīya."
Having formed this thought, he ascended into the air with his fourfold army and proceeded from Jambudvīpa, gradually arriving at that place.
Once the king had arrived there, he enjoyed the most excellent food, drink, and requisites; the people of the land were peaceful, secure, and lived in abundance and joy.
Within the royal palace, it rained jewels for seven days, no different from what occurs throughout Jambudvīpa; the king resided there for hundreds of thousands of millions of years.
At that time, King Mandhātṛ reflected again:
"I have heard that to the east there is a great continent called Videha."
Having formed this thought, he ascended into the air with his fourfold army and proceeded gradually from Goḍānīya-dvīpa to that place.

Once the king arrived there, he enjoyed exquisite and supreme food and drink; he governed the people with transformation and healing so that they lived in peace, security, abundance, and joy, and likewise rained down treasures within the palace for seven days, no different from what occurred in Goḍānīya-dvīpa. The king resided there for hundreds of thousands of years.
"Great King!
That King Mandhātṛ again reflected to himself:
'I have heard that in the north there is the continent of Uttarakuru, where the people do not give rise to the conceptualization of "I" and "mine. I shall now go there to test them.'"
Having formed this thought, he ascended into the void together with his fourfold army and traveled from Videha to that very place.
Once the king arrived there, he examined his retinue and realized it was indeed so; they enjoyed supreme and wondrous pleasures for immeasurable years.
"Great King!
King Mandhātṛ further reflected:
'I have heard that there are the Thirty-three Gods who dwell individually upon the summit of Mount Sumeru; I shall now go there to behold them with my own eyes.'"
Having formed this thought, he traveled through the air with his fourfold army and arrived at that place from the continent of Kuru.
At that time, the Lord of the Gods was gathered with the sons of gods in the Hall of Sublime Dharma, discussing matters pertaining to the heavens.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing King Mandhātṛ approaching from afar, went out to meet him and spoke these words: "Welcome,
Great King!"
“...have come this far.
He then offered half of his seat and bade the king sit together with him.
When King Mandhātṛ took that seat, he excelled the Lord of Devas in ten respects:
First, longevity;
second, dignified demeanor; third, renown.
Fourth, happiness;
fifth, sovereignty;
sixth, physical excellence.
Seventh, the voice;
eighth, the fragrance of the body.
Ninth, the taste of food;
tenth, subtle touch.
At that time, King Mandhātṛ and the Lord of the Devas were identical in appearance and enjoyment, with the sole distinction being the blinking of their eyes.
"Yet the sons of the gods, by means of this eloquence, know that there is a distinction between the lord of heaven and the king of men.
The Buddha said,
"Great King!"

King Mandhātṛ was born among humans with a physical appearance identical to that of the Lord of Devas; his extraordinary karmic rewards were unprecedented, and having dwelt in that celestial realm for immeasurable years, he attained the status of the most supreme and sovereign Lord of Devas.
Supremely honored for his wealth and prosperity over the four continents, King Mandhātṛ ruled as a co-sovereign with Śakra, yet his mind remained unsatisfied.
Then, at one time, King Mandhātṛ suddenly conceived a different thought:
"I myself can now alone be the Lord of Devas; what need is there for Śakra?"
"It would be appropriate to repel him.
Having formed this thought, the king, together with his fourfold army, descended from the heavens into the most excellent grove of the city of Ayojjhā in Jambudvīpa.
At the time of his descent, the king’s majestic radiance pervaded Jambudvīpa, shining everywhere and eclipsing the light of the sun and moon.
When the people went out of the city to observe, they saw this unprecedented occurrence and were struck with wonder. They immediately entered the city and proclaimed:
"Now a celestial being, together with the fourfold army, has descended from the sky into the most excellent garden."
"Great King!

At that time, the king and the people within the city immediately prepared various kinds of ointments, powdered incense, song and dance, music, precious banners, flags and canopies, flower garlands, necklaces, and ornaments for adorning the body, and quickly proceeded to that most excellent garden."
"Great King!

When King Mandhātṛ first descended into the human realm, the earth shook in six ways. At that time, all the people took whatever supreme ornaments and most excellent, wondrous fragrances they possessed and brought them each to the Most Victorious Garden (Puṣpavana), using them to anoint the king’s body as an offering."

At that time, King Mandhātṛ had long enjoyed the exquisite pleasures of the celestial palaces; unable to endure the provisions of the human realm, he was like clarified butter placed upon hot sand—his limbs exhausted and weary, with not even a moment’s peace.
At that time, the king within the city asked him, saying:
"Who is this being from heaven who has fallen here? He then replied:
"Have you ever heard before of a Wheel-Turning King named Mandhātṛ?
The king and his people all replied,

"We have indeed heard of a king named Mandhātṛ, who possessed great majesty and virtue, ruled over the four continents, and without departing from the human realm, led his fourfold army to ascend to the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
Then the deva who had fallen from his station addressed him, saying:
"I myself was King Mandhātṛ in the past; it was because of insatiability that I came to this state."
"Who is it that finds contentment in the fruits of merit?
At that time, the king within the city and his ministers and subjects asked in verse:
"I have heard from the elders' accounts that in the past there was a Wheel-Turning King."
Named Mandhātṛ, endowed with vast majesty and power,
he ascended to the Heaven of the Thirty-three with his retinue of the fourfold army;
there he taught and transformed the devas and humans, preaching the True Dharma for them.
"That King Mandhātṛ, having abandoned celestial bliss to undergo suffering,
was overcome by the power of impermanence because his mind knew no contentment.
Then all the people joined their palms and prostrated at the feet of the Great King:
"What virtuous words did the King leave behind that I shall speak in the future?
Then King Mandhātṛ addressed the multitude, saying:
"Because of my attachment to pleasure, I have fallen from heaven."
Possessing great majestic power, he ruled over the four continents;
yet never satiated in his pursuit of sensual pleasures, he fell from heaven.
Formerly, within his own palace, he rained down precious jewels for seven days.
Insatiable in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, he falls from heaven.
That Lord Śakra, sharing half his throne and ruling together with him,
was tormented by evil thoughts and fell away from heaven.
Never satiated with sensual pleasures, they do not have faith in or accept the Buddha’s words;
destroying their own meritorious karma, they wander through the ocean of saṃsāra.
Yet there are great wise ones in the world who are able to leave behind the darkness of desire and delusion.
One can also teach others to practice contentment and observe well.
If one abides in right reflection and accords with all wholesome dharmas,
one will destroy the activities of saṃsāra, as well as the calamities of birth, old age, and death.
One contemplates contact as a blazing fire, and one contemplates feeling in the same way;
by understanding this well, desire does not arise.
The fool is attached to sense objects, just like hearing the sound of music.
Realizing that the faculties and their objects are fundamentally empty, one knows that phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
When the six sense bases are not at peace, they are merely pervasive conceptualization;
if one realizes that form and the rest are empty, then attachment will not arise.
"The wise one guards well, Feeling weary of and terrified by the suffering of saṃsāra;
With the eye of wisdom constantly illuminating, They attain liberation from all faults and afflictions.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Great King!
As for King Mandhātṛ at that time, could he have been anyone else?
Do not view it otherwise; it was I myself."
Because they rely on their majestic power, the force of merit, and sovereign control, yet remain insatiable in their greed, they eventually meet their end.
Therefore, Great King, you should renounce the arrogance and self-importance born of wealth and status; abide in a pure mind and do not give way to negligence.

If one abandons negligence and benefits both oneself and others, giving rise to all roots of goodness and abiding in the principle of equality, then one can realize and enter the true nature of reality (dharmatā).
Great King!

You should know that whether it be the conditioned realm or the unconditioned realm, these two are equal; they possess neither male characteristics nor female characteristics, nor do they belong to the past, present, or future. You should settle your own mind within this Dharma, observe it with certainty and correct insight, and not follow the instructions of others.
“Great King!

In the past there was a king named Nimi who appeared in the world and ruled according to the True Dharma. His mind was always tranquil and he never gave rise to negligence; in various places he remained free from negligent conduct, and because he feared those evils, he did not commit them again.”
"Great King!

That King Nimi is firm in his resolve and constantly dwells in the contemplation of the equality of the three periods of time. He contemplates all dharmas of the past as abiding in the principle of equality, fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature; that all dharmas of the present and future are likewise devoid of intrinsic nature is also thus."
"Great King!
That King Nimi contemplates the dharmas of the three periods of time as perfectly equal and remains free from grasping or attachment.

Furthermore, he observes all sentient beings in the world who are deluded and attached by the four inversions: they perceive purity within the impure, pleasure within suffering, permanence within impermanence, and a self within what is non-self."
At that time, King Nimi thought to himself:

"The fools of this world are deeply pitiable; though the self-nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent, they are shrouded by delusion and ignorance and do not realize it. I must employ skillful means through the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to transform these sentient beings and cause them to give rise to faith and compliance."
He then said to him:

"You should understand that all phenomena are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature. If a phenomenon is devoid of intrinsic nature, you should know that such a phenomenon is neither past, nor present, nor future."
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
If a phenomenon is empty of intrinsic nature, it cannot be conceptually distinguished as past, present, or future.

“Great King! After that King Nimi had thus demonstrated the Dharma of the equality of the three periods of time, at that moment, hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings in the assembly heard the Dharma, attained realization, and achieved the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).”

At that time, the sons of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven gathered in the Sudharmā Hall and deliberated among themselves. With their divine eyes, they saw from afar that in Jambudvīpa there was King Nimi, who governed and transformed his realm through the ten virtuous paths; all the people obtained the benefits of the Dharma, and he benefited sentient beings through skillful means.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was in another place; with his pure divine ear, he heard what had been said above.
Then that Lord of the Devas came to the assembly and sat down, asking the sons of the gods:
"What were you discussing just now?"
He replied immediately:

"The people of Jambudvīpa have truly gained the benefit of the Dharma. King Nimi has profoundly penetrated all dharmas and, through skillful means, gathers and transforms sentient beings; he causes those dwelling in perversion to leave perversion behind. What was discussed previously refers precisely to this matter."
Then the Lord of the Devas said to the son of heaven:
"This King Nimi has planted roots of virtue in past lives and is fully endowed with the power of majestic spiritual authority.
Do you wish to see this King Nimi?"
The devas all said,
"We wish to see him.
At that time, Śakra immediately commanded his charioteer, named Mātali:
"You should prepare the thousand-spoked precious chariot along with your retinue and proceed to the presence of King Nimi of Jambudvīpa, and speak thus:
'Great King!'"
"This is the thousand-spoked precious chariot sent by Śakra to welcome the King; we pray that you will mount it and not give way to fear.
Those sons of the gods wish to behold the Holy King."
The charioteer replied:
"Your Majesty is now ascending to heaven; there are two paths by which you may go:
shall you take the path of inverted beings, or the path of non-inverted beings?"
The King immediately replied,
"You may take me between those two paths and proceed.
Then the charioteer Mātali said, "I shall follow Your Majesty’s command and advance along the middle path."
The King spoke again, saying:
"You may stop the carriage and rest for a short while;
I shall go to observe the dwelling place of those deluded sentient beings."

Then, by the power of his compassionate vow, King Nimi, in a mere instant, caused immeasurable sentient beings to each attain the samādhi of sporting in tranquil supernormal powers as well as the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
In this brief interval, that King Nimi was able to accomplish great benefit.
Why is this? It is because he had long practiced the conduct of heedfulness and was skillful in means for bringing about the welfare and happiness of sentient beings.
Then Mātali gradually proceeded forward and led the king to the summit of Mount Sumeru.
From afar, the king first saw the lush greenery of the forest trees and said to the charioteer,
"This place must surely be the dwelling of beings who are not deluded."

The charioteer replied, "This grove belongs to the Heaven of the Thirty-three. There, those sons of the gods in the Hall of Wondrous Dharma gaze with single-minded devotion, desiring to see Your Majesty. Please do not hesitate or fear; you should ascend to this hall."
At that time, King Nimi’s countenance was serene and joyful, and his body and mind remained unmoving. Seeing him from afar, Śakra rose immediately to receive him, saying:
"Welcome, Great King!"
"I humbly entreat you to deign with your majestic power; may you not be exhausted.
He then divided his seat in half and offered it to the king. After they had exchanged greetings and inquiries, the king took his seat and said:
"Excellent!"
"Great King!
You have swiftly attained excellent benefit, being able to cause the Buddha-dharma to blaze forth and increase.
Then Śakra addressed the sons of the gods, saying:
"This King Nimi has long planted roots of goodness and has accomplished inconceivable merit.

Through skillful means, in a short period of time, he has transformed eighty koṭis of sentient beings, causing them to leave behind their inverted views and dwell securely in the Buddha-dharma, yet Matali was entirely unaware of this."
Then King Nimi, having extensively expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the sons of the gods, addressed the Lord of Devas, saying:
"I shall now return to Jambudvīpa."
"Why is this? It is because he wishes to protect and uphold the True Dharma of the Buddha.
Then the Lord of Devas said:
"May Your Majesty do as you wish," [the king replied]. The Buddha said,
"Great King!"
The King Nimi of old was myself.
The power of non-negligence is inconceivable;
even when Śakra offered me half his seat, I felt no attachment.
Therefore, you should know that within the Buddha-dharma one must apply oneself with diligent effort and abide in heedfulness.
Great King,
what is meant by "Buddha-dharma"?
"All dharmas are the Buddha-dharma.
When King Śuddhodana heard these words, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If all phenomena were the Buddha-dharma, then all sentient beings would necessarily be Buddhas.
The Buddha said,
"Great King!"
Sentient beings who do not abide in perverted views are themselves the Buddha!

Great King, that which is called "Buddha" is sometimes named True Suchness (tathatā), sometimes named the Reality Limit (bhūtakoṭi), and sometimes named the Dharma Realm (dharmadhātu). These are merely expressions sought through conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya); they are not spoken thus according to ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
"Great King!
All dharmas are fundamentally without arising or ceasing; this is called the *A-kṣara-dhāraṇī-mukha*:
it is without intrinsic nature, without fabrication, without characteristics, without causes or conditions, and without coming or going."
There is no sentient being, no life-span possessor, no nourisher, no person,
no conceptual proliferation, no form, no limit, no defilement, no residual habituation, no agent, no one who cuts off,
no bondage and no liberation, no advancing and no retreating, and no superior and no inferior.
Without distraction and without error; neither knowing nor not knowing; neither seeing nor not seeing;
neither precept nor non-precept; neither remorse nor freedom from remorse; neither joy nor absence of joy; neither craving nor absence of craving;
neither tranquility nor absence of tranquility; neither concentration nor absence of concentration; neither stillness nor absence of stillness.
Tranquility is neither craving nor freedom from craving; neither liberation nor freedom from liberation; neither wisdom nor lack of wisdom;
neither action nor non-action; neither retribution nor absence of retribution.
"O Great King!
If one can enter into and understand this gateway of the letter A, then one can enter into and understand all phenomena.
O Great King!"

Form is devoid of intrinsic nature; it has not existed in the past, does not exist in the present, and will not exist in the future. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise devoid of that intrinsic nature, and thus do not exist throughout the three periods of time.
"Great King!
For example, an echo is not something that has existed, does not exist now, and will not exist in the future;
likewise, from form up to consciousness, they do not exist across the three periods of time."
"Great King!
For example, a mirage has not existed, does not exist, and will not exist;
likewise, from form through to consciousness, they do not exist across the three periods of time."
"Great King, it is like a mass of foam, which has not existed in the past, does not exist in the present, and will not exist in the future;
so too, from form up to consciousness, they do not exist across the three periods of time."
"Great King!
It is like a barren woman who dreams of having given birth to a son; that son has not existed in the past, does not exist in the present, and will not exist in the future.
Likewise, from form through to consciousness, they do not exist across the three periods of time."
"Great King!
Space has no support; from form up to consciousness, there is likewise nothing upon which they depend.
Great King!"
Form has no arising, and so on up to consciousness, which also has no arising.
Great King!
Form has no cessation, and so on up to consciousness, which also has no cessation.
"Great King!
In the realm of nirvāṇa there is neither arising nor ceasing; from form up to consciousness, there is likewise neither arising nor ceasing.
Great King!"
The Dharma-realm is without arising or ceasing; from form through to consciousness, there is likewise no arising or ceasing.
Great King!

This Dharma is the sphere of activity of the Tathāgata—an inconceivable and subtle realm that is neither grasped nor abandoned, neither attained nor lost, and is beyond the reach of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or ordinary worldlings.
Why is this? Great King!
All dharmas are fundamentally without intrinsic nature; whether grasped or relinquished, they are all unobtainable.
"O King, take delight in this Dharma by settling your own mind in peace; observe it with right mindfulness, and do not follow the teachings of others.

When King Śuddhodana heard these words, he understood them clearly and thoroughly, realizing that there is not even the slightest dharma that can be obtained or not obtained. At that time, this teaching was called "The Buddha’s Teaching on This Dharma."
At that time, King Śuddhodana and seventy thousand members of the Śākya clan each attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Then the World-Honored One, knowing that King Śuddhodana had awakened to this Dharma and was firm in his profound resolve, immediately emitted various rays of light from his mouth. These lights shone throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds, surpassing the Brahma realm, and then re-entered through the crown of the Tathāgata’s head.
Then the Venerable Aśvajit rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in salutation, and addressed the Buddha in verse:
"O Heroic and Great Holy One, you manifest this rare event;
You radiate pure light everywhere, Illuminating the Brahma world throughout."
O Guide of All-Knowledge, for what reason do you manifest this auspicious omen?
We pray that you explain its cause and origin to dispel our doubts.
Since the Tathāgata attained the Way, he has extensively benefited all sentient beings.
To deliver the Śākyas, the Tathāgata emits radiance, bringing joy to gods and humans;
awakening all the sons of the Buddha,
he teaches them to practice according to the Dharma, so that they shall attain unsurpassed wisdom.
"The Buddha is the Lord of the three realms, supreme and beyond compare;
he can shatter all doubts, and his pure mind is at peace.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣu Aśvajit:
"Aśvajit, listen attentively: now I emit this pure radiance for the benefit and happiness of the Śākya clan, so that they may perceive true wisdom.
Having thoroughly understood it, they realize that all phenomena are ungraspable."
Within my True Dharma, his mind dwells in tranquility.
This scion of the Śākya clan of great renown has realized that all phenomena are without support;
having attained freedom from doubt, he shall become a Buddha in the future.
From this final body, one shall attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
born by transformation within a lotus flower, one shall reverently behold Amitāyus.
Abiding securely in that Buddha-field, one shall practice with diligence without regression.
Wandering and transforming throughout the ten directions, you served billions of buddhas.
In each and every world, you offered various kinds of worship;
for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, you diligently sought the unsurpassed path.
Passing through each and every Buddha-field, they establish all manner of Buddha-works;
sustained by the Tathāgata’s empowerment, their courageous minds are firm and steadfast.
For immeasurable billions of kalpas, they have reverently held exquisite incense and flowers.
Having made offerings to all the World-Honored Ones, you shall later attain perfect enlightenment.
In the presence of each and every Buddha, you shall proclaim and assist in the transformation of the Dharma,
maturing all sentient beings so that they all attain clear realization of the mind.
Furthermore, in those buddha-fields, there are no pratyekabuddhas or śrāvakas;
there are only assemblies of pure bodhisattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna.
The lifespan of each buddha is immeasurable koṭis of years.
He spoke of transforming and benefiting sentient beings; when his conditions were exhausted, he was like a lamp extinguished.
After that Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, the sons of the Buddhas remained to uphold the Dharma, dwelling securely in the world and skillfully proclaiming the dharma of emptiness and stillness.
Such a community of disciples, having gathered and transformed all sentient beings and disciplined their own minds, attained realization of the dharma of emptiness.
Abiding in heedful practice, they contemplate the self-nature of phenomena as empty.
By practicing well according to the truth, one shall attain all-encompassing wisdom.
These members of the Śākya clan and others, having heard the Dharma, were all awakened;
the devas and the people of the world felt great joy in their hearts.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:
"I shall now expound this wondrous samādhi of the true nature of reality; if bodhisattvas hear this teaching, they will swiftly awaken and reach the other shore."

Why is this? This samādhi clarifies that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is neither existent nor non-existent, and that within a person (pudgala), not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended.
If there is anything apprehended, that is not awakening.
If there is no awakening, then there is no teaching;
if there is no teaching, then there is no comprehension;
and if there is no comprehension, that is the Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
"Śāriputra!
I now entrust to you this samādhi-door of seeing true reality; you should receive, uphold, recite, and extensively explain it to others."
Śāriputra! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family abides in the Mahāyāna and practices the five pāramitās for ten kalpas, with the exception of the prajñāpāramitā.
If a person were to approach, listen to, and receive this samādhi-gate of seeing true reality, the merit they would obtain would exceed even that.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If, moreover, there should be another person who, having heard this Dharma during ten kalpas, is even able to explain it for the sake of a single individual, the merit they obtain would exceed that of the former.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If someone were to hear this Dharma for ten kalpas and then explain it to others, their merit would not equal that of another person who, for even a single kṣaṇa, practices and contemplates it; the latter’s merit would exceed the former’s.
Śāriputra! You should, with single-minded focus, analyze and explain this for the sake of all bodhisattvas, so that it shall not be interrupted. Why is this?
If one is able to realize this samādhi, one will swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and shall surely attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

When this Dharma was thus spoken, the Venerable Śāriputra and the other bhikṣus, King Śuddhodana and others, the devas including Śakra and Brahmā, asuras, gandharvas, humans, and non-humans, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Compendium of the Father and Son Sūtra, Volume Twenty.
